where sj ∈ S, i |λi | ≤ 1 and j |µij | ≤ 1 for any i. If we remove the angular
brackets, the equation we obtain looks like the usual distributivity relation,
written for arbitrary octahedral combination of octahedral combinations of
some sj ∈ S.
2.14.9. Since any formal octahedral combination involves only finitely many

2.14.10. Note that all αn , hence also α, are completely determined by α2 :
Σ∞ (2) × X 2 → X. Indeed, for α0 and α1 we have α1 (λ; x) = α2 (λ, 0; x, x)
and α0 = α2 (0, 0; x, x) for any x ∈ X (note that X has to be non-empty,
otherwise we won’t be able to retrieve its zero element α0 ). For αn , n ≥ 3,
we prove this statement by induction, using identity

 αn (λ1 , . . . , λn−2 , λn−1, λn ; x1 , . . . , xn−2 , xn−1 , xn ) =
 αn−1 (λ1 , . . . , λn−2 , µ; x1 , . . . , xn−2 , α2 (λn−1 /µ, λn /µ; xn−1 , xn )) (2.14.10.1)
when µ := |λn−1 | + |λn | 6= 0; if it is zero, we use (2.14.9.2) instead.
   We see that we might describe a Z∞ -module X as a triple (X, α0 , α2 ),
where X is a set, α0 ∈ X is its marked element (“zero”), and α2 : Σ∞ (2) ×
X 2 → X is the binary octahedral combination evaluation map discussed
above. These data have to satisfy several axioms, which do not seem to be
especially enlightening, so we don’t list them here. The most interesting
among them is the associativity/distributivity axiom for α2 :
      α2 (λ′ ν ′ , µ; x, α2 (ν, ρ; y, z)) = α2 (λ′ , µρ; α2 (ν ′ , ρ′ ; x, y), z),   (2.14.10.2)
for any x, y, z ∈ X, whenever µν = λ′ ρ′ , |λ′ ν ′ | + |µ| ≤ 1, |λ′ | + |µρ| ≤ 1,
|ν| + |ρ| ≤ 1 and |ν ′ | + |ρ′ | ≤ 1.
    In this form the definition of (abstract) Z∞ -modules is very similar to
that of abstract convex sets, which in fact can be obtained in the same way
starting from the monad ∆ that maps any set S into the simplex with vertices
{s}, i.e. the convex hull of all basis elements {s} of R(S) .
2.14.11. We see that any Z∞ -module X has a marked element, namely,
α0 := αX (0); we denote it by 0X or 0, and call it the zero element of X.
We have also a map α1 : Z∞ × X → X, which defines an action of Z∞ ,
considered as a multiplicative monoid, on X, i.e. α1 (λ, α1 (µ, x)) = α1 (λµ, x)
for any x ∈ X and |λ|, |µ| ≤ 1. Of course, α1 (λ, x) is usually written as λ · x
or λx, so the above formula can be written simply as λ(µx) = (λµ)x. Note
that 0X is a fixed point for this action, i.e. λ · 0X = 0X for any |λ| ≤ 1, and
0 · x = 0X for any x ∈ X. However, this structure of a set with marked point,
equipped by an action of monoid Z∞ = [−1, 1], doesn’t determine uniquely
α2 , i.e. the structure of a Z∞ -module on X.
2.14.12. We see that a Z∞ -module X can be described as an algebraic
system X = (X, α0 , α2 ), consisting of a set X, its element α0 and a map
α2 : Σ∞ (2) × X 2 → X, subject to a finite set of axioms. Therefore, the
category of Z∞ -modules has all the usual properties of categories defined by
algebraic systems. We list some of these properties below without proof;
most of them can be easily checked directly, and all of them will be proved
later in 4.6 for the categories of modules over arbitrary generalized rings.
2.14. Abstract Z∞ -modules                                                  113


   • Arbitrary projective limits exist in Z∞ -Mod; they can be essentially
     computed in Sets (i.e. ΓZ∞ : Z∞ -Mod → Sets commutes with arbitrary
     projective limits).

   • Arbitrary inductive limits exist in Z∞ -Mod (this is the only complicated
     statement in this list).

   • Filtered inductive limits exist in Z∞ -Mod; they can be computed in
     Sets, i.e. ΓZ∞ commutes with filtered inductive limits.

   • A Z∞ -linear map f : M → N is a monomorphism in Z∞ -Mod iff it is
     injective as a map of sets (i.e. iff ΓZ∞ (f ) is injective).

   • A Z∞ -linear map f : M → N is a strict epimorphism iff it is surjective
     as a map of sets.

   • Given an injective map of sets f : N → M and a Z∞ -module structure
     on M, there is at most one Z∞ -module structure (called the induced
     structure) on N, compatible with f . Therefore, subobjects (i.e. Z∞ -
     submodules) of M are in one-to-one correspondence with those subsets
     N of M, which admit an induced Z∞ -module structure.

   • Similarly, given a surjective map of sets f : M → Q and a Z∞ -module
     structure on M, there is at most one Z∞ -module structure on Q, com-
     patible with f . Strict quotients of M are in one-to-one correspondence
     with certain quotient sets Q of M.

   • Any Z∞ -homomorphism f : M → N decomposes into a strict epimor-
     phism p : M → I, followed by a monomorphism i : I → N. As a set, I
     coincides with f (M); its Z∞ -module structure can be described either
     as one induced from N or as one induced from M. We denote I by
     f (M) or Im f and say that it is the image of f .

2.14.13. Consider the Z∞ -module Q = F∞ , constructed as follows. Its
underlying set consists of three elements, denoted 0, +1 and −1. The Σ∞ -

with zero; this explains our alternative notation F∞ and Z∞ /m∞ for Q.
    Note that for any non-zero object A = (AZ∞ , AR ) of Z∞ -Fl.Mod the

hence it is infinite. Since Q 6= 0 and it is finite, we see that it cannot
be isomorphic to any I(A), i.e. it doesn’t lie in the essential image of I :
Z∞ -Fl.Mod → Z∞ -Mod, hence I cannot be an equivalence of categories.
2.14.14. Clearly, I : Z∞ -Fl.Mod → Z∞ -Mod is faithful, since Γ′ ◦ I =

2.14.15. Henceforth we shall identify Z∞ -Fl.Mod with a full subcategory of
Z∞ -Mod by means of the functor I constructed in 2.14.2. Recall that the
category of R-vector spaces R-Vect has been identified in 2.9.3 with a full
subcategory of Z∞ -Fl.Mod, hence it is now identified with a full subcategory
of Z∞ -Mod. In other words, we have a canonical Z∞ -structure αV on any
R-vector space V ; it is easy to see that αV : Σ∞ (V ) → V simply evaluates
any given formal octahedral combination of elements of V in the natural way
by means of the R-vector space structure on V .
    Let us denote the functor just constructed by ρ∗ : R-Vect → Z∞ -Mod. It
is not very hard to prove that it admits both a left adjoint ρ∗ and a right
adjoint ρ! , similarly to what we had before for flat Z∞ -modules. We will see
later that formulas ρ∗ M = R ⊗Z∞ M and ρ! M = HomZ∞ (R, M) are still
valid in this context, so we can denote ρ∗ M also by M(R) or even MR .
2.14.16. Existence of M(R) and of a Z∞ -linear map iM : M → M(R) , universal
with respect to Z∞ -linear maps from M into R-vector spaces, can be shown
directly in several different ways. For example, we can construct M(R) as the
quotient of free R-vector space R(M ) by the R-vector subspace generated by
all elements of the form {λ1 x1 + · · · + λn xn } − λ1 {x1 } − · · · − λn {xn }, for all
n ≥ 0 and all octahedral combinations of n elements of M.
    Second construction: we can characterize R-vector spaces as those Z∞ -
modules, on which all elements of S := Z∞ − {0} act bijectively; then the
required universal property of M(R) is that of S −1 M, so we have to compute
S −1 M, and this can be done by means of filtered inductive limits in the same
way as in 2.13.4. In particular, this means that all elements of M(R) can be
written in form x/s for some x ∈ M and s ∈ Z∞ , s 6= 0, and x/s = y/t iff
there is some u 6= 0, such that utx = usy.
    Finally, we can develop first the theory of tensor products in Z∞ -Mod,
and construct M(R) as R ⊗Z∞ M.

Definition 2.14.17 We say that a Z∞ -module M is a torsion-free Z∞ -
module if the canonical map iM : M → M(R) is injective, i.e. a monomorphism
in Z∞ -Mod. We say that M is a (pure) torsion Z∞ -module if M(R) = 0. Fi-
nally, we denote by Mtf the image of M in M(R) ; it is the largest torsion-free
quotient of M.
116                             Chapter 2. Z∞ -Lattices and flat Z∞ -modules


     Note that by the universal property of M(R) , we have that M is torsion-free
iff there exists an embedding (=monomorphism) of M into an R-vector space.
This shows that Mtf ⊂ M(R) is indeed torsion-free. Any map f : M → N
from M to a torsion-free N induces an R-linear map f(R) : M(R) → N(R) ; since
iN : N → N(R) is injective, and f(R) ◦ iM = iN ◦ f , this implies immediately
that f factorizes through iM (M) = Mtf , as stated above. In other words,
M 7→ Mtf is a left adjoint to the embedding of the full subcategory of torsion-
free Z∞ -modules into Z∞ -Mod.
2.14.18. Let us show that the torsion-free Z∞ -modules are exactly those
which lie in the essential image of I : Z∞ -Fl.Mod → Z∞ -Mod, i.e. which are
isomorphic to some I(A). This will characterize internally Z∞ -Fl.Mod as a
subcategory of Z∞ -Mod, and it will show that M 7→ Mtf is a left adjoint
to I.
    Clearly, any Z∞ -module of form I(A) = AZ∞ for some object A =
(AZ∞ , AR ) embeds into some R-vector space, namely, AR , so it must be
torsion-free. Conversely, if M is torsion-free, we put AR := M(R) and AZ∞ :=
Mtf = iM (M) ∼  = M. Then AZ∞ ⊂ AR is stable under all octahedral combi-
nations of its elements, hence it is symmetric and convex; it also generates
the whole of AR = M(R) , as it easily follows either from the universal prop-
erty or from any of the three constructions of M(R) given in 2.14.16, hence
A ∈ Ob Z∞ -Fl.Mod and M ∼    = I(A).
2.14.19. (Torsion Z∞ -modules.) By definition, M is a torsion Z∞ -module
iff M(R) = S −1 M = 0, where S = Z∞ − {0}. Our description of localizations
shows immediately that this condition is equivalent to the following: For any
x ∈ M there is some λ ∈ S (i.e. a non-zero λ ∈ Z∞ ), such that λx = 0
in M. For example, the Z∞ -module F∞ considered in 2.14.13 is torsion,
since (1/2)x = 0 for any x ∈ F∞ .
2.14.20. (Limits in Z∞ -Fl.Mod and Z∞ -Mod.) Since I : Z∞ -Fl.Mod →
Z∞ -Mod has a left adjoint M 7→ Mtf , it commutes with arbitrary projective
limits, i.e. arbitrary projective limits of torsion-free Z∞ -modules can be still
computed as in 2.8. This is in general not true for arbitrary inductive lim-
its: we have only the formula I(limα Mα ) = (limα I(Mα ))tf , which follows
                                     −→            −→
immediately from the fact that I is fully faithful and admits a left adjoint
M 7→ Mtf .
    However, this is still true for filtered inductive limits, since in both cat-
egories they can be essentially computed in Sets, and for arbitrary direct
sums as well. In the latter case we are to check that arbitrary direct sums of
torsion-free modules are still torsion-free. For this we first write a direct sum
over an arbitrary index set I as a filtered inductive limit of direct sums over
2.14. Abstract Z∞ -modules                                                    117


all finite subsets J ⊂ I, thus reducing to the case of a finite direct sum, and
then by induction it suffices to check the statement for a direct sum M ⊕ N.
     So let M and N be torsion-free Z∞ -modules, P := M ⊕ N be their direct
sum in Z∞ -Mod. Notice that i1 : M → M ⊕ N is injective, since it admits a
left inverse π1 : M ⊕ N → M ⊕ 0 ∼     = M, and similarly for i2 : N → M ⊕ N,
so we can identify M and N with subsets of M ⊕ N. Let us check that P is
torsion-free, i.e. that P → S −1 P is injective. Let z, z ′ ∈ P be two elements
of P , such that z/1 = z ′ /1 in S −1 P , i.e. νz = νz ′ for some 0 < ν ≤ 1. We’ll
check in 4.6.15 that elements z, z ′ ∈ P = M ⊕ N can be always represented
as octahedral combinations z = λx + µy, z ′ = λ′ x′ + µ′ y ′ with x, x′ ∈ M,
y, y ′ ∈ N. Applying π1 : P → M to νz = νz ′ , we obtain νλx = νλ′ x′ ,
hence λx = λ′ x′ , M being torsion-free. Furthermore, if |λ| ≥ |λ′ |, we get
λ · (λ′ /λ)x′ = λx, whence x = (λ′ /λ)x′ , unless both λ = λ′ = 0. Substituting
this into z = λx + µy, we get z = λ′ x′ + µy, i.e. we can assume λ = λ′ ,
x = x′ . Case |λ′ | ≥ |λ| is dealt with similarly, and if both λ = λ′ = 0, then z
and z ′ ∈ N, hence z = z ′ , N being torsion-free, so this case can be excluded.
Next, we can consider cases |µ| ≥ |µ′ |, |µ′ | ≥ |µ| and µ = µ′ = 0, and deduce
from N being torsion-free that we can assume µ = µ′ , y = y ′ as well. We see
that z = λx + µy = z ′ , so P → S −1 P is indeed injective and P = M ⊕ N is
torsion-free, q.e.d.
2.14.21. (Linear algebra, ⊗-structure etc.) Given any three Z∞ -modules M,
N and P , we say that a map Φ : M × N → P is Z∞ -bilinear if for any x ∈ M
the map sΦ (x) : y 7→ Φ(x, y) is a Z∞ -linear map N → P , and, similarly, for
any y ∈ N the map dΦ (y) : x 7→ Φ(x, y) is Z∞ -linear.
    Proceeding as in 2.10, we construct tensor products and inner Homs in
Z∞ -Mod, obtaining an ACU ⊗-structure on this category. This leads to a
natural definition of a Z∞ -algebra and of a module over such an algebra; we
can construct their localization theory and their spectra exactly in the same
way we did it in 2.13.
    Again, we shall return to all these questions later in a more general con-
text. We would like to finish this quite long chapter by remarking that
I : Z∞ -Fl.Mod → Z∞ -Mod commutes with tensor products and inner Homs
(the reader is invited to check this easy statement once tensor products and
inner Homs over arbitrary generalized rings are defined in 5.3), so almost all
our previous considerations and computations inside Z∞ -Fl.Mod will retain
their validity in Z∞ -Mod.

Chapter 3. Generalities on monads                                          119


3    Generalities on monads
In this chapter we want to collect some general facts on monads, which will
be of use to us in the remaining part of this work. Almost all of these facts
are very well known and can be found, for example, in [MacLane]. We recall
also some proofs, especially in the cases where we need to generalize them
later to the case of inner monads.
    After that we study the concept of inner endofunctors and inner monads
on a Cartesian closed category (e.g. a topos). This theory doesn’t seem to be
widely known; however, most definitions and proofs appear just as natural
generalizations of their counterparts in the theory of monads.
    Later we shall usually consider monads on the category of sets, and inner
monads on topoi; we shall see that the latter intuitively correspond to sheaves
of monads over the category of sets, hence their significance for our further
developments.
3.1. (AU ⊗-categories.) Let A be an AU (associative with unity) ⊗-category.
This means that we are given a bifunctor ⊗ : A × A → A, an associativity
                                                                             ∼
constraint α, i.e. a family of functorial isomorphisms αX,Y,Z : (X ⊗ Y ) ⊗ Z →
X ⊗ (Y ⊗ Z) satisfying the pentagon axiom for quadruple tensor products,
and that we are given an unit object 1A together with functorial isomor-
phisms 1A ⊗ X ∼  =X∼   = X ⊗ 1A , compatible with the associativity constraint
in a natural way which need not be explained explicitly here. By a well-
known theorem of MacLane, this data allows us to define multiple tensor
products of any (possibly empty) finite sequence of objects of A, and to
establish canonical isomorphisms between tensor products of such multiple
products. In short, we get a notion of tensor product on A, enjoying all
usual properties of tensor product of modules over a commutative ring, apart
from commutativity, since we don’t impose any commutativity constraint.
We’ll profit by this remark by working with this tensor product in the cus-
tomary way, without bothering to write down explicitly all arising canonical
isomorphisms.
3.1.1. (External ⊗-action.) Once the AU ⊗-category A is fixed, we can
consider its external (left) ⊗-action, or ;-action, on some category B. This
means that we are given some “external tensor product” ; : A × B → B
(which will be also denoted by the same symbol ⊗ as the tensor product of
A, when no confusion can arise), together with some external associativity
                                                                  ∼
constraint, i.e. a family of functorial isomorphisms (X ⊗ Y ) ; M → X ; (Y ;
M), satisfying a variant of the pentagon axiom with respect to quadruple
products of sort X ⊗ Y ⊗ Z ; M, where X, Y , Z are in A and M is in B.
                                                         ∼
We also require some functorial isomorphisms 1A ; M → M to be given and
120                                        Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


to be compatible with given external associativity constraint.
   As before, we don’t use these canonical isomorphisms explicitly, but sim-
ply write down multiple tensor products X1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ Xn ; M, for any Xi in A
and M in B, and use different canonical isomorphisms between them without
explaining or even naming them.
   We have also the notion of a right external ⊗-action (also called ⊘-action)
of A on B, given by some bifunctor ⊘ : B × A → B together with some
external associativity and unit constraints. This case can be reduced to one
considered before by permuting the order of arguments to ⊗ and ⊘.
3.1.2. Of course, we have both a left and a right external ⊗-action of A
on itself. Another example, even more trivial, is given by taking for B the
empty or the point category.
3.1.3. We have the notion of a ⊗-functor F : A → A′ between two AU
⊗-categories A and A′ . By definition, this is a functor F : A → A′ , together
                                                             ∼
with a family of functorial isomorphisms F (X ⊗A Y ) → F (X) ⊗A′ F (Y )
                                ∼
and an isomorphism F (1A ) → 1A′ , compatible with associativity and unit
constraints on A and A′ .
     If we are given some external ⊗-action of A on some B, and of A′ on B′ , we
can speak about external ⊗-functors (or ;-functors) G : B → B′ , compatible
with F . By definition, this means that we are given some functor G : B →
                                                             ∼
B′ , together with functorial isomorphisms G(X ;B M) → F (X) ;B′ G(M),
compatible with external associativity and unit constraints on B and B′ in a
natural way.
     In particular, we can apply this definition in case A′ = A, F = IdA . Then
we are given external ⊗-actions of A on two categories B and B′ , and study
;-functors G : B → B′ compatible with these ⊗-actions.
     Another special case is given by B = A, B′ = A′ . Then we see that F is
compatible with itself.
3.1.4. We have also a notion of natural transformation ζ : G → G′ of two ;-
functors G, G′ : B → B′ , compatible with same ⊗-functor F : A → A′. This
is simply a natural transformation ζ : G → G′ of corresponding underlying
functors, such that the following square is commutative for all X ∈ Ob A
and Y ∈ Ob B, where the horizontal arrows come from the ;-structure on G
and G′ :
                                    ∼ /
                    G(X ; M)            F (X) ; G(M)               (3.1.4.1)

                               ζX;M               1F (X) ;ζM

                                                  
                                      ∼
                     G′ (X ; M)           / F (X) ; G′ (M)

Natural transformations of ⊘-functors are defined similarly.
3.1. AU ⊗-categories                                                         121


3.1.5. Let’s mention some important examples of ⊗-categories and ⊗-actions.
    a) Take A := Sets, and ⊗ := ×, i.e. we consider the the cartesian products
on the category of sets. Of course, this is an AU (even ACU) ⊗-category,
and it acts on itself.
    b) Take A := K-Mod for any commutative ring K, and let ⊗ := ⊗K be
the usual tensor product of K-modules. Again, this is clearly an AU (even
ACU) ⊗-category, acting on itself.
    c) Let K ′ be any (associative) K-algebra. Let A := K-Mod as before,
and B := K ′ -Mod. Then any tensor product X ⊗K M, where X is a K-
module and M is a (left) K ′ -module, has a canonical K ′ -module structure,
so we get an external tensor product ; : A × B → B. It satisfies indeed
all requirements for an external ⊗-action, so we get an external ⊗-action of
K-Mod on K ′ -Mod.
    d) If F : A → A′ is an ⊗-functor, then it induces both a left and a right
⊗-action of A on A′ , given by X ; M := F (X) ⊗A′ M (resp. M ⊘ X :=
M ⊗A′ F (X)). If K ′ was commutative in the previous example, we see that
that example can be recovered in this manner starting from the ⊗-functor
F : K-Mod → K ′ -Mod given by X 7→ X(K ′ ) = K ′ ⊗K M.
3.1.6. (Algebras.) By definition, an algebra in an AU ⊗-category A is a triple
A = (A, µ, ε), consisting of an object A of A, a “multiplication” morphism µ :
A ⊗ A → A and a “unit” morphism ε : 1 → A, subject to usual associativity
and unit axioms: µ◦(1A ⊗µ) = µ◦(µ⊗1A ) : A⊗A⊗A → A and µ◦(1A ⊗ε) =
1A = µ ◦ (ε ⊗ 1A ). Note that in the first of these axioms we have to identify
A ⊗ (A ⊗ A) with (A ⊗ A) ⊗ A by means of the associativity constraint, and,
similarly, we have implicitly used the unit constraint in the second axiom.
So AU ⊗-categories are actually the minimal possible context sufficient to
consider algebras. Note that we cannot impose any commutativity conditions
on A without a commutativity constraint on A.
    An algebra homomorphism f : (A, µA , εA ) → (B, µB , εB ) in A is by defi-
nition a morphism f : A → B, such that µB ◦(f ⊗f ) = f ◦µA and f ◦εA = εB .
In this way we construct the category of algebras in A, denoted by Alg(A).
    This category has an initial object, called unit or initial algebra, given by
the natural algebra structure on 1A coming from the canonical isomorphism
1A ⊗ 1A ∼  = 1A . Indeed, the only algebra homomorphism from 1A to an
arbitrary algebra A = (A, µ, ε) is defined by ε : 1A → A. If A has a final
object eA , it admits a unique algebra structure, thus becoming the final
object in Alg(A).
3.1.7. Of course, this definition is motivated by the situation of 3.1.5b),
where we recover the notion of an associative K-algebra with unity. In other
situations we obtain other interesting notions, e.g. in 3.1.5a) we recover the
122                                        Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


category of monoids.
3.1.8. (Projective limits of algebras.) Note that all the projective limits
which exist in A, exist also in Alg(A), and they can be computed in A.
Indeed, if we have to compute lim(Aα , µα , εα), we compute first A := lim Aα
                                   ←−                                      ←−
in A, denote the canonical projections by πα : A → Aα , and define µ :
A ⊗ A → A and ε : 1A → A starting from compatible families of morphisms
µα (πα ⊗πα ) : A⊗A → Aα and εα : 1A → A. We see that the forgetful functor
Alg(A) → A commutes with arbitrary projective limits, and in particular is
left exact, if finite projective limits exist in A. In this situation it preserves
monomorphisms, and since in addition it is faithful, we see that ϕ : A′ → A
is a monomorphism in Alg(A) iff ϕ is a monomorphism in A.
3.1.9. (Subalgebras.) Given an algebra A = (A, µ, ε) in Alg(A) and a
monomorphism i : A′ → A, we see that there is at most one algebra struc-
ture (µ′ , ε′ ) on A′ compatible with i, since we must have iµ′ = µ(i ⊗ i) and
iε′ = ε. Note that whenever µ′ and ε′ satisfying these relations exist, they
satisfy the associativity and unit axioms automatically, thus giving required
algebra structure on A′ . In particular, we can apply this to embeddings
A′ → A of subobjects A′ ⊂ A. If a compatible algebra structure on A′ exists,
we call it the induced structure, and say that A′ is a subalgebra of A. If finite
projective limits exist in A, then the subalgebras of a fixed algebra A are the
same thing as the subobjects of A in Alg(A).
3.1.10. (Modules over an algebra.) Suppose we are given a (left) external
⊗-action of A on B, and an algebra A = (A, µ, ε) in A. Then a (left) A-
module in B is by definition a pair M = (M, α), consisting of an object M
of B, and a left action α of A on M, i.e. a morphism α : A ; M → M, such
that α ◦ (µ ; 1M ) = α ◦ (1A ; α) and α ◦ (ε ; 1M ) = 1M . Note that we have
again implicitly used here the external associativity and unity constraint for
the ⊗-action of A on B, so our context seems to be the most general context
in which the notion of an A-module makes sense.
    Of course, a morphism of A-modules f : (M, αM ) → (N, αN ) in B is
just a morphism f : M → N in B, compatible with given A-actions, i.e.
f ◦ αM = αN ◦ (1A ; f ). In this way we obtain the category of A-modules in
B, denoted by BA .
    If we have a right ⊗-action ⊘ : B × A → B of A on B, we can define right
A-modules M = (M, α) in B in a similar way. In this case α : M ⊘ A → M
is required to satisfy α ◦ (1M ⊘ µ) = α ◦ (α ⊘ 1A ) and α ◦ (1M ⊘ ε) = 1M .
This yields the category BA of right A-modules in B. Usually we will state
and prove the statements only for left modules, leaving their counterparts
for right modules to the reader.
3.1. AU ⊗-categories                                                          123


   In particular, we can always take the canonical left and right ⊗-action
of A on itself. This leads to a definition of left and right A-modules in A,
which are usually called simply left and right A-modules. For example, the
multiplication µ gives both a left and a right A-module structure on A itself.
3.1.11. Of course, this definition is motivated by the situation of 3.1.5b)
again, where we recover the usual notions of a left or right A-module over an
associative K-algebra A. In the situation of 3.1.5a) we recover the notion
of a (left or right) action of a monoid on a set, and in 3.1.5c) we obtain the
notion of an A ⊗K K ′ -module.
3.1.12. (Submodules and projective limits.) Similarly to what we had in
3.1.8, all projective limits existing in B exist also in BA and can be essentially
computed in B; if finite projective limits exist in B, then ϕ : N → M is a
monomorphism in BA iff it is a monomorphism in B. In this situation we
have a notion of submodules M ′ of a module M = (M, α), i.e. subobjects
M ′ ⊂ M in B, such that α(1A ; i) factorizes into iα′ , thus yielding an A-
module structure on M ′ ; here i : M ′ → M is the canonical embedding.
Again, when finite projective limits exist in B, the set of submodules of M
is actually the set of subobjects of M in BA .
3.1.13. (Scalar restriction.) We have a very natural notion of scalar restric-
tion in this setup. Namely, if f : A → A′ is an algebra homomorphism
in A, and we are given a (left) A′ -module N = (N, α′) in some category
B on which A ⊗-acts, then we can define its scalar restriction with respect
to f , denoted by f ∗ N, to be the same object N of B equipped with (left)
A-action α := α′ ◦ (f ; 1N ) : A ; N → N. As usual, this gives us a functor
        ′
f ∗ : BA → BA .
3.1.14. (Scalar extension.) In some cases the scalar restriction functor has
a left adjoint, called the scalar extension functor. In general it can be not so
easy to construct it, but we’ll consider now a very simple special case. Fix
an algebra A = (A, µ, ε) and consider the scalar restriction ε∗ : BA → B1A
with respect to the only homomorphism ε : 1A → A from the initial algebra
1A into A. Clearly, B1A is canonically equivalent (even isomorphic) to B,
since any object of B admits exactly one 1A -module structure, and ε∗ can be
identified with the forgetful functor Γ = ΓA : BA → B, (M, α) 7→ M.

Proposition. For any algebra A = (A, µ, ε) in A and any ;-action of A on
B the forgetful functor Γ = ΓA : BA → B, (M, α) 7→ M, has a left adjoint L =
LA : B → BA , given by X 7→ (A ; X, µ ; 1X ). The functorial isomorphism
                    ∼
HomBA (L(X), M) → HomB (X, Γ(M)) maps an A-module homomorphism
ϕ : A ; X → M into ϕ♭ : X → M given by ϕ♭ := ϕ ◦ (ε ; 1X ), and

its inverse maps a morphism ψ : X → M into ψ ♯ := α ◦ (1A ; ψ), where
α : A ; M → M is the multiplication of M. Moreover, the adjointness

explicitly as follows: ξX = ε ; 1X : X → A ; X for any X ∈ Ob B, and
η(M,α) = α : (A ; M, µ ; 1M ) → (M, α).

Proof. We have to check that ψ ♯ = α ◦ (1A ; ψ) is indeed an A-module
homomorphism (A ; X, µ ; 1X ) → (M, α) for any ψ : X → M. This means

This is clear since α ◦ (1A ; α) = α ◦ (µ ; 1M ) and (1A ; ψ) ◦ (µ ; 1X ) =

α ◦ (ε ; ψ) = α ◦ (ε ; 1M ) ◦ ψ = ψ. This completes the proof of adjointness
of L and Γ. The formulas for ξ and η follow immediately from ξX = (1L(X) )♭
and η(M,α) = (1M )♯ .

3.1.15. (Application of functors.) Given an ⊗-functor F : A → A′ , we can
apply it to any algebra
                           A = (A, µ, ε) in A, obtaining an algebra F (A) =
 F (A), F (µ), F (ε) , where we identify for simplicity F (A ⊗ A) with F (A) ⊗
F (A), and F (1A ) with 1A′ . Clearly, F transforms algebra homomorphisms
into algebra homomorphisms, hence it induces a functor Alg(F ) from the
category Alg(A) of algebras in A into the category Alg(A′ ) of algebras in
A′ ; this functor will be usually denoted by the same letter F .
     Similarly, if we have an ⊗-action of A on B and of A′ on B′ , and an
external ⊗-functor G : B → B′ compatible with F , then we can apply G to
any A-module M = (M, α) in B, thus obtaining an F (A)-module G(M) =
 G(M), G(α) in B′ . It is clear again that this gives us actually a functor
G̃ (or simply G) from the category BA of A-modules in B into the category
B′ F (A) of F (A)-modules in B′ .
     Furthermore, any natural transformation of ;-functors ζ : G → G′ in-
duces an F (A)-module homomorphism ζM : G(M) → G′ (M) in B′ for any A-
module M in B, thus effectively defining a natural transformation ζ̃ : G̃ → G̃′
of functors BA → B′ F (A) .
3.2. (Categories of functors.) Recall that the category of all categories Cat
is actually a (strictly associative) 2-category. In other words, the set of
functors Funct(C, D) = HomCat (C, D) between two arbitrary categories C
and D is not just a set, but a category, since we have the notion of a natural
transformation between two functors from C to D, and the composition map
3.2. Categories of functors                                                       125


◦ : Funct(D, E) × Funct(C, D) → Funct(C, E) is not just a map of sets, but a
functor.
      This means that, apart from the usual composition of natural transfor-
mations ξ ′ ◦ ξ = ξ ′ ξ : F → F ′′ , defined for any natural transformations
ξ ′ : F ′ → F ′′ , ξ : F → F ′ between functors F, F ′, F ′′ : C → D, we have also
the notion of ⋆-composition η ⋆ ξ : GF → G′ F ′ for any natural transforma-
tions ξ : F → F ′ : C → D and η : G → G′ : D → E. The requirement for ◦
to be a functor means that idG ⋆ idF = idGF and (η ′ ⋆ ξ ′)(η ⋆ ξ) = (η ′ η) ⋆ (ξ ′ξ).
      We adopt the usual convention and denote η ⋆ idF simply by η ⋆ F , and
idG ⋆ξ by G ⋆ ξ. Hence we have η ⋆ ξ = (η ⋆ F ′ )(G ⋆ ξ) = (G′ ⋆ ξ)(η ⋆ F ).
3.2.1. Let’s make these operations with natural transformations of functors
more explicit. First of all, a natural transformation ξ : F → G between
two functors from C to D is by definition a collection of morphisms in D
(ξX )X∈Ob C , indexed by objects of C, where ξX : F (X) → G(X) are required
to satisfy ξY ◦ F (ϕ) = G(ϕ) ◦ ξX for any morphism ϕ : X → Y in C.
Therefore, we would like to have explicit descriptions of our operations with
natural transformations in terms of such families.
    a) First of all, the usual composition ξ ′ ξ = ξ ′ ◦ ξ : F → F ′′ of two natural
transformations ξ : F → F ′ and ξ ′ : F ′ → F ′′ of functors from C to D is
computed in the obvious way: (ξ ′ ξ)X := ξX   ′

    b) Now, given a functor G : D → E, we would like to obtain a natural
transformation G ⋆ ξ = idG ⋆ξ : GF → GF ′ . This is done in a very natural
way: (G ⋆ ξ)X := G(ξX ) : GF (X) → GF ′ (X).
    c) Similarly, given a natural transformation η : G → G′ , we have to define
η ⋆ F = η ⋆ idF : GF → G′ F . Again, the most natural way of doing this is
correct: (η ⋆ F )X := ηF (X) : GF (X) → G′ F (X).

means that Cat is a (strictly associative) 2-category.
3.2.2. Now we can exploit this 2-category structure on Cat to obtain some
important examples of AU ⊗-categories and their external ⊗-actions. First
of all, consider the category of endofunctors Endof (C) := Funct(C, C) on any
category C. Let’s take the composition functor ◦ : Endof (C) × Endof (C) →
Endof (C) as the tensor product on Endof (C). In other words, we put G ⊗
F := GF for any two endofunctors G and F on C, and for any two natural
transformations η : G → G′ and ξ : F → F ′ of such endofunctors we put
η ⊗ ξ := η ⋆ ξ : GF → G′ F ′ . Of course, the identity functor IdC of C is the
unity for this ⊗-structure.
    In this way we obtain an AU ⊗-structure on Endof (C). Clearly, it is
even strictly associative (i.e. we have (X ⊗ Y ) ⊗ Z = X ⊗ (Y ⊗ Z), and
the associativity constraint is identity), since Cat is strictly associative (i.e.
(XY )Z = X(Y Z)).
3.2.3. Moreover, for any other category D we have a left ⊗-action of A :=
Endof (C) on Funct(D, C), and a right ⊗-action of A on Funct(C, D), given
in both cases by the composition functor ◦ : Endof (C) × Funct(D, C) →
Funct(D, C) (resp. ◦ : Funct(C, D) × Endof (C) → Funct(C, D)). Therefore,
in both cases we have F ; H = F H (resp. H ⊘ F = HF ) for any F ∈
Ob Endof (C) and H : D → C (resp. H : C → D), and the action on natural
transformations is given by the ⋆-product.
3.2.4. Any functor H : D → D ′ defines functors H∗ : Funct(C, D) →
Funct(C, D ′ ) and H ∗ : Funct(D ′ , C) → Funct(D, C), given again by the com-
position functors in Cat, i.e. H∗ : G 7→ HG, η 7→ H ⋆ η and H ∗ : G 7→
GH, η 7→ η ⋆ H. It is immediate that H∗ (resp. H ∗ ) is compatible with right
(resp. left) external ⊗-action of A = Endof (C) on corresponding categories,
i.e. H∗ is an ⊘-functor, and H ∗ is an ;-functor.
     Moreover, any natural transformation ζ : H → H ′ induces a natural
transformation of ;-functors ζ ∗ : H ∗ → H ′∗ , given by (ζ ∗ )G := G ⋆ ζ :
GH → GH ′ , and a natural transformation of ⊘-functors ζ∗ : H∗ → H∗′ ,
given by (ζ∗ )G := ζ ⋆ G : HG → H ′ G.
3.2.5. So far this reasoning was valid in any 2-category. Let’s do something
more specific now. Put D := h∗i — the point (or final) category, consisting
of exactly one object ∗ and only one morphism — the identity of ∗. Then
we get a right external ⊗-action of A = Endof (C) on Funct(C, h∗i), which
is not really interesting since this category is equivalent (even isomorphic)
to h∗i, and a left ⊗-action of A on Funct(h∗i, C). This is more interesting,
since Funct(h∗i, C) is canonically isomorphic to C itself.
    Therefore, we get an external ⊗-action of A = Endof (C) on C, ; :
3.2. Categories of functors                                                   127


Endof (C) × C → C, which is easily seen to be the evaluation map: F ; X =
F (X) for any endofunctor F and any object X of C, and ξ ; f = ξY ◦ F (f ) =
F ′ (f ) ◦ ξX : F (X) → F ′ (Y ) for any natural transformation ξ : F → F ′ and
any morphism f : X → Y in C. In particular, ξ ; X = ξX and F ; f = F (f ).
     The situation of 3.2.4 also admits a similar special case, if we put D :=
h∗i, and rename D ′ to D. We see that for any object Z ∈ Ob D the corre-
sponding “evaluation functor” Z ∗ : Funct(D, C) → C, Z ∗ : G 7→ G(Z), η 7→
ηZ is an ;-functor with respect to the external ⊗-action of A on Funct(D, C)
and on C. In this case any morphism ζ : Z → Z ′ in D gives rise to a natural
;-transformation ζ ∗ : Z ∗ → Z ′ ∗ of corresponding evaluation functors, given
by ζG∗ := G(ζ).
3.2.6. (Set-theoretical issues.) Strictly speaking, the category of all cate-
gories is no more legal mathematical object than the set of all sets. Therefore,
we encounter some set-theoretical complications, which really do not affect
anything important for us. However, we would like to explain here how we
are going to avoid them, without paying too much attention to similar issues
in future.
     To do this we work in Tarski–Grothendieck set theory, i.e. we accept
the usual Zermelo–Frenkel axiomatics for set theory and mathematics (re-
call that all mathematical objects are sets in this picture), and we accept
Grothendieck’s universe axiom as well, which tells us that any set can be
embedded into an universe, i.e. a set U closed under all usual set-theoretical
operations with its elements (e.g. the union of a family of sets ∈ U indexed
by a set ∈ U also belongs to U). Usually we fix such an universe from the
very beginning, choosing it as to contain all sets of interest to us (e.g. the
set of integers Z). Then all usual constructions produce sets ∈ U, and we
restrict ourselves to working with such sets (cf. appendix to SGA 4 I).
     A set is said to be U-small (or just small, when U is fixed) if it belongs
to U, or in some cases if we can establish a bijection between this set and an
element of U. A category is said to be U-small, or just small when U is fixed,
if it belongs to U, i.e. if both its set of objects and its set of morphisms are
U-small. There is also a notion of a U-category C, where the only requirement
is for all individual Hom-sets HomC (x, y) to be U-small for the less restrictive
understanding of U-smallness (cf. SGA 4 I for more details).
     When we consider the categories Sets, Ab, . . . of, say, sets, abelian groups
and so on, we actually consider the categories U-Sets, U-Ab . . . of U-small
sets, U-small abelian groups and so on (i.e. we require these sets, abelian
groups, . . . to belong to U). In this way we obtain U-categories, which,
however, are not U-small.
     Now, if we consider the category U-Cat of U-small categories, this per-
128                                       Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


fectly makes sense, and all previous constructions can be applied. For ex-
ample, for any two U-small categories C and D the category of functors
Funct(C, D) is also U-small.
    However, this approach is too restrictive for our purposes, since we cannot
even consider the category of endofunctors on the category of sets. Therefore,
we choose a larger universe V ∋ U, and consider the category Cat := V-U-
Cat of V-small U-categories. Then all previous constructions begin to make
sense; however, observe that even in this case Funct(C, D) usually will not
be an U-category, but only a V-category. For example, Endof (Sets) is not
an U-category.
    We’ll deal with this minor problem later by restricting our attention to
certain full subcategories of Funct(C, D), which will be actually U-categories.
Then the output of our constructions won’t involve the larger universe V, and
won’t depend on its choice, even if it is required at some intermediate stages.
One example of such full U-subcategory of a category of functors is given
by the subcategory of algebraic endofunctors in Endof (Sets), which will be
studied in the next chapter.
3.3. (Monads.) Now we combine the AU ⊗-structure on the categories of
endofunctors Endof (C) studied in 3.2 with the definition 3.1.6 of algebras
in ⊗-categories and of modules over such algebras. Of course, we thus obtain
just the definition of monads. Our choice of this approach is motivated by the
theory of inner endofunctors and inner monads to be developed later. The
statements for this second case will be almost the same, but direct proofs
tend to be more lengthy and slightly more complicated.

Definition 3.3.1 A monad Σ on (or over) some category C) is an algebra
(cf. 3.1.6) in the category Endof (C) with respect to its AU ⊗-structure
defined in 3.2.2. In other words, a monad Σ over C is a triple Σ = (Σ, µ, ε)
consisting of an endofunctor Σ : C → C and two natural transformations:
the multiplication µ : Σ2 = ΣΣ → Σ and the unit ε : IdC → Σ, required to
satisfy the associativity axiom µ ◦ (Σ ⋆ µ) = µ ◦ (µ ⋆ Σ) : Σ3 → Σ and the
unit axiom µ ◦ (Σ ⋆ ε) = idΣ = µ ◦ (ε ⋆ Σ).
    A morphism of monads ϕ : Σ → Ξ is simply a morphism of algebras in
Endof (C), i.e. a natural transformation of underlying endofunctors ϕ : Σ →
Ξ, such that ϕ◦εΣ = εΞ and ϕ◦µΣ = µΞ ◦(ϕ⋆ϕ). The category of all monads
over C will be denoted by Monads(C). Hence Monads(C) = Alg(Endof (C)).
3.3.2. The definition of a monad Σ = (Σ, µ, ε) over some category C can
be made even more explicit in terms of individual components of natural
transformations µ : Σ2 → Σ and ε : IdC → Σ, i.e. morphisms µX : Σ2 (X) →
Σ(X) and εX : X → Σ(X) parametrized by X ∈ Ob C. The requirement for
3.3. Monads                                                                 129


µ and ε to be natural transformations translates into Σ(f ) ◦ µX = µY ◦ Σ2 (f )
and Σ(f ) ◦ εX = εY ◦ f for any morphism f : X → Y in C, and our axioms
translate into µX ◦ Σ(µX ) = µX ◦ µΣ(X) : Σ3 (X) → Σ(X) and µX ◦ Σ(εX ) =
idΣ(X) = µX ◦ εΣ(X) for all X ∈ Ob C.
    Similarly, a morphism of monads ϕ : Σ → Ξ is simply a collection of
morphisms ϕX : Σ(X) → Ξ(X), parametrized by X ∈ Ob C, such that
ϕY ◦Σ(f ) = Ξ(f )◦ϕX for any morphism f : X → Y in C, and ϕX ◦εΣ,X = εΞ,X
and ϕX ◦µΣ,X = µΞ,X ◦Ξ(ϕX )◦ϕΣ(X) = µΞ,X ◦ϕΞ(X) ◦Σ(ϕX ) for all X ∈ Ob C.
Here, of course, Ξ(ϕX ) ◦ ϕΣ(X) = (ϕ ⋆ ϕ)X = ϕΞ(X) ◦ Σ(ϕX ), so only one
equality has to be checked in the last axiom.
3.3.3. (Submonads and projective limits of monads.) Note that all projective
limits that exist in C, exist also in A = Endof (C), since they can be computed
componentwise: (lim Fα )(X) := lim Fα (X). We say that F ′ is a subfunctor
                     ←−              ←−
of F , if F ′ (X) ⊂ F (X) for all X ∈ Ob C. When C has finite projective limits,
the subfunctors of some endofunctor F are actually its subobjects in A, and
we are in position to apply 3.1.8 and 3.1.9 to Monads(C) = Alg(A).
    We see that all projective limits existing in C exist also in Monads(C),
and they can be computed componentwise. Moreover, we obtain the notion
of a submonad Σ′ of a monad Σ: by definition it is a subfunctor Σ′ ⊂ Σ
stable under multiplication and unit of Σ, or equivalently a monad Σ′ , such
that Σ′ (X) ⊂ Σ(X) for all X ∈ Ob C, and Σ′ → Σ is a morphism of monads.
3.3.4. Once we have the definition of a monad Σ over C as an algebra in
AU ⊗-category A := Endof (C), we can use the left (resp. right) ⊗-action
of this category on Funct(D, C) and C (resp. on Funct(C, D)) explained
in 3.2.3 and 3.2.5 to define the categories of left (resp. right) Σ-modules
in Funct(D, C) and C (resp. in Funct(C, D)) according to 3.1.10; the corre-
sponding categories of modules are denoted by Funct(D, C)Σ and C Σ (resp.
Funct(C, D)Σ ), according to conventions of loc.cit. In all of these situations
we have a faithful forgetful functor Γ, acting from corresponding category of
modules into the underlying category.
3.3.5. (Category of Σ-modules.) Let’s make these definitions more explicit,
starting from the category C Σ of (left) Σ-modules in C. Its objects are pairs
M = (M, α), consisting of an object M of C, and a Σ-structure or Σ-action
α on M, i.e. a morphism α : Σ ; M = Σ(M) → M, such that α ◦ µM =
α ◦ Σ(α) : Σ2 (M) → M and α ◦ εM = idM . Objects of C Σ , i.e. these pairs
M = (M, α) = (M, αM ) are called Σ-modules or Σ-objects; if C = Sets,
we also call them Σ-sets. Another classical terminology is “Σ-algebras”; we
avoid it since in our setup these are modules over algebra Σ, not algebras.
    Morphisms f : (M, αM ) → (N, αN ) in C Σ are simply those morphisms
f : M → N in C, which agree with given Σ-structures, i.e. such that f ◦
130                                       Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


αM = αN ◦ Σ(f ). When no confusion can arise, the subset HomC Σ (M, N) ⊂
HomC (M, N) is denoted simply by HomΣ (M, N).
3.3.6. Let’s consider the category Funct(D, C)Σ now. First of all, any functor
H : D ′ → D induces an ;-functor H ∗ : Funct(D, C) → Funct(D ′ , C), hence
a functor H ∗ : Funct(D, C)Σ → Funct(D ′ , C)Σ , and natural transformations
ζ : H → H ′ induce natural transformations ζ ∗ : H ∗ → H ′ ∗ (cf. 3.2.4 and
3.1.15).
    Similarly, the evaluation functor Z ∗ : Funct(D, C) → C, M 7→ M(Z),
defined by any Z ∈ Ob D, is an ;-functor (cf. 3.2.5), hence it induces a
functor Z ∗ : Funct(D, C)Σ → C Σ , and morphisms ζ : Z → Z ′ induce natural
transformations ζ ∗ : Z ∗ → Z ′ ∗ of these functors.
    In other words, for any M = (M, α) ∈ Ob Funct(D, C)Σ , where M : D →
C is a functor and α : M → ΣM is a natural transformation, such that
α ◦ (µ ⋆ M) = α ◦ (Σ ⋆ α) : Σ2 M   → M, we get an object Z ∗ M of C Σ , easily
seen to be M(Z) = M(Z), αZ , and any ζ : Z → Z ′ induces a Σ-morphism
ζ ∗M = M(ζ) : M(Z) → M(Z ′ ).
    In this way we obtain a functor M̃ : D → C Σ , which is usually de-
noted with the same letter M, since it coincides with M on the level of the
underlying objects; applying this for different Σ-modules M and their homo-
morphisms, we construct a functor Funct(D, C)Σ → Funct(D, C Σ ), which is
now easily seen to be an equivalence, and even an isomorphism of categories.
One can say that C Σ “represents” the functor Funct(−, C)Σ on the category
of all categories. Let’s state this result separately:

Proposition 3.3.7 For any monad Σ over a category C and any category D
we have a canonical isomorphism of categories Funct(D, C)Σ → Funct(D, C Σ )
which maps (M, α : M → ΣM) into the functor Z 7→ (M(Z), αZ ). This iso-
morphism of categories is compatible with corresponding forgetful functors,
i.e. it identifies Funct(D, C)Σ → Funct(D, C) with (ΓΣ )∗ : Funct(D, C Σ ) →
Funct(D, C), where ΓΣ : C Σ → C is the forgetful functor for C Σ . Moreover, the
functor Funct(D, C)Σ → Funct(D ′ , C)Σ induced by any functor H : D ′ → D
is identified with H∗ : Funct(D, C Σ ) → Funct(D ′ , C Σ ), and this statement
extends to natural transformations arising from any ζ : H → H ′ . A similar
statement is also true for evaluation functors Z ∗ : Funct(D, C)Σ → C Σ arising
from objects Z of D.

Proof. The functor mentioned in the statement has been constructed be-
fore. It remains to check that it is an isomorphism of categories, but this
is quite straightforward, once we understand that this statement actually
means that to give a left Σ-module structure on a functor F : D → C is the
same thing as to give a left Σ-structure on each individual F (X), depending
3.3. Monads                                                                  131


functorially on X ∈ Ob D. Another possibility — construct the inverse func-
tor directly, by first introducing a left Σ-functor structure on Γ : C Σ → C, and
then applying F̃ ∗ to it for any F̃ : D → C Σ , thus obtaining a left Σ-functor
structure on ΓF̃ : D → C.
3.3.8. In particular, we see that the category AΣ of left Σ-modules in A :=
Endof (C) is isomorphic to Funct(C, C Σ ). Since the multiplication µ defines
                                                                      Σ
                          we obtain a functor L = LΣ : C → C , such
a left Σ-action on Σ itself,
that L(X) = Σ(X), µX for any object X in C, and L(f ) is given by Σ(f )
for any morphism f : X → Y in C. Moreover, L(X) can be described as
(Σ ; X, µ ; idX ) in terms of the ;-action of A on C, so we are in position to
apply 3.1.14:

Proposition. The forgetful functor Γ = ΓΣ : C Σ → C, (M, α) 7→ M,
has a left adjoint L = LΣ : C → C Σ , given by X 7→ Σ(X), µX . The
                                               ∼
adjointness isomorphism HomC Σ L(X), (M, α) → HomC (X, M) transforms
a Σ-morphism ϕ : L(X) = Σ(X) → M into ϕ♭ := ϕ ◦ εX , and its inverse
transforms ψ : X → Γ(M) = M into ψ ♯ := α ◦ Σ(ψ).
   Moreover, ΓL = Σ, and the natural transformations ξ : IdC → ΓL = Σ
and η : LΓ → IdC Σ defined by adjointness of L and Γ are given by ξ = ε and
η(M,α) = α.
   Finally, the pair of adjoint functors L and Γ completely determines the
monad Σ = (Σ, µ, ε) since Σ = ΓL, ε = ξ and µ = Γ ⋆ η ⋆ L : ΓLΓL = Σ2 →

Proof. All statements but the last one follow immediately from 3.1.14.
Let’s check the formula for µ: (Γ ⋆ η ⋆ L)X = Γ(ηL(X) ) = Γ(η(Σ(X),µX ) ) =
Γ(µX ) = µX .
3.3.9. Since LΣ is a left adjoint to the forgetful functor ΓΣ , the Σ-object
LΣ (X) = (Σ(X), µX ) will be called the free Σ-object (or Σ-module) generated
by X, and Σ-objects isomorphic to some LΣ (X) will be called free. Since the
underlying object of LΣ (X) is equal to Σ(X), this Σ-object will be often
denoted simply by Σ(X), when no confusion can arise. In other words, when
we consider Σ(X) as a Σ-object, we endow it with the Σ-structure given by
µX , unless otherwise specified.
3.3.10. We have seen that the monad Σ over C is completely determined by
the pair of adjoint functors L : C → C Σ and Γ : C Σ → C.
    This construction can be generalized as follows. Suppose we are given two
adjoint functors F : C → D and G : D → C with adjointness transformations
ξ : IdC → GF and η : F G → IdD , i.e. we have (ξ ⋆ G)(G ⋆ η) = idG and
132                                         Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


(η ⋆ F )(F ⋆ ξ) = idF . Put Σ := GF ∈ Ob Endof (C), µ := G ⋆ η ⋆ F :
Σ2 = GF GF → Σ = GF and ε := ξ : IdC → Σ. Then it is easy to see that
Σ := (Σ, µ, ε) is a monad over C. Indeed, µ(Σ⋆µ) = (G⋆η⋆F )(GF G⋆η⋆F ) =
G ⋆ η ⋆ η ⋆ F = µ(µ ⋆ Σ), µ(Σ ⋆ ε) = (G ⋆ η ⋆ F )(GF ⋆ ξ) = G ⋆ idF = idΣ , and
µ(ε ⋆ Σ) = idΣ is checked similarly.
    Moreover, α := G ⋆ η : ΣG → G determines a left Σ-module structure
on G : D → C: indeed, α(Σ ⋆ α) = (G ⋆ η)(GF G ⋆ η) = G ⋆ η ⋆ η =
(G ⋆ η)(G ⋆ η ⋆ F G) = α(µ ⋆ G) and α(ε ⋆ G) = (G ⋆ η)(ξ ⋆ G) = idG . Therefore,
according to 3.3.7 our left Σ-functor (G, G⋆η) ∈ Ob Funct(D, C)Σ determines
in a unique way a functor G̃ : D → C Σ , such that G̃(Z) = G(Z), G(ηZ )
for any Z ∈ Ob D. Clearly, G = ΓΣ G̃, i.e. we have shown that G : D → C
factorizes through C Σ in a natural way. It is also easy to see that G̃F = LΣ .

Definition 3.3.11 A functor G : D → C is called monadic, if it admits a left
adjoint F : C → D, and if the induced functor G̃ : D → C Σ is an equivalence
of categories, where Σ is the monad over C defined by F and G as described
above.
   Clearly, in this case we can replace D with C Σ , G with ΓΣ , and F with
the left adjoint LΣ of ΓΣ .
   Note that the monadicity of G doesn’t depend on the choice of its left
adjoint F , since such an adjoint is unique up to a unique isomorphism.
3.3.12. The concept of monadicity is very important since it allows us to
replace some categories D with the categories of Σ-objects inside a simpler
category C with respect to a certain monad Σ over C, thus providing a uniform
description of these categories D. There are several interesting criteria of
monadicity, e.g. the Beck’s monadicity theorem (cf. [MacLane]). However,
what is really important for us is that if C is the category of sets and D is
a category defined by some algebraic structure (e.g. the category of groups,
monoids, rings, left modules over a fixed ring, . . . ), then the forgetful functor
F : D → Sets is monadic, i.e. any of these “algebraic” categories is equivalent
(usually even isomorphic) to Sets Σ for a suitable monad Σ over Sets. In fact,
such categories are defined by a certain special class of monads, which we
call algebraic; they will be studied in some detail in the next chapter.
3.3.13. We have seen in 3.3.7 that C Σ in a certain sense represents the
category of left Σ-functors Funct(D, C)Σ for variable category D. Is a similar
result true for the categories of right Σ-functors Funct(C, D)Σ ? The answer
turns out to be positive:

Proposition. Given a monad Σ = (Σ, µ, ε) over a category C, denote by
CΣ the category with the same objects as C, and with morphisms given
3.3. Monads                                                                  133


by HomCΣ (X, Y ) := HomC (X, Σ(Y )) ∼   = HomC Σ (LΣ (X), LΣ (Y )). The com-
position of morphisms is given by the second description of HomCΣ ; in
terms of the first description it is given by (ψ, ϕ) 7→ µZ ◦ Σ(ψ) ◦ ϕ, where
ϕ ∈ HomCΣ (X, Y ) and ψ ∈ HomCΣ (Y, Z). In other words, CΣ is equivalent to
the full subcategory of free objects in C Σ .
    Consider the functor I = IΣ : C → CΣ , which is identical on objects
and maps ϕ : X → Y into εY ◦ ϕ ∈ HomCΣ (X, Y ). Then the category
Funct(C, D)Σ of right Σ-functors C → D is canonically isomorphic to the
category Funct(CΣ , D), and under this isomorphism the forgetful functor is
identified with I ∗ : Funct(CΣ , D) → Funct(C, D).
    More explicitly, F = (F, α) ∈ Ob Funct(C, D)Σ , where F : C → D and
α : F Σ → F , corresponds under this isomorphism to the functor F̃ : CΣ → D
which coincides with F on objects, and transforms ϕ : X → Σ(Y ) into
F̃ (ϕ) := αY ◦ F (ϕ) : F (X) → F (Y ).

Proof. Let’s check first the equivalence of the two descriptions of compo-
sition in CΣ . In the notations of 3.3.8 this amounts to check ψ ♯ ◦ ϕ♯ =
(µZ ◦ Σ(ψ) ◦ ϕ)♯ , i.e. µZ ◦ Σ(ψ) ◦ µY ◦ Σ(ϕ) = µZ ◦ Σ(µZ ) ◦ Σ2 (ψ) ◦ Σ(ϕ); this
equality follows immediately from Σ(ψ) ◦ µY = µΣ(Z) ◦ Σ2 (ψ) and from the
associativity condition µZ ◦ Σ(µZ ) = µZ ◦ µΣ(Z) .
     Now we want to construct a functor Funct(CΣ , D) → Funct(C, D)Σ , in-
verse to one constructed above. To do this we construct first a right Σ-
structure β : IΣ → I on I : C → CΣ , and then apply to it the ⊘-functor
F̃∗ for any F̃ : CΣ → D, thus obtaining a right Σ-functor F̃∗ (I, β) =
(F̃ I, F̃ ⋆ β); this construction, being functorial in F̃ , yields the required
functor Funct(CΣ , D) → Funct(C, D)Σ .
     So we have to construct β : IΣ → I. For any X ∈ Ob C we must
produce some βX ∈ HomCΣ (Σ(X), X) = HomC (Σ(X), Σ(X)); of course, we
take idΣ(X) . It remains to check that β is indeed a right Σ-action on I, and
that our two functors between Funct(C, D)Σ and Funct(CΣ , D) are inverse to
each other; we leave these verifications to the reader.

3.3.14. Note that I = IΣ : C → CΣ admits a right adjoint K = KΣ : CΣ → C,
given by K(X) := Σ(X), K(ϕ) := µY ◦ Σ(ϕ) for any ϕ : X → Σ(Y ). Clearly,
KI = Σ, and IK : CΣ → CΣ coincides with Σ on objects and transforms
ϕ : X → Σ(Y ) into εΣ(Y ) ◦µY ◦Σ(ϕ). The adjointness natural transformations
ξ : IdC → KI = Σ and η : IK → IdCΣ are computed as follows: ξ = ε and
ηX ∈ HomCΣ (Σ(X), X) = HomC (Σ(X), Σ(X)) is given again by idΣ(X) .
    It is easy to see that this pair of adjoint functors I : C → CΣ and K :
CΣ → C determines by the recipe of 3.3.10 the original monad Σ = (Σ, µ, ε):
indeed, we have already seen that KI = Σ and ξ = ε, and K ⋆ η ⋆ I = µ is
134                                                 Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


quite easy to check: (K ⋆ η ⋆ I)X = K(ηI(X) ) = K(idΣ(X) ) = µX .
3.3.15. Moreover, if we are given two adjoint functors F : C → D and
G : D → C with adjointness natural transformations ξ : IdC → GF and
η : F G → IdD , defining a monad Σ = (GF, G⋆η⋆F, ξ) as described in 3.3.10,
we obtain a right Σ-action η ⋆ F : F Σ → F on F , hence by 3.3.13 there is
a unique functor F̃ : CΣ → D, such that F̃ I = F and F̃ ⋆ β = η ⋆ F .
    In this respect the situation is quite similar (or rather dual) to that
of 3.3.10, where we obtained a functor G̃ : D → C Σ . We see that among all
pairs of adjoint functors (F, G), defining the same monad Σ on C, we have
an initial object (IΣ , KΣ ) and a final object (LΣ , ΓΣ ).
3.3.16. Proposition 3.3.13 is important for us since it allows us to identify
the category AΣ of right Σ-modules in A := Endof (C) with the category
Funct(CΣ , C) of functors from CΣ to C.

p ◦ τ = idΣ(M ) and q ◦ τ = σ ◦ α. This together with α ◦ p = α ◦ q implies the
right exactness of this diagram in C, and, since this splitting is preserved by
any functor, the right exactness of this diagram after an application of Σ.
     Now, given any Σ-morphism ϕ : (Σ(M), µM ) → (N, β), such that ϕ ◦
p = ϕ ◦ q, we want to show the existence and uniqueness of a Σ-morphism
ψ : M → N, such that ϕ = ψ ◦ α. Right exactness in C implies existence and
uniqueness of such a morphism ψ in C; it remains to check that this is a Σ-

this follows from ψ◦α◦Σ(α) = ψ◦α◦µM = ϕ◦µM = β◦Σ(ϕ) = β◦Σ(ψ)◦Σ(α).
3.3.21. We have seen that any monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ induces
a scalar restriction functor ρ∗ : C Ξ → C Σ , such that ΓΣ ρ∗ = ΓΞ . We claim
that any functor H : C Ξ → C Σ , such that ΓΣ H = ΓΞ , is equal to ρ∗ for a
uniquely determined monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ. To show this we
first observe that by 3.3.7 such functors H : C Ξ → C Σ are in one-to-one
correspondence with left Σ-structures β : ΣΓΞ → ΓΞ on ΓΞ . For example,
H = ρ∗ corresponds to β = (ΓΞ ⋆ ηΞ ) ◦ (ρ ⋆ ΓΞ ), where ηΞ : LΞ ΓΞ → IdC Ξ and
ξΞ = εΞ : IdC → Ξ = ΓΞ LΞ are the usual adjointness natural transformations.
Notice that ρ is uniquely determined by β since ρ = ρ ◦ µΣ ◦ (Σ ⋆ εΣ ) =
µΞ ◦ (ρ ⋆ ρεΣ ) = µΞ ◦ (ρ ⋆ εΞ ) = µΞ ◦ (ρ ⋆ Ξ) ◦ (Σ ⋆ εΞ ) = (β ⋆ LΞ ) ◦ (Σ ⋆ εΞ ).
In general we put ρ := (β ⋆ LΞ ) ◦ (Σ ⋆ εΞ) for an arbitrary left Σ-action β
on ΓΞ . We check that ρ : Σ → Ξ is a monad homomorphism using the fact
that β is a left Σ-action. For example, we use β ◦ (εΣ ⋆ ΓΞ ) = idΓΞ to prove
ρ◦εΣ = (β⋆LΞ )◦(Σ⋆εΞ)◦εΣ = (β⋆LΞ )◦(εΣ ⋆εΞ) = (β⋆LΞ )◦(εΣ ⋆ΓΞLΞ )◦εΞ =
εΞ . The compatibility with multiplication µΞ ◦ (ρ ⋆ ρ) = ρ ◦ µΣ is checked
similarly but longer, using µΞ = ΓΞ ⋆ ηΞ ⋆ LΞ , (ΓΞ ⋆ ηΞ ) ◦ (εΞ ⋆ ΓΞ ) = idΓΞ and
3.4. Examples of monads                                                                            137


β ◦ (Σ ⋆ β) = β ◦ (µΣ ⋆ ΓΞ ). Finally, we have to check that (ΓΞ ⋆ ηΞ ) ◦ (ρ ⋆ ΓΞ )
will give back the original β. Indeed, this expression equals (ΓΞ ⋆ ηΞ ) ◦ (β ⋆
LΞ ΓΞ )◦(Σ⋆εΞ ⋆ΓΞ ) = (β ⋆ηΞ )◦(Σ⋆εΞ ⋆ΓΞ ) = β ◦(ΣΓΞ ⋆ηΞ )◦(Σ⋆εΞ ⋆ΓΞ ) = β.
3.4. (Examples of monads.) Now we would like to give some examples of
monads which will be important for us later. The most important of them
are those defined by pairs of adjoint functors F : C → D and G : D →
C (cf. 3.3.10), where usually C := Sets, D is some “algebraic category”
(category of sets with some algebraic structure, e.g. the category of groups,
rings and so on), G = Γ : D → Sets is the forgetful functor, and F is a
left adjoint of G. This gives us a monad Σ on the endofunctor GF over
the category of sets, and the forgetful functor G usually turns out to be
monadic (cf. 3.3.11), i.e. the induced functor G̃ : D → Sets Σ turns out to
be an equivalence and even an isomorphism of categories, thus identifying D
with Sets Σ . Another important source of monads is obtained by considering
submonads of previously constructed monads (cf. 3.3.3).
3.4.1. (The monad of words.) Let’s take C := Sets, D := Mon be the
category of monoids, G : Mon → Sets be the forgetful functor, and F :
Sets → Mon be its left adjoint, which maps any set X into the free monoid
F (X) generated by X. Recall that F (X) consists of all finite words x1 . . . xn
in alphabet X, i.e. all xi ∈ X, n ≥ 0, the multiplication on F (X) is given
by the concatenation of words, and the unit of F (X) is the empty word ∅,
i.e. the only word of length zero. According to 3.3.10, this defines a monad
W = (W, µ, ε) over the category of sets, which will be called the monad of
words.                              F
     We see that W (X) = n≥0 X n for any set X. Sequences (x1 , x2 , . . . , xn )
lying in X n ⊂ W (X) are usually called words of length n over X, and are
written simply as x1 x2 . . . xn ; the individual components xi of a word are
usually called letters. When some of xi are replaced by more complicated
expressions, or when there is some other source of potential confusion, we
enclose some or all of them into braces, thus writing {x1 }{x2 } . . . {xn } instead
of x1 x2 . . . xn or (x1 , x2 , . . . , xn ). For example, {x} is the one-letter word
corresponding to an element x ∈ X. The empty word will be usually denoted
by ∅, or on some occasions by {}.
     Now the unit ε : IdSets → W and the multiplication µ : W 2 (X) → W (X)
can be described explicitly as follows. εX : X → W (X) maps any x ∈ X
into the corresponding one-letter word {x} ∈ W (X). As to the multipli-
cation µX : W 2 (X) → W (X), it “removes one layer of braces”, i.e. maps
{x1 x2 . . . xn }{y1y2 . . .} . . . {z1 . . . zm } into x1 x2 . . . xn y1 y2 . . . z1 . . . zm . The ax-
ioms of a monad can be checked now directly. For example, the associativity
condition µX ◦ µW (X) = µX ◦ W (µX ) : W 3 (X) → W (X) means simply that
138                                        Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


if we have an expression with two layers of braces, and remove first the in-
ner layer and then the outer layer, or conversely, then the resulting word
in W (X) is the same in both cases. So we might have defined the monad
W = (W, µ, ε) directly, without any reference to the category of monoids.
3.4.2. Of course, the forgetful functor G : Mon → Sets is monadic, i.e.
the induced functor G̃ : Mon → Sets W is an equivalence, and even an iso-
morphism of categories. In other words, the structure of a monoid on some
set X is essentially the same thing as a W -structure α : W (X) → X, and
W -morphisms are exactly monoid morphisms.
     Let’s show how this works in this situation. If we have a monoid structure
(X, ∗, e) on X, where ∗ : X × X → X is the multiplication and e ∈ X is
the unit, then the corresponding W -structure α : W (X) → X simply maps
a word x1 x2 . . . xn ∈ W (X) into the corresponding product x1 ∗ x2 ∗ · · · ∗ xn
(this actually follows from the description of G̃ given in 3.3.10). Conversely,
if we are given a W -structure α : W (X) → X on a set X, we can recover a
monoid structure on X by setting e := α({}) and x∗y := α({x}{y}) = α(xy).
The associativity and unit axioms for this choice of operations on X follow
from the axioms α ◦ W (α) = α ◦ µX and α ◦ εX = idX for α. For example,
(x ∗ y) ∗ z = α({α(xy)}{z}) = α({α(xy)}{α(z)}) = (α ◦ W (α))({xy}{z}) =
α(µX ({xy}{z})) = α(xyz), and x ∗ (y ∗ z) = α(xyz) is shown similarly, thus
proving the associativity of ∗.
     The fact that W -morphisms f : (X, α) → (Y, β) are exactly monoid
homomorphisms is also checked similarly. For example, if f is a W -morphism,
i.e. β ◦ W (f ) = f ◦ α, then f (x ∗X y) = f (α(xy)) = (β ◦ W (f ))({x}{y}) =
β({f (x)}{f (y)}) = f (x) ∗Y f (y).
3.4.3. This construction generalizes
                            F           to any (Grothendieck) topos E, where
we can also put WE (X) := n≥0 X n for any X ∈ Ob E. Then E WE is of course
just the category Mon(E) of monoids in E. If E is the category S̃ of sheaves
(of sets) on some site S, then E WE is the category of sheaves of monoids on S.
We’ll see later that both W and WE are examples of algebraic monads, and
that WE is the pullback of W with respect to the canonical morphism of
topoi E → Sets.

3.4.5. Note that the above construction is functorial in U, so we get canonical
monad homomorphisms ζf : ΣU → ΣV for any f : U → V , given by ζf,X :=
Σ(f ⊔ idX ) : Σ(U ⊔ X) → Σ(V ⊔ X), and homomorphisms ζU : Σ → ΣU ,
ζU,X := Σ(jX ) : Σ(X) → Σ(U ⊔ X) as well.
3.4.6. In particular, we can apply this to the monad of words W on the
category of sets, or to its topos counterpart WE , thus obtaining a family of
new monads W hUi = WU parametrized by sets (resp. objects of E) U. The
alternative notation W hUi reflects the fact that this is something like “the
algebra of polynomials over W in non-commuting variables from U”. More
precisely, Sets WU is the category of pairs (M, ϕ), consisting of a monoid M
and some “choice of constants”, i.e. an arbitrary map of sets ϕ : U → M.
    Clearly, the elements of WU (X) = W (U ⊔ X) are simply words in the
alphabet U ⊔X. Usually we don’t enclose the letters from U in braces, even if
we do it with some other letters of the same word, thus obtaining expressions
like u1 {x1 }u2 {x2 }{x3 }. The unit morphism ε′X : X → WU (X) still maps
any x ∈ X into the corresponding “variable” (one-letter word) {x}, and the
multiplication µ′X : WU2 (X) → WU (X) is given by the concatenation of words
and subsequent identification of “constants”, i.e. letters from U, coming from
different layers. For example, µ′X (u1 {u2 {x1 }{x2 }}{u3}) = u1 u2 {x1 }{x2 }u3.
This property is actually the reason which allows us to omit braces around
letters from U in almost all situations.
3.4.7. The importance of these monads WU obtained from the monad of
words W is due to the fact that any algebraic monad appears as a subquotient
of a monad of this form. We’ll return to this issue in the next chapter.
3.4.8. (Monads defined by rings.) Now fix any ring R (required to be associa-
tive, with unity, but not necessarily commutative) and consider the forgetful
functor ΓR : R-Mod → Sets and its left adjoint LR : Sets → R-Mod, which
transforms any set X into the corresponding free module R(X) . As usual, this
defines a monad ΣR = (ΣR , µ, ε) over Sets with the underlying endofunctor
equal to ΓR LR . In other words, ΣR (X) is simply the underlying set of R(X) ,
i.e. the set of all formal R-linear combinations λ1 {x1 } + · · · + λn {xn }, where
n ≥ 0, all λi ∈ R, xi ∈ X, and where we have denoted by {x} the basis
element corresponding to x ∈ X. Another description: ΣR (X) = {λ : X →
R | λ(x) = 0 for almost all x ∈ X}.
     Clearly, the unit εX : X → ΣR (X) maps any x ∈ X into the correspond-
ing basis element {x}, and µX : Σ2R (X) → ΣR (X) computes   P         linear combi-
                                                                      P
nationsP  of formal linear combinations (cf. 2.14.8): µX          λ

equals i,j λi µij {xj }.
     Now a ΣR -structure α : ΣR (X) → X on some set X can be considered as a
way of evaluating formal linear combinations of elements of X. In particular,
3.4. Examples of monads                                                        141


we can define an addition and an action of R on X by setting x + y :=
α({x}+{y}) and λ·x := α(λ{x}). Similarly to what we had in 3.4.2, one can
check directly that this addition and R-action satisfy the axioms for a left R-
module, thus obtaining a one-to-one correspondence between ΣR -structures
and left R-module structures. This shows that the categories R-Mod and
Sets ΣR are equivalent and actually isomorphic, hence ΓR is monadic.
3.4.9. (The underlying set of a monad.) Can we recover the ring R, or at least
its underlying set, starting from the corresponding monad ΣR ? The answer
is positive, since R = ΣR (1), where 1 = {1} is the standard one-element set
(i.e. a final object of Sets). Moreover, we can recover the multiplication on
R, as well as the action of R on the underlying set of any ΣR -module X.
     To do this observe that Rs := LΣR (1) is actually the ring R, considered
as a left module over itself. Now R ∼      = EndR (Rs )op = EndΣR (LΣR (1))op ,
and this is an isomorphism of monoids, if we consider the multiplication on
End’s defined by composition of endomorphisms. Moreover, the action of R
on any R-module (i.e. ΣR -module) M can be recovered from the canonical
isomorphism HomSets (1, M) ∼    = HomΣR (LΣR (1), M) = HomR (Rs , M), and
from the right action of EndR (Rs ) on this set, given again by the composition
of homomorphisms.
     This construction can be generalized to any monad Σ over Sets. For
any such monad we define its underlying set |Σ| (sometimes denoted simply
by Σ) by |Σ| := Σ(1). Clearly, |Σ| ∼    = HomSets (1, Σ(1)) ∼  = EndΣ (LΣ (1)) ∼  =
EndSets Σ (1), and we introduce a monoid structure on |Σ| by transporting the
natural monoid structure of EndΣ (LΣ (1)) given by composition of endomor-
phisms and taking the opposite. This defines the underlying monoid of Σ,
which will be also denoted by |Σ|. Clearly, {1} := ε1 (1) ∈ |Σ| is the unit for
this multiplication.
     Moreover, for any Σ-module M we get a canonical right action of monoid
EndΣ (LΣ (1)) on HomΣ (LΣ (1), M) ∼   = HomSets (1, M) ∼ = M, hence a left action
                                ∼
of the opposite monoid |Σ| = EndΣ (LΣ (1))op . All these constructions are
functorial: for example, any Σ-homomorphism f : M → N is at the same
time a map of |Σ|-sets, any homomorphism of monads ρ : Σ → Ξ induces
a monoid homomorphism |ρ| := ρ1 : |Σ| → |Ξ|, and the scalar restriction
functors ρ∗ : Sets Ξ → Sets Σ are compatible with these constructions as well,
i.e. the |Σ|-action on ρ∗ N coincides with the scalar restriction of the |Ξ|-action
on N with respect to |ρ|.
     Of course, in any particular case there is some extra information which
cannot be recovered by this general construction. For example, the addition
of R or of an R-module is not recovered in this way from ΣR .

monads. In other words, any monad homomorphism ζ : ΣR → ΣS is of form
Σρ for a (uniquely determined) ring homomorphism ρ : R → S. Clearly, we
must have ρ = |ζ| : R → S. We postpone some details of the proof until 4.8,
where we develop a suitable machinery for such tasks. Up to these details
the proof goes as follows.
    We know already that ρ := |ζ| is a monoid homomorphism, and we’ll
check later that it respects addition as well. Thus we are reduced to check
Σρ,X = ζX : ΣR (X) → ΣS (X) for any set X. Since both ΣR and ΣS commute
with filtered inductive limits and any set is a filtered inductive limit of its
finite subsets, we can assume X to be finite, e.g. X = n = {1, 2, . . . , n}. Then
we construct canonical projections pri : ΣR (n) → ΣR (1) = |ΣR | = R, using
only the monad structure of ΣR , and combine them to obtain a canonical
                          ∼
isomorphism ΣR (n) → Rn . Since this construction uses only the monad
structure of ΣR , it has to be compatible with ζ, i.e. it fits into a commutative
diagram relating ζn with (ζ1 )n = ρn . This proves ζn = Σρ,n . This also proves
that ρ respects addition as well, since the only map 2 = {1, 2} → 1 induces
a map R2 ∼   = ΣR (2) → R = ΣR (1), which is nothing else than the addition
of R. Now the functoriality of this construction with respect to ζ : ΣR → ΣS
and the identification of ζ2 with ρ2 proves the compatibility of ρ with the
addition on R and S.

3.4.11. (Monads as generalized rings.) We have embedded the category
of rings into the category of monads over Sets as a full subcategory. We
will often identify a ring R with the corresponding monad ΣR , thus writing
LR instead of LΣR , and on some occasion even R(X) instead of ΣR (X).
Moreover, we can treat arbitrary monads over Sets as some sort of non-
commutative generalized rings, and transport some notations usual for rings
into this more general context. For example, we write Σ-Mod instead of
Sets Σ , HomΣ instead of HomSets Σ , and even Σ(X) instead of Σ(X) or LΣ (X).
3.4. Examples of monads                                                        143


    However, one should be careful with these identifications, since to obtain
the correct category of non-commutative generalized rings we have to impose
the algebraicity condition, satisfied by all monads we considered so far. For
example, infinite projective limits computed in the category of all monads
(cf. 3.3.3) and in the category of algebraic monads are different.
    Notice that R 7→ ΣR is left exact, i.e. it commutes with finite projec-
tive limits. Indeed, given such a limit R = lim Rα , we first observe that
                                                    ←−
ΣR (X) ∼ = lim ΣRα (X) is true for a finite X, since in this case ΣR (n) ∼    = Rn
            ←−
and similarly for ΣRα , and then extend this result to the case of an arbi-
trary X by representing X as a filtered inductive limit of finite sets and
observing that filtered inductive limits commute with finite projective limits.
    Nevertheless, if we compute for example Ẑp := lim Z/pn Z in the category
                                                         ←−
of monads, we obtain a monad Ẑp which is not algebraic and in particular is
different from Zp , regardless of the fact that |Ẑp | = Zp . Actually the category
of Ẑp -modules turns out to be quite similar to that of topological Zp -modules.
In particular, it doesn’t have the usual properties of a category of modules
over a ring.
3.4.12. (Subrings and submonads.) Clearly, if R′ is a subring of R, then
ΣR′ (X) ⊂ ΣR (X) for any set X, i.e. ΣR′ is a submonad of ΣR (cf. 3.3.3).
However, not all submonads of ΣR come from subrings of R. Let’s give some
examples of such submonads.
                                                           (X)
    a) Consider the submonad Z≥0 of Z, defined by Z≥0 := {formal lin-
ear combinations of elements of X with non-negative integer coefficients}.
Clearly, Z≥0 is a subfunctor of Z = ΣZ , and it is compatible with the multi-
                                                                      (X)
plication and the unit of ΣZ , since all basis vectors {x} belong to Z≥0 , and
a linear combination with non-negative integer coefficients of several such

coefficients. Hence Z≥0 is indeed a submonad of Z. Notice that |Z≥0 | is
indeed the multiplicative monoid of all non-negative integers, as suggested
by our notation. It is easy to see that Z≥0 -Mod is actually the category of
commutative monoids, and that the scalar restriction functor for the inclu-

groups to the category of commutative monoids. We have also a unique (sur-

restriction functor is simply the embedding of the category of commutative
monoids into the category of all monoids.

3.4.13. All monads of the above examples a)–h) turn out to be algebraic,
i.e. they commute with filtered inductive limits of sets. Let’s construct a
                                                                (X)
monad Ẑ∞ ⊃ Z∞ which  P is not algebraic. For this we takePẐ∞ to be the
set of all expressions x λx {x}, where all λx are real, and x |λx | ≤ 1. (In
particular, only countably many of λx are 6= 0, otherwise this sum would be
+∞.) In several respects the relationship between Z∞ and Ẑ∞ is similar to
the relationship between Zp and Ẑp (cf. 3.4.11).
3.4.14. All of the above monads, maybe with the only exception of W and
WU , behave themselves very much like ordinary rings. Let’s consider an
example where this is definitely not so. For this consider the monad Σ
defined by the forgetful functor from the category of commutative rings to the
category of sets. This functor turns out to be monadic, so Σ-Mod is actually
the category of commutative rings. Furthermore, Σ(X) = Z[X] is the set of
polynomials in variables from X with integer coefficients. In particular, |Σ|
is the set Σ[T ] of polynomials in one variable T , and the monoid structure on
|Σ| is given by the application of polynomials: f ∗ g = f (g). This is definitely
not what somebody expects from the multiplicative monoid of a ring.
3.5. (Inner functors.) Given a monad Σ over a topos E, we would like to be
able to localize it, i.e. to obtain a monad ΣS over E/S for any S ∈ Ob E.
However, this requires some additional structure on functor Σ. We suggest
one possible choice of such a structure, sufficient for our purposes.

Definition 3.5.1 Let P : C → D be a functor between two cartesian cate-
gories (i.e. categories with finite products). A diagonal structure (ρ, θ) on P
consists of a morphism θ : eD → P (eC ), where eC and eD are the final objects
146                                                  Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


of C and D, and a family of morphisms {ρX,Y : P (X) × P (Y ) → P (X × Y )}
in D, parametrized by couples of objects X, Y of C, required to satisfy the
following axioms:

 ρ0) ρX,Y : P (X) × P (Y ) → P (X × Y ) is functorial in X and Y , i.e. for any
     two morphisms f : X → X ′ and g : Y → Y ′ we have P (f × g) ◦ ρX,Y =
     ρX ′ ,Y ′ ◦ (P (f ) × P (g));

             θ×idP (X)                    ρeC ,X
 ρ1) P (X)       / P (eC ) × P (X)                 / P (eC × X) ∼
                                                                = P (X) is the identity of
     P (X) for any X ∈ Ob C;

 ρ2) For any X, Y , Z ∈ Ob C we have ρX×Y,Z ◦ (ρX,Y × idP (Z) ) = ρX,Y ×Z ◦
     (idP (X) ×ρY,Z ):

                                                ρX,Y ×idP (Z)
                P (X) × P (Y ) × P (Z)                          / P (X × Y ) × P (Z)

                                idP (X) ×ρY,Z                                 ρX×Y,Z
                                                  ρX,Y ×Z                
                  P (X) × P (Y × Z)                              / P (X × Y × Z)


A diagonal (inner) functor P = (P, ρ, θ) : C → D is a functor P : C → D
endowed with a diagonal structure. A natural transformation ξ : (P, ρ, θ) →
(P ′, ρ′ , θ′ ) of diagonal functors is simply a natural transformation ξ : P →
P ′, compatible with diagonal structures: ξeC ◦ θ = θ′ and ξX×Y ◦ ρX,Y =
ρ′X,Y ◦ (ξX × ξY ). The category of all diagonal functors between two cartesian
categories will be denoted by DiagFunct(C, D); if D = C, we also write
DiagEndof (C).
3.5.2. Any left exact functor P : C → D admits a unique diagonal structure,
given by canonical isomorphisms P (X ×Y ) ∼ = P (X) ×P (Y ) and P (eC ) ∼
                                                                        = eD .
In particular, IdC can be considered as a diagonal endofunctor on C.
3.5.3. If (P, ρ, θ) : C → D and (Q, ρ′ , θ′ ) : D → E are two diagonal functors,
we obtain a diagonal structure (ρ′′ , θ′′ ) on QP : C → E as follows. We put
θ′′ := Q(θ)◦θ′ : eE → QP (eC ), and ρ′′X,Y := Q(ρX,Y )◦ρ′P (X),P (Y ) . This actually
defines a functor ◦ : DiagFunct(D, E)×DiagFunct(C, D) → DiagFunct(C, E).
Combining together these categories of diagonal functors, we obtain a strictly
associative 2-category with cartesian categories for objects and diagonal func-
tors for morphisms. We can replace the 2-category of all categories with this
new 2-category in our previous considerations, thus obtaining an AU ⊗-
structure on DiagEndof (C), its ;-action on DiagFunct(D, C) and C, and its
⊘-action on DiagFunct(C, D).

3.5.4. Of course, a diagonal (inner) monad Σ over a cartesian category C is
simply an algebra Σ = (Σ, µ, ε) in DiagEndof (C). Natural transformations
µ : Σ2 → Σ and ε : IdC → Σ define a monad structure on the underlying
endofunctor Σ, and the category C Σ is the same for the diagonal monad Σ
and for its underlying usual monad, also denoted by Σ.
   We see that a diagonal monad Σ over C is just a usual monad Σ = (Σ, µ, ε)
over C, together with a diagonal structure (ρ, θ) on Σ, compatible in a certain
sense.
   For example, the compatibility of ε with θ actually means θ = εeC : eC →
Σ(eC ), so we don’t have to specify θ separately. Compatibility of ε with ρ
means ρX,Y ◦ (εX × εY ) = εX×Y . Next, the compatibility of µ with θ = εeC
means ρeC ,X ◦ (εeC × idΣ(X) ) = idΣ(X) , and the remaining compatibility of µ
with ρ means µX×Y ◦ Σ(ρX,Y ) ◦ ρΣ(X),Σ(Y ) = ρX,Y ◦ (µX × µY ):

                        ρΣ(X),Σ(Y )                               Σ(ρX,Y )
  Σ2 (X) × Σ2 (Y )                    / Σ(Σ(X) × Σ(Y ))                      / Σ2 (X × Y )       (3.5.4.1)
              µX ×µY                                                                      µX×Y
                                            ρX,Y                                     
   Σ(X) × Σ(Y )                                                              / Σ(X × Y )


Definition 3.5.5 Given a diagonal functor (P, ρ, θ) : C → D, we define a P -
inner functor F = (F, α) : C → D as follows: F is a functor C → D, and α is
a P -inner structure on F , i.e. a family of morphisms {αX,Y : P (X)×F (Y ) →
F (X × Y )}X,Y ∈Ob C , subject to the following conditions, similar to ρ0)–ρ2)
of 3.5.1:

 α0) αX,Y : P (X) × F (Y ) → F (X × Y ) is functorial in X and Y , i.e. for any
     two morphisms f : X → X ′ and g : Y → Y ′ we have F (f × g) ◦ αX,Y =
     αX ′ ,Y ′ ◦ (P (f ) × F (g));

               θ×idF (X)                       αeC ,X
 α1) F (X)       / P (eC ) × F (X)                      / F (eC × X) ∼
                                                                     = F (X) is the identity of
     F (X) for any X ∈ Ob C;

 α2) For any X, Y , Z ∈ Ob C we have αX×Y,Z ◦ (ρX,Y × idF (Z) ) = αX,Y ×Z ◦
     (idP (X) ×αY,Z ):

                                                     ρX,Y ×idF (Z)
                  P (X) × P (Y ) × F (Z)                             / P (X × Y ) × F (Z)

                                     idP (X) ×αY,Z                                   αX×Y,Z
                                                       αX,Y ×Z                  
                       P (X) × F (Y × Z)                              / F (X × Y × Z)
