A natural transformation of P -inner functors ζ : (F, α) → (F ′ , α′) is a natural
transformation ζ : F → F ′ , such that ζX×Y ◦ αX,Y = αX,Y ′
                                                               ◦ (idP (X) ×ζY ) :

P (X)×F (Y ) → F (X ×Y ). The category of P -inner functors will be denoted
by InnFunct /P (C, D).

3.5.6. Given a P -inner functor (F, α) : C → D and a Q-inner functor
(G, α′) : D → E, we have a canonical QP -inner structure α′′ on GF : C → E,
            ′′
given by αX,Y   = G(αX,Y ) ◦ αP′ (X),F (Y ) : QP (X) × GF (Y ) → GF (X × Y ).
In this way we construct the composition functors ◦ : InnFunct /Q (D, E) ×
InnFunct /P (C, D) → InnFunct /QP (C, E).
3.5.7. Notice that P = (P, ρ, θ) is itself a P -inner functor, since the axioms
α0)–α2) specialize to ρ0)–ρ2) when we put F := P , α := ρ. Hence the state-
ments proved for inner functors over a diagonal functor can be transferred
to diagonal inner functors themselves.
3.5.8. If C = D, we can take P = IdC , thus obtaining the category of plain
inner endofunctors InnEndof (C), which consists of endofunctors F : C → C,
endowed with a plain inner structure α, αX,Y : X × F (Y ) → F (X × Y ). We
have an AU ⊗-structure on InnEndof (C); the algebras with respect to this
⊗-structure will be called (plain) inner monads. Clearly, a plain inner monad
Σ = (Σ, µ, ε, α) is simply a usual monad (Σ, µ, ε) over C, together with some
plain inner (i.e. IdC -inner) structure α on Σ, subject to some compatibility
conditions similar to those considered before. Namely, we must have

Proposition 3.5.9 Any endofunctor F over Sets admits a unique plain in-
ner structure, i.e. the ⊗-categories InnEndof (Sets) and Endof (Sets) are iso-
morphic. In particular, any monad over Sets uniquely extends to a plain
inner monad.

Proof. For any set X and any element x ∈ X denote by x̃ : eSets = 1 =
{1} → X the only map with image x. Then x̃ × idY : Y → X × Y is the map
y 7→ (x, y) for any set Y . A plain inner structure {αX,Y : X ×F (Y ) → F (X ×
Y )} is functorial with respect to X and Y ; applying this to x̃ and taking α1)
into account we see that αX,Y ◦(x̃×idF (Y ) ) = F (x̃×idY ) : F (Y ) → F (X ×Y ),
i.e. αX,Y (x, w) = (F (x̃ × idY ))(w) for any x ∈ X, w ∈ F (Y ). This shows the
uniqueness of α, and also gives a way of defining it. It is immediate that the
family {αX,Y } defined by this formula indeed satisfies α0)–α2).

3.5.10. For example, the plain inner structure on the monad of words W
is given by αX,Y (x, y1 y2 . . . yn ) = {x, y1 }{x, y2 } . . . {x, yn }, where we write
{x, y} instead of {(x, y)}. For the monad WU of words with constants
from U the situation is similar, but the constants are not affected, e.g.
αX,Y (x, y1 u1 y2 y3 u2 ) = {x, y1 }u1 {x, y2 }{x, y3}u2 .
3.5.11. (Alternative description of inner structures.) A P -inner structure
{αX,Y : P (X) × F (Y ) → F (X × Y )} on a functor F : C → D admits an
alternative description in terms of a natural transformation γ of functors
C 0 × C 0 × C → Sets, γX,Y,Z : HomC (X × Y, Z) → HomD (P (X) × F (Y ), F (Z)).
Namely, for any ϕ : X × Y → Z we put γX,Y,Z (ϕ) := F (ϕ) ◦ αX,Y , and
conversely, any such γ defines (by Yoneda) a family αX,Y , functorial in X
and Y ; actually, αX,Y = γX,Y,X×Y (idX×Y ). Moreover, the axioms α0)–α2)
can be rewritten directly in terms of γ:

 γ0) γX,Y,Z : HomC (X × Y, Z) → HomD (P (X) × F (Y ), F (Z)) is functorial
     in X, Y and Z ∈ Ob C;

 γ1) The following diagram is commutative for any X and Y in C:
                                         γeC ,X,Y

3.5.12. (Inner structures over cartesian closed categories.) Now suppose
that both C and D are cartesian closed, i.e. they are cartesian, and the
functor Hom(− × Y, Z) is representable by some object Hom(Y, Z) (local

or inner Hom), for any couple of objects Y and Z from C or from D. The

3.5.13. Consider now a P -inner structure α on some functor F : C →
D. We know already that it admits a description in terms of morphisms
γX,Y,Z : HomC (X × Y, Z) → HomD (P (X) × F (Y ), F (Z)), functorial in X,
Y and Z (cf. 3.5.11). Since we have assumed C and D to be cartesian
closed, we can interpet γX,Y,Z as a morphism HomC (X, HomC (Y, Z)) →
HomD (P (X), HomD (F (Y ), F (Z)). By Yoneda such a functorial family of
morphisms is determined by its value on idHomC (Y,Z) , so we put βY,Z :=
γHom(Y,Z),Y,Z (evY,Z )♭ : P (HomC (Y, Z)) → HomD (F (Y ), F (Z)). This gives
another equivalent description of a P -inner structure on a functor between
two cartesian closed categories, and in fact it is possible to restate the ax-
ioms in terms of these morphisms β. For example, β0) states that βY,Z :
P (HomC (Y, Z)) → HomD (F (Y ), F (Z)) is functorial in Y and Z, axiom β1)
relates β with the global section functors, and β2) relates β with the composi-
tion morphisms oX,Y,Z : Hom(Y, Z)×Hom(X, Y ) → Hom(X, Z). Actually,
it states βX,Z ◦ P (oX,Y,Z ) ◦ ρHom(Y,Z),Hom(X,Y ) = oF (X),F (Y ),F (Z) ◦ (βY,Z ×βX,Y ).
We omit the verification of equivalence of this set of axioms β0)–β2) with our
other sets of axioms. Let’s just remark that this description shows that an
inner structure can be thought of as an extension of F (−) : HomC (Y, Z) →
HomD (F (Y ), F (Z)) to the local Homs. This also shows again that in case
C = D = Sets there is always a unique plain inner structure, since in this
case local Homs coincide with the usual ones.

can retrieve a plain inner structure α on the same monad by putting αX,Y :=
ρX,Y ◦(εX ×idΣ(Y ) ). Conversely, we might try to extend a plain inner structure

     Strictly speaking, we have to check that these formulas indeed define
some plain inner structure α starting from a diagonal inner structure ρ, and
study the exact conditions under which a plain inner monad extends to a
diagonal inner monad in this manner; it is true in general that we always
obtain a diagonal inner structure on the underlying endofunctor of Σ, which
need not be compatible with the monad structure. The verifications are
straightforward but lengthy; we omit them and consider an example instead.
     Let C = Sets, Σ = W be the monad of words (cf. 3.4.1), and consider the
only compatible plain inner structure α on W (cf. 3.5.9); αX,Y : X ×W (Y ) →
W (X ×Y ) is given by (x, y1 y2 . . . yn ) 7→ {x, y1 }{x, y2} . . . {x, yn } (cf. 3.5.10).
Then the corresponding diagonal inner structure ρX,Y : W (X) × W (Y ) →
W (X × Y ) maps a pair of words (x1 x2 . . . xm , y1 y2 . . . yn ) into the word
{x1 , y1 }{x1 , y2} . . . {x1 , yn }{x2 , y1 } . . . {xm , yn }, i.e. we list all pairs of letters
(xi , yj ) of the two original words in the lexicographical order with respect to
the pair of indices (i, j). Notice that this is indeed a diagonal inner struc-
ture on the underlying endofunctor W , but it is not compatible with the
monad structure. For example, put X := {a, b}, Y := {x, y, z} and con-
sider the two maps W 2 (X) × W 2 (Y ) → W (X × Y ) which have to be equal
by (3.5.4.1). The images of ({{a}{b}}, {{x}{y}}{{z}}) ∈ W 2 (X) × W 2 (Y )
under these two maps are distinct: {a, x}{a, y}{a, z}{b, x}{b, y}{b, z} 6=
{a, x}{a, y}{b, x}{b, y}{a, z}{b, z}.

in general does not commute:

on Σ, also restricting to the same plain inner structure α.
    We say that a diagonal (resp. plain) inner monad is commutative if ρ′ = ρ
(resp. if this is true for diagonal inner structure constructed above), i.e. if this
diagram commutes. Since any monad over Sets extends uniquely to a plain
inner monad, the notion of commutativity makes sense in this context as
well. For example, the monad of words is not commutative, while the monad
ΣR defined by an associative P    ring R is commutative

    An interesting statement is that if the diagonal inner structure ρ defined

compatible with the monad structure of Σ. It seems to be known in similar
contexts (cf. 3.5.19 below), so we omit the proof. We won’t use it anyway.
3.5.18. Let Σ = (Σ, µ, ε, α) be a plain inner monad over a cartesian closed
category C, and let M = (M, σ) and N = (N, τ ) be two objects of C Σ . Then
we can construct “local inner Homs” HomC,Σ (M, N) = HomΣ (M, N) ⊂
Hom(M, N), such that ΓC (HomΣ (M, N)) = HomΣ (M, N). To do this con-
sider an arbitrary morphism i : H ′ → H := Hom(M, N), which corresponds
by adjointness to some i♯ : H ′ × M → N. We say that H ′ acts by Σ-
morphisms from M to N if the following diagram commutes:
                                                    idH ′ ×σ
                      H ′ × Σ(M)                                   / H′ × M     (3.5.18.1)
                                 αH ′ ,M                                   i♯
                                          Σ(i♯ )                      

                      Σ(H ′ × M)                    / Σ(N)           /N

In particular, we can take H ′ = H, i = idH and obtain two morphisms
H × Σ(M) ⇒ N, which correspond by adjointness to some p, q : H ⇒
Hom(Σ(M), N). In general the above diagram commutes for some i :
H ′ → H iff p ◦ i = q ◦ i, i.e. iff i factorizes through the kernel H0 =
HomΣ (M, N) := Ker(p, q) ⊂ H. In other words, H0 is the largest sub-
object of Hom(M, N) which acts by Σ-homomorphisms, so it is a natural
candidate for HomΣ (M, N). Notice that ΓC (H0 ) corresponds to morphisms
i : eC → Hom(M, N) which factorize through H0 , i.e. which make the above
diagram commutative; using α1) we see that this is equivalent to i♯ : M → N
being a Σ-homomorphism, i.e. ΓC (HomΣ (M, N)) ∼     = HomΣ (M, N).
     Of course, one can check directly that the composition morphisms oM,N,P :
Hom(N, P ) × Hom(M, N) → Hom(M, P ) respect these subobjects HomΣ
once we fix Σ-structures on M, N and P ; we’ll prove this later for algebraic
monads over a topos in another way.
154                                    Chapter 3. Generalities on monads


    Notice that in general HomΣ (M, N) doesn’t inherit a Σ-structure from
Hom(M, N) (cf. 3.5.15), i.e. it is a subobject of Hom(M, N), but not nec-
essarily a Σ-stable subobject. Actually, we’ll prove later that HomΣ (M, N)
is a Σ-subobject of Hom(M, N) for all choices of M and N from C Σ iff Σ is
commutative.
3.5.19. A terminological remark: if we consider on a cartesian category C
the ACU ⊗-structure defined by the direct product (A ⊗ B := A × B), then
our notion of plain inner structure corresponds (up to some minor details)
to what people call tensorial strength, and plain inner monads – to strong
monads. Furthermore, our diagonal inner monads correspond to monoidal
(or tensorial ) monads, and our commutativity condition seems to be known
either under the name of commutativity or symmetry condition in this setup.
Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems                         155


4    Algebraic monads and algebraic systems
This chapter is dedicated to the study of a very important class of endo-
functors and monads — the algebraic endofunctors and monads over the
category of sets, and their topos counterparts — algebraic (plain inner) end-
ofunctors and monads over a (Grothendieck) topos E. These notions admit
both category-theoretic descriptions (in terms of some functors and monads)
and algebraic descriptions (as sets or sheaves with some operations on them,
in the spirit of universal algebra). Both these approaches are important:
for example, the first of them enables us to construct (arbitrary) projective
limits of algebraic monads, while the second is equally indispensable for the
construction of some inductive limits (e.g. tensor products). That’s why we
carefully develop some language and some notation to simplify transition
between these two alternative descriptions.
    Let us emphasize once more that the notion of an algebraic monad (resp.
algebraic inner monad over a topos) is extremely important in the sequel
since in our setup it corresponds to the notion of a “(non-commutative)
generalized ring” (or a sheaf of such generalized rings); in this sense the
content of this chapter should be viewed as some generalization of the basic
theory of (sheaves of) associative rings and algebras.
    Notations. All endofunctors and monads considered in this chapter,
unless otherwise specified, will be defined over a base category C, which will
be supposed to be equal either to Sets, or to a topos E. Sometimes E is the
topos of sheaves (of sets) on some site S; then we write E = S̃. We also
denote by A the AU ⊗-category Endof (C).
4.1. (Algebraic endofunctors on Sets.) The definition itself is very simple:

Definition 4.1.1 We say that an endofunctor Σ : Sets → Sets is alge-
braic if it commutes with filtered inductive limits. The full ⊗-subcategory of
A = Endof (Sets), consisting of all algebraic endofunctors, will be denoted
Endof alg (Sets) or Aalg . Thus an algebraic monad is simply an algebra in
Aalg , i.e. a monad over Sets, the underlying functor of which commutes with
arbitrary inductive limits.
Clearly, if F and G commute with filtered inductive limits, the same is true
for F ⊗ G = F ◦ G, so Aalg is indeed a ⊗-subcategory of A.
4.1.2. Notice that any set X is a filtered inductive limit of the ordered set
of all its finite subsets I ⊂ X, hence an algebraic endofunctor Σ is com-
pletely determined by its values on finite sets: Σ(X) = limfinite I ⊂ X Σ(I).
                                                            −→
On the other hand, any finite set is isomorphic to some standard finite set
n = {1, 2, . . . , n}, n ≥ 0. Let us denote by N the full subcategory of Sets,
156                       Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


consisting of all standard finite sets. Sometimes we identify the objects of N
with the set of non-negative integers, and write n instead of n. Let us denote
by J = JSets : N → Sets the inclusion functor.
    We see that J is fully faithful, and that its essential image is the category
of all finite sets. Since any algebraic endofunctor Σ is completely determined
by its restriction to the category of finite sets, which is equivalent to N, we
see that the canonical functor J ∗ : A → Funct(N, Sets) = Sets N , given by
F 7→ F ◦ J, induces an equivalence between Aalg and a full subcategory of
Sets N . Let’s make a more precise statement:

Proposition 4.1.3 Consider the inclusion functor J : N → Sets, the cor-
responding restriction functor J ∗ : A = Endof (Sets) → Sets N , F 7→ F ◦ J,
and its left adjoint (i.e. left Kan extension of J) J! : Sets N → A, defined
by the usual formula (J! G)(X) = limN/X G(n), where N/X is the category
                                      −→
of all maps from standard finite sets into a set X. Then J! is fully faithful,
and its essential image equals Aalg , hence it induces an equivalence between
Sets N and Aalg , and J ∗ |Aalg is the quasi-inverse equivalence. Moreover, J ∗
commutes with arbitrary limits of functors, and J! commutes with arbitrary
inductive and finite projective limits, hence Aalg ⊂ A is stable under these
types of limits in A.

Proof. The existence of J! follows from the existence of inductive limits of
sets, and the explicit formula for (J! G)(X) is well-known and can be either
checked directly or found in SGA 4 I, for example. Full faithfulness of J!
is a consequence of that of J, since (J! G)(m) is computed as the limit of
G(n) along the category N/m of all maps n → m, which has a final object
idm , hence (J! G)(m) ∼   = G(m), i.e. G → J ∗ J! G is an isomorphism, hence J!
is fully faithful. Notice that N/X is a filtered category, and limN/X n ∼    = X,
                                                                    −→
                                                                ∼
hence for any algebraic endofunctor F we have F (X) = limN/X F (n) =
                                                                   −→
(J! J ∗ F )(X), i.e. any algebraic functor lies indeed in the essential image of J! .
To prove the converse we use the alternative description of (J! G)(X) in terms
of inductive limits and finite products, given in Lemma 4.1.4 below, and
the fact that filtered inductive limits in Sets commute with finite projective
limits; this shows immediately that J! G is indeed algebraic. This fact also
shows that J! commutes with finite projective limits, and it has to commute
with arbitrary inductive limits since it has a right adjoint; this proves the
remaining statements.

4.1.5. Notice that the injective maps n → X form a cofinal set in N/X,
hence it is sufficient to take the inductive limit along only such maps in

factorizes through Falg . We also know that F 7→ Falg commutes with arbi-

(infinite) projective limits can be computed in Aalg by first computing it
(componentwise) in A, and then taking the largest algebraic subfunctor; al-
ternatively, we might first restrict everything to N by applying J ∗ , compute
(componentwise) the projective limit in Sets N , and then extend resulting
functor N → Sets to an algebraic endofunctor by means of J! .
4.1.6. Observe that if Σ is a monad over Sets, then Σalg ⊂ Σ is a submonad
                                                               µ
of Σ (cf. 3.3.3). Indeed, Σ2alg is algebraic, hence Σ2alg → Σ2 → Σ factorizes
158                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


through Σalg ⊂ Σ, and similarly ε : IdSets → Σ factorizes through Σalg since
IdSets is algebraic. Clearly, Σalg → Σ is universal among all homomorphisms
from algebraic monads into Σ. In other words, the inclusion functor from
the category of algebraic monads into the category of all monads admits a
right adjoint Σ 7→ Σalg , hence it commutes with arbitrary inductive limits of
algebraic monads.
4.1.7.
S         We see that the algebraicity of a monad Σ means that Σ(X) =
  finite I⊂X Σ(I). If we think of Σ(X) as “the set of all formal Σ-linear combi-
nations of elements of X”, this condition means that any such Σ-linear com-
bination actually involves only finitely many elements of X. This explains
why all monads defined by algebraic systems (in terms of some operations
and relations between them), e.g. the monads W and ΣR = R for an asso-
ciative ring R, or any of the monads listed in 3.4.12, are actually algebraic
in the sense of 4.1.1. However, monads Ẑ∞ (cf. 3.4.13) and Ẑp (cf. 3.4.11)
are clearly not algebraic; their largest algebraic subfunctors (which turn out
to be submonads) are Z∞ and Zp , respectively.

4.1.8. Notice that these monads like Ẑ∞ still have a similar property: any
formal Ẑ∞ -linear combination of elements of a set X involves only at most
countably many elements of X. This means that if we replace N by the
category of all ordinals ≤ ω, these monads will lie in the essential image of
the corresponding left Kan extension J≤ω,! . This leads to the idea of cardinal
filtration on the category of all endofunctors, when we consider those end-
ofunctors which lie in the essential image of J≤α,! or J<α,! for some “small”
cardinal α (e.g. belonging to the chosen universe U). The set of all end-
ofunctors which belong to some step of the cardinal filtration forms a full
subcategory of A, stable under ⊗ (i.e. composition of functors) and arbi-
trary projective and inductive limits (along small index categories). We call
such endofunctors accessible (cf. SGA 4 I); clearly, their category Aacc is
a very good (rigorous) replacement for A = Endof (Sets), which contains
all interesting endofunctors and at the same time avoids all set-theoretical
complications (e.g. it is a U-category).
4.1.9. Since J ∗ induces an equivalence between categories Aalg and Sets N ,
and since it is nothing else than the restriction functor, we usually denote an
algebraic endofunctor F and its restriction J ∗ F by the same letter F . We
also often write F (n) instead of F (n) or (J ∗ F )(n). In this sense an algebraic
endofunctor F is something like a (co)simplicial object: we get a collection of
sets {F (n)}n≥0, together with some transition maps F (ϕ) : F (m) → F (n),
defined for any map of finite sets ϕ : m → n. In this context we think of J! F
(denoted again by F ) as some sort of extension of F to arbitrary sets.
4.1. Algebraic endofunctors on Sets                                                             159


4.1.10. In particular, we see that the category Aalg ∼        = Sets N really makes
sense, i.e. it is not “too large” (it is a U-category in the language of universes),
so in this way we avoid the set-theoretical complications of 3.2.6.
4.2. (Operations with algebraic endofunctors.) Let’s express some category-
theoretic operations with algebraic endofunctors in terms of corresponding
“cosimplicial objects”.
4.2.1. We have already seen that an algebraic endofunctor F corresponds
to a “cosimplicial set”, i.e. to a collection of sets {F (n)}n≥0, together with
some maps F (ϕ) : F (m) → F (n), defined for any map of finite sets ϕ :
m → n, subject to usual conditions F (ψ ◦ ϕ) = F (ψ) ◦ F (ϕ) and F (idn ) =
idF (n) . Moreover, a natural transformation β : F → G from an algebraic
endofunctor F into another endofunctor G is given by a collection of maps
βn : F (n) → G(n), such that G(ϕ) ◦ βm = βn ◦ F (ϕ) for any ϕ : m → n.
4.2.2. Consider an algebraic endofunctor Σ, two arbitrary sets X and Y ,
and some map α : Σ(X) → Y (if X = Y , we say that any such map is a

H1 (X) ⇒ H0 (X)), given in 4.1.4. It shows immediately that to give such an
α : Σ(X) → Y is equivalent to giving a family of maps {α(n) : Σ(n) × X n →
Y }n≥0 , subject to condition

of maps (“operations”) [t]α : X n → Y for each “formal n-ary operation”

4.2.7. In particular, the algebraic subfunctors F ′ of a given algebraic functor
F are given by collections of subsets {F ′(n) ⊂ F (n)}n≥0 , stable under all

in Aalg . Notice that after we extend F ′ and F to endofunctors on Sets, we
still have F ′ (X) ⊂ F (X) for any set X. Another interesting consequence:
an algebraic equivalence relation R on some algebraic functor F is given
by a family of equivalence relations R(n) ⊂ F (n) × F (n), compatible with
all maps F (ϕ). In this case we can construct the quotient F/R, given by
4.3. Algebraic monads                                                                       161


(F/R)(n) = F (n)/R(n). It is again an algebraic functor, and, if we extend
everything to arbitrary sets X, we still have (F/R)(X) = F (X)/R(X), and
F → F/R is a strict epimorphism with kernel R both in A and Aalg .
4.2.8. Notice that any morphism ρ : F → G of algebraic endofunctors
has an algebraic kernel pair R := F ×G F as well as an algebraic image
I = ρ(F ) ∼
          = F/R. Of course, these notions can be computed componentwise:
R(n) ⊂ F (n)×F (n) is the equivalence relation defined by ρn : F (n) → G(n),
and F (n)/R(n) ∼ = ρn (F (n)) = I(n) ⊂ G(n). Moreover, these formulas
extend to arbitrary sets X, i.e. R(X) ⊂ F (X) × F (X) is still the kernel of
ρX : F (X) → G(X) and so on.
4.2.9. What about natural transformations ε : IdSets → F from the iden-
tity functor into an arbitrary (algebraic) endofunctor F ? Since IdSets =
Hom(1, −), we see by Yoneda that such an ε is uniquely determined by an
element e := ε1 (1) ∈ F (1), which can be chosen arbitrarily. In this case we
get εX (x) = (F (x̃))(e) for any set X and any x ∈ X, where x̃ : 1 → X
is the only map with image x. In particular, for an algebraic F the maps
εn : n → F (n) can be reconstructed from e ∈ F (1) in this way.

4.3. (Algebraic monads.) Now we want to combine together some of pre-
vious considerations to obtain a “naı̈ve” description of an algebraic monad
162                            Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


Σ = (Σ, µ, ε) (i.e. an algebra in Aalg , or equivalently, a monad over Sets with
an algebraic underlying endofunctor) in terms of a sequence of sets {Σ(n)}n≥0
and some maps between these sets and their products, subject to some con-
ditions. This naı̈ve approach has its advantages: for example, it immediately
generalizes to the case of an arbitrary category C, and it is completely clear
how to apply left exact functors to such objects (e.g. pullback, direct image
or global sections functors between topoi), or how to define sheaves of them
over any site S. However, we’ll develop a (plain inner) monad interpretation
in the topos case as well, since it also has its advantages.

                                        n

is an example of an algebraic structure, hence Σ-Mod = Sets Σ has all the
properties of a category defined by an algebraic structure.
4.3.8. Given any set X, we can construct its “absolute endomorphism ring”
END(X). It is an algebraic monad defined by (END(X))(n) := HomSets (X n ,
X); we take eΞ to be equal to idX , and µn : Hom(X k , X)×Hom(X n , X)k ∼
                                         (k)
                                                                        =
Hom(X k , X) × Hom(X n , X k ) → Hom(X n , X) are the usual composition
166                            Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


maps. The conditions of 4.3.3 obviously hold, and we have a canonical action
of END(X) on X. Furthermore, the considerations of 4.3.7 show that giving
an action α : Σ(X) → X of an algebraic monad Σ on X is equivalent to giving
a monad homomorphism (“representation”) ρ : Σ → END(X), and then the
Σ-action on X can be recovered from the canonical END(X)-action on X by
means of scalar restriction along ρ.
     We say that X is a faithful Σ-module if the corresponding homomorphism
ρ : Σ → END(X) is injective, i.e. if [t]X = [t′ ]X implies t = t′ for any
t, t′ ∈ Σ(n) and any n ≥ 0. In general case we denote the image ρ(Σ) of ρ by
ΣX ; clearly, this is the only strict quotient of Σ which acts faithfully on X.
4.3.9. (Terminology and notations.) Given any algebraic monad Σ, we call
the elements of Σ(0) constants (of Σ), elements of |Σ| = Σ(1) — unary
operations, elements of Σ(2) — binary operations,                  F . . . , elements of Σ(n) —
n-ary operations (of Σ). We say that kΣk := n≥0 Σ(n) is the set of all
operations of Σ; if t ∈ Σ(n), we say that the arity of t is equal to n, and
sometimes write t[n] or r(t) = n to emphasize this fact. Cleary, an operation
t of arity n induces a map [t]X : X n → X on any Σ-module X. We often write
tX (x1 , . . . , xn ), t(x1 , . . . , xn ) or even t x1 . . . xn instead of [t]X (x1 , . . . , xn ). In
particular, if λ ∈ |Σ| is a unary operation, we write λX (x) or λx instead of
[λ]X (x); this is especially useful when λ is denoted by some sign like −; then
we write −x instead of [−]X (x), and −X : X → X instead of [−]X . Notice
that (λt)(x1 , . . . , xn ) = λ(t(x1 , . . . , xn )) for any λ ∈ |Σ|, t ∈ Σ(n) (this is a
special case of (4.3.2.2)), so the notation λt(x1 , . . . , xn ) is unambiguous.
    Similarly, if a binary operation is denoted by some sign like +, ∗, × . . . ,
which is usually written in infix form, we write x1 +x2 instead of [+]X (x1 , x2 );
notice that [+] = [+]Σ(2) ({1}, {2}) = {1} + {2} in Σ(2). We obey the usual
precedence rules while using such notations, inserting parentheses when nec-
essary; if an operation + is associative, we write x+y +z instead of (x+y)+z
or x + (y + z). For example, any R-linear combination t = (λ1 , . . . , λn ) ∈
ΣR (n) = Rn , where λi ∈ R, R is any associative ring (cf. 3.4.8), can be safely
written now in form t = λ1 {1}+λ2 {2}+· · ·+λn {n}, where λi ∈ R = |ΣR | are
interpreted as unary operations of ΣR , and [+] = (1, 1) ∈ ΣR (2) is of course
a binary operation of ΣR . In this situation we also have a unary operation
[−] := −1 ∈ |ΣR |, and a constant 0 ∈ ΣR (0).
4.3.10. In particular, for any constant c ∈ Σ(0) and any Σ-module X we
get the value cX = [c]X ∈ X of this constant in X. Of course, any Σ-
homomorphism f : X → Y has to preserve all constants: f (cX ) = cY . For
example, if i : 0 = ∅ → 1 is the canonical embedding, then the unary op-
eration i∗ c = c|Σ| ∈ Σ(1) acts on any Σ-module X by mapping all elements
of X into cX , i.e. [i∗ c]X (x) = cX . This shows that Σ(i) : Σ(0) → Σ(1) is in-
4.3. Algebraic monads                                                                  167


jective: indeed, i∗ c = i∗ c′ implies [i∗ c]Σ(0) = [i∗ c′ ]Σ(0) , hence c = [i∗ c]Σ(0) (x) =
[i∗ c′ ]Σ(0) (x) = c′ , where we can take any auxiliary element x ∈ Σ(0) (e.g.
x = c).
     This fact, combined with the observation that any monomorphism (i.e.
injective map) f : X → Y with non-empty source splits in Sets (i.e. admits a
left inverse), hence Σ(f ) : Σ(X) → Σ(Y ) has to be injective when X is non-
empty, shows that Σ(f ) is in fact injective even if X is empty. In particular,
all maps Σ(ϕ) : Σ(m) → Σ(n) for injective     S      ϕ : m → n are injective; if we
put Σ(∞) := Σ(Z≥0 ) = limn≥0 Σ(n) = n Σ(n), we see that Σ(n) is a subset
                             −→
of Σ(∞), and these subsets form a filtration on Σ(∞), so we can combine all
Σ(n) into one large filtered set Σ(∞).
4.3.11. Notice that Σ(0) = LΣ (∅) is an initial object of Σ-Mod = Sets Σ .
We say that Σ is a monad without constants if Σ(0) = ∅; in this case the
empty set is (the only) initial object of Σ-Mod, in particular, the empty set
admits a (unique) Σ-action. We have already seen some examples of monads
without constants like F∅, ∆ or Aff R (cf. 3.4.12). We can also consider the
submonad W+ ⊂ W given by W+ (X) = W (X) if X 6= ∅, W+ (∅) = ∅; this is
also a monad without constants, and W+ -Mod is the category of semigroups.
4.3.12. If Σ(0) consists of exactly one constant, usually denoted by 0, we
say that Σ is a monad with zero. In this case Σ(0) = {0} is both a initial and
a final object, i.e. a zero object 0 := Σ(0) of Σ-Mod, and conversely, since
Σ(0) is always initial and 1 is always final in Σ-Mod, if Σ-Mod has a zero
object, then Σ is a monad with zero. In this case any Σ-module X has a
pointed element 0X = 0, which has to be respected by any Σ-homomorphism;
in particular, X cannot be empty. Moreover, any set HomΣ (M, N) has a
pointed element — the zero homomorphism 0M N : M → 0 → N. Almost all
monads considered by us up to now have been monads with zero, with the
exception of WU and of those listed in 4.3.11.
4.3.13. (Triviality of a monad.) Recall that the category of all monads over
Sets admits a final object — the trivial or final monad 1, such that 1(X) is
the one-point set 1 for any set X. Clearly, this monad is algebraic, so it is
a final object in the category of algebraic monads. We say that Σ is trivial
if it is isomorphic to 1; in this case we write Σ ∼ = 1 or even Σ = 1. In some
cases we write 0 or 0 instead of 1, since 1 is the monad defined by the trivial
ring 0. Let’s list some criteria for triviality of a monad:

Proposition. The following conditions for an algebraic monad Σ are equiv-
alent: (i) Σ is trivial; (ii) Σ-Mod is a trivial category, i.e. all its objects
are final; (ii’) The only sets which admit a Σ-structure are the one-element
sets; (iii) εX : X → Σ(X) is not injective for at least one set X, and
168                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


Σ(0) 6= ∅; (iii’) ε2 : 2 → Σ(2) is not injective, i.e. {1}2 = {2}2 , and
Σ(0) 6= ∅; (iv) e ∈ Σ(1) comes from a constant c ∈ Σ(0), i.e. e = [c]Σ(1) .

Proof. (i)⇒(ii): Indeed, for any Σ-module X the action α : Σ(X) = 1 → X
has to be surjective, and this is possible only if X ∼
                                                     = 1; (ii)⇔(ii’) is evident.
(ii’)⇒(i): All sets Σ(n) admit a Σ-structure, so we must have Σ(n) ∼    = 1, i.e.
Σ = 1. The implications (i)⇒(iii’)⇒(iii) are also evident. (iii)⇒(iii’): If we
have εX (x) = εX (y) for some x 6= y ∈ X, consider the map f : X → 2,
such that f (x) = 1 and f (z) = 2 otherwise; applying Σ(f ) to our equality
we get (iii’). (iii’)⇒(ii’): Since {1} and {2} act on any Σ-module X by
means of corresponding projections X 2 → X, we see that {1} = {2} implies
the equality of these projections, hence X consists of at most one element;
it cannot be empty since Σ(0) 6= ∅. Now (i)⇒(iv) is again trivial, and
(iv)⇒(ii’) follows from the fact that if e = [c]|Σ| for some constant c, then
for any Σ-module X the identity map idX = [e]X has to coincide with the
constant map which maps all elements of X into the value cX ∈ X of the
constant, hence X = {cX } is an one-element set.

   2) If u ∈ Uk is any generator of arity k, and t1 , . . . , tk ∈ Σ′ (n) for some

from requirement 2) by induction on the number of applications of rules 1)

property since ϕ∗ t = [t]Σ(n) ({ϕ(1)}n , . . . , {ϕ(m)}n).

4.4.4. The above definitions admit a useful generalization. Suppose that we
are given some algebraic monad homomorphism ρ : Σ0 → Σ, and some set
U ⊂ kΣk. Then we denote by Σ0 hUi the smallest algebraic submonad of
Σ that contains both ρ(Σ0 ) and U; we say that this is the submonad of Σ
generated over Σ0 by U. Clearly, Σ0 hUi = U ∪ kρ(Σ0 )k , and ρ : Σ0 → Σ
factorizes through Σ0 hUi ⊂ Σ. Of course, we write Σ0 hu1 , . . . , un i when U
is a finite set. This notion has similar properties to those considered above.
For example, if Σ is generated by U over Σ0 , a Σ-structure on any set X is
completely determined by its scalar restriction along ρ : Σ0 → Σ together
with the action of the generators [u]X : X r(u) → X, u ∈ U.
4.4.5. (Finite generation and pre-unarity.) Given an algebraic monad homo-
morphism ρ : Σ → Ξ, we say that Ξ is finitely generated over Σ if there is a
finite set U ⊂ kΞk, such that Ξ = ΣhUi. In this case we can choose a finite
subsystem of generators V0 ⊂ V from any other system V of generators of Ξ
over Σ: indeed, according to 4.4.3, any operation t ∈ kΞk can be expressed
in terms of a finite number of operations from ρ(Σ) and V ; let’sSdenote by
V0 (t) the finite set of involved operations from V , and put V0 := u∈U V0 (u).
     We say that Ξ is generated over Σ by operations of arity ≤ r, or that
F Σ → Ξ is of arity ≤ r if Ξ = ΣhV i for some subset V ⊂ kΞk≤r :=
ρ  :
   n≤r Ξ(n) ⊂ kΞk; clearly, in this case we can always take V = kΞk≤r . On
the other hand, if at the same time Ξ is finitely generated over Σ, we can
find a finite system of generators of arity ≤ r.
     Finally, we say that Ξ is pre-unary over Σ, or that Ξ is a pre-unary
extension of Σ, or that ρ : Σ → Ξ is a pre-unary homomorphism if Ξ = ΣhV i
for some set of unary operations V ⊂ Ξ(1). In this case we can again take
V = |Ξ| = Ξ(1); if Ξ is finitely generated over Σ, we can choose a finite set
of unary generators V ⊂ |Ξ|.
4.4.6. (Examples.) For example, Z = ΣZ is finitely generated (absolutely,
i.e. over F∅) by operations of arity ≤ 2: we can choose 0 ∈ ΣZ (0), [−] :=
−1 ∈ Z = ΣZ (1) and [+] := (1, 1) ∈ Z2 = ΣZ (2) as a system of generators
of Z. Any ring R is pre-unary over Z; we’ll show later they are actually
unary and that all unary extensions of Z come from associative rings. An
associative ring R is (absolutely) finitely generated iff it is finitely generated
over Z in the usual sense. Notice that Z and Z∞ are not pre-unary extensions
of F1 or F±1 , but are generated in arity ≤ 2. Another interesting example:
while R × R (= ΣR × ΣR ) is a unary extension of R = ΣR for any associative
ring R, algebraic monad Z∞ × Z∞ is not a pre-unary extension of Z∞ .
4.4.7. (Strict quotients and equivalence relations.) Recall that the coker-
nels and the fibered products are computed in Aalg componentwise, hence a
4.4. Algebraic submonads and strict quotients                                 171


morphism ρ : Σ → Ξ in Aalg ∼   = Sets N is a strict epimorphism iff all its compo-
nents ρn : Σ(n) → Ξ(n) are strict epimorphisms in Sets, i.e. surjective maps.
We see that the strict quotients of an algebraic endofunctor Σ are given by
“surjective” maps ρ : Σ → Ξ, i.e. natural transformations ρ, such that all
ρn : Σ(n) → Ξ(n) are surjective, or equivalently, such that kρk : kΣk → kΞk
is surjective. Such (algebraic) strict quotients are in one-to-one correspon-
dence with algebraic equivalence relations R ⊂ Σ × Σ, given by some systems
of equivalence relations R(n) ⊂ Σ(n) × Σ(n), compatible with all maps Σ(ϕ)
as usual (cf. 4.2.8); in this case Ξ = Σ/R and Ξ(n) = Σ(n)/R(n).
   Now suppose Σ has an algebraic monad structure. We say that its strict
quotient Σ/R (in Aalg ) is compatible with the monad structure of Σ, or
that equivalence relation R is compatible with the monad structure of Σ, if
Ξ = Σ/R admits a (necessarily unique) monad structure, for which Σ → Σ/R
becomes a monad homomorphism.
    Clearly, in this case Σ/R is a quotient of Σ modulo R in the category of
algebraic monads as well, so Σ → Σ/R is still a strict epimorphism in this
category. Conversely, an algebraic monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ is a
strict epimorphism iff ρ is surjective, i.e. is of the form just discussed, and
then Ξ ∼= Σ/R in both categories for some compatible algebraic equivalence
relation R on Σ. To see this we just consider the decomposition of any
algebraic monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ into a surjection ρ̃ : Σ → ρ(Σ)
and an embedding of a submonad i : ρ(Σ) → Ξ (cf. 4.4.1), and R := Σ ×Ξ Σ
is the kernel of both ρ and ρ̃, hence it is necessarily a compatible equivalence
relation, and ρ(Σ) ∼ = Σ/R both as a monad and as an algebraic endofunctor.
This also shows that ρ is a strict epimorphism iff ρ(Σ) = Ξ, i.e. iff ρ is
surjective.

4.4.10. (Finitely generated and unary equivalence relations.) We introduce
for compatible equivalence relations R on algebraic monads Σ and corre-
sponding strict quotients Ξ := Σ/R a terminology similar to that of 4.4.5.
For example, we say that R is finitely generated , or that Ξ is obtained from
Σ by imposing finitely many relations (or conditions, or equations), if R is
generated by some finite set of equations E. We say that R is generated in
arity ≤ k, or generated by equations or relations of arity ≤ k, or that Ξ is
obtained from F Σ by imposing relations in arity ≤ k, if R is generated by some
subset E ⊂ 0≤n≤k Σ(n) × Σ(n); if R is also finitely generated, then such a
set of equations can be chosen to be finite. Finally, we say that R is unary
if it is generated by some subset of Σ(1) × Σ(1).
4.5. (Free algebraic monads.) Now we would like to construct a very im-
portant class of algebraic monads, namely,Fthe free algebraic monads. For
this purpose we fix some “graded set” U = n≥0 Un , consider F the category of
couples (Σ, ϕ), where Σ is an algebraic monad and ϕ = n≥0 ϕn : U → kΣk
is a graded map of sets (i.e. essentially a collection of maps ϕn : Un → Σ(n)),
and define the free algebraic monad F∅hUi to be the initial object of this
category.
4.5.1. By definition, we must have a graded map j : U → kF∅hUik, such that
any graded map ϕ : U → Σ induces a uniquely determined monad homo-
morphism ρ : F∅hUi → Σ, for which ϕ = kρk ◦ j. In other words, monad ho-
momorphisms ρ : F∅hUi → Σ are in one-to-one correspondence with graded
maps ϕ : U → kΣk, i.e. with families of maps {ϕn : Un → Σ(n)}n≥0 . Apply-
ing this to Σ = END(X), we see that F∅hUi-Mod is equivalent to the cate-
gory of sets X, equipped with an arbitrary family of maps [u]X : X r(u) → X,
defined for each u ∈ U, where r : U → Z≥0 is the arity map (i.e. r(u) = n iff
u ∈ Un ).
4.5.2. Of course, we have to show the existence of free algebraic monads
F∅hUi. For this purpose we construct such a monad as a certain submonad
WU,r of the monad WU of words with constants from U (cf. 3.4.6). Recall
that WU (X) = W (U ⊔ X) consists of all words in alphabet U ⊔ X, usually
written in form u1 {x1 }{x2 }u2 {x3 } (we omit braces around constants, i.e.
letters from U). Informally speaking, F∅hUi = WU,r ⊂ WU is constructed as
the set of all valid expressions, constructed with the aid of operations from U
from the variables from X, and written in the prefix notation. For example, if
r(u1 ) = 1 and r(u2) = 2, then {x}, u1 {z} and u2 u1{x}u2 {y}{z} are elements
of WU,r ({x, y, z}). We present a more formal construction below, which has
the advantage of allowing a straightforward generalization to the topos case.
4.5.3. Let us denote by S the set of all maps ϕ from the set {−∞} ∪ Z≥0
174                       Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


into itself, which satisfy the following conditions: 1) ϕ(−∞) = −∞; 2)
ϕ(x) 6= −∞ for at least one x; 3) ϕ(x + 1) = ϕ(x) + 1 whenever ϕ(x) 6= −∞.
Clearly, this set is closed under composition and contains the identity map,
hence S is a monoid. We call S the syntax monoid. Its elements ϕ are
classified by pairs of integers r, s ≥ 0, where r is the smallest x ≥ 0 for
which ϕ(x) ≥ 0, and s = ϕ(r). We denote the corresponding element of S
by Gr,s . Notice that G0,s is the only element ϕ ∈ S, such that ϕ(0) = s. In
particular, G0,0 is the identity of S. We can compute Gr,s Gr′ ,s′ explicitly: if
r ≤ s′ , it is equal to Gr′ ,s+s′ −r , otherwise it equals Gr+r′−s′ ,s .
4.5.4. Now we define the verification maps dX : WU (X) = W (U ⊔ X) → S
as follows. Recall that WU (X) is a free monoid generated by U ⊔ X, so
dX is completely determined by its values on generators U ⊔ X, if we also
require it to be a monoid homomorphism. We put dX (u) := Gr(u),1 for any
u ∈ U, i.e. dX (u) = Gn,1 for u ∈ Un , and dX (x) := G0,1 for any x ∈ X; then
dX (z1 z2 . . . zs ) = dX (z1 )dX (z2 ) . . . dX (zs ) for any zi ∈ U ⊔ X.
    Put WU,r (X) := d−1       X (G0,1 ) ⊂ WU (X), i.e. this is the set of all words
t ∈ WU , such that dX (t) = G0,1 , or equivalently such that (dX (t))(0) = 1;
we call such words t valid expressions or terms with respect to the set of

hence (WU (f ))(WU,r (X)) ⊂ WU,r (Y ), so WU,r is indeed a subfunctor of WU ,
and even an algebraic subfunctor, since it commutes with filtered inductive

4.5.5. We have to check that WU,r ⊂ WU is indeed a submonad, i.e. that
if we replace in some term t some variables {xi } (or even {ti }) with some
other terms ti , then the resulting word t̃ is necessarily a term. This is clear,
since the expression for d(t̃) ∈ S is obtained from that of d(t) by replacing
d({xi }) with d(ti ); but d(ti ) = G0,1 = d({xi }) since all ti are terms, hence
d(t̃) = d(t) = G0,1 , hence t̃ is indeed a term.
4.5.6. (Structural induction.) Notice that we have some general rules for
constructing new terms:

  1) Any variable x ∈ X defines a one-letter term {x} ∈ WU,r (X).

  2) If u ∈ Un is an operation of arity n and t1 , . . . , tn are terms, then
     u t1 . . . tn is also a term.

Conversely, one checks in the usual way that any term t ∈ WU,r (X) is nec-
essarily non-empty, and that it is either of form 1), when the first letter of t
belongs to X, or of form 2) with uniquely determined u ∈ U and terms of
smaller length t1 , . . . , tn ∈ WU,r (X), when the first letter of t is an operation
4.5. Free algebraic monads                                                             175


from U; moreover, if t = u t1 . . . tn for some operation u ∈ U and some terms
ti , then necessarily n = r(u), and such a list of ti is unique.
      The fact that any term of WU,r (X) can be uniquely written either in form
1) or 2) allows us to prove statements by induction on length of a term t,
proving them first for case t = {x}, and then proving them for t = u t1 . . . tn ,
assuming them to be already proved for all ti ; this sort of induction is called
structural induction.

4.5.9. We have already seen that F∅hUi = WU,r is generated by U ∼    = j(U) ⊂
kWU,r k. This justifies the notation F∅hUi. Moreover, if we have any subset
U ⊂ kΣk, it induces a canonical homomorphism ρ : F∅hUi → Σ, and its
image is exactly the submonad Σ′ of Σ generated by U, which has been also
denoted before by F∅hUi. In particular, U generates Σ iff ρ : F∅hUi → Σ
is surjective, i.e. a strict epimorphism. If it is an isomorphism, we say that
U freely generates Σ, or that U is a system of free generators of Σ. For
example, the free algebraic monad F∅hUi is freely generated by j(U) ∼   = U.

4.5.10. In general we tend to use capital letters for the elements of U when
Σ is freely generated by U, to distinguish this situation from the case when
U is just any system of generators of Σ. Of course, we follow the conventions
of 4.4.2 when U is a finite set, thus writing for example F∅hN [0] , T [1] , U [2] i to
denote the free monad generated by one constant, one unary, and one binary
generator.

4.5.11. (Algebraic monads from algebraic systems.) Now suppose given
a graded set of operations U = ⊔n≥0 Un , or equivalently, a set U together
with an arity map r : U → Z≥0 , and any set of “equations” or “relations”
E ⊂ kF∅hUi × F∅hUik. Then we can construct the compatible algebraic
equivalence relation hEi on F∅hUi generated by E, and consider the quotient
Σ := F∅hUi/hEi. This quotient will be denoted F∅hU|Ei or even hU|Ei;
when U and E are finite we adopt the conventions of 4.4.2 and 4.4.9, thus
writing expressions like F∅h0[0] , ζ [1] | ζ0 = 0, ζ n {1} = {1}i (this is actually
F1n ) or F∅hU [2] | U{1}{2} = U{2}{1}, U{1}U{2}{3} = UU{1}{2}{3}i. We
usually prefer to replace the free variables like {1}, {2}, . . . , with some
(arbitrarily chosen) letters like x, y, . . . , and of course we use the infix
notation and parentheses when appropriate, thus writing the second of the
above examples in form F∅h+[2] | x + y = y + x, x + (y + z) = (x + y) + zi.
Another useful convention: we often write unary equations without naming
the free variable e = {1}1 explicitly, using the monoid structure of |Σ| = Σ(1)
instead. Thus we write ζ n = e instead of ζζ · · · ζ{1} = {1}, and ϕ2 = ϕ + e
instead of ϕϕ{1} = ϕ{1}+{1}; we can also write −2 = e instead of −(−x) =
x (here ζ, ϕ and − are unary, and + is binary). This is possible because of
the associativity relation t(u1 , . . . , uk ) · x = t(u1 (x), . . . , uk (x)), true for any
t ∈ Σ(k), ui ∈ |Σ|, and for any x from a Σ-module X, e.g. for e ∈ |Σ|.
    We call such couples (U, E) as above algebraic systems, and F∅hU|Ei is
the algebraic monad defined by algebraic system (U, E). If Σ ∼              = F∅hU|Ei, we
say that (U, E) is a presentation of algebraic monad Σ. Of course, in this case
the image of U in Σ generates Σ, and all relations from E are fulfulled in Σ,
and all other relations between operations of Σ can be deduced from E, so
we have indeed something very similar to the usual description of an algebra
in terms of a list of generators and relations.
    Clearly, algebraic monad homomorphisms ρ : F∅hU|Ei → Ξ are in one-
to-one correspondence with graded maps ϕ : U → kΞk, such that the image
under ρ of any equation from E is fulfilled in Ξ. Taking here Ξ = END(X)
for some set X, we see that F∅hU|Ei-Mod is exactly the category of sets X
with an algebraic structure of species defined by the algebraic system (U, E).
In this way the study of any algebraic structure is reduced to the study of
modules over some algebraic monad. Of course, different algebraic systems
4.5. Free algebraic monads                                                   177


can correspond to isomorphic algebraic monads.
4.5.12. Conversely, any algebraic monad Σ admits some presentation (U, E),
since one can always take for U any system of generators of Σ (e.g. U = kΣk),
and then take for E any system of generating equations for the equivalence
relation R on the free monad F∅hUi, defined by the canonical surjection
F∅hUi → Σ (we can always take E = R). In this sense the study of cate-
gories of sets equipped with some algebraic structures, i.e. universal algebra,
is nothing else than the study of categories of modules over algebraic mon-
ads. For example, we see immediately that the forgetful functors from any
of these categories into Sets is monadic. However, the category of algebraic
monads themselves is more convenient for different category-theoretic oper-
ations (e.g. computation of projective limits) than the category of algebraic
systems (since even the definition of a morphism of algebraic systems is quite
difficult to handle when written without monads).
4.5.13. The above constructions generalize to the case when we replace F∅
with an arbitrary algebraic monad Σ0 . For example, for any graded set we
can construct an algebraic monad Σ0 hUi over Σ0 (i.e. a homomorphism of
algebraic monads Σ0 → Σ0 hUi), which is an initial object in the category
of triples (Σ, ρ, ϕ), consisting of an (algebraic) monad Σ, a homomorphism
ρ : Σ0 → Σ, and a graded map ϕ : U → kΣk. Then the category of Σ0 hUi-
modules consists exactly of Σ0 -modules X together with arbitrarily chosen
maps [u]X : X r(u) → X for all u ∈ U. This actually shows that the canonical
map j : U → kΣ0 hUik is injective unless Σ0 = 1 or Σ0 ∼   = 1+ ⊂ 1.
    We have to show the existence of such free monads Σ0 hUi, but this is sim-
ple: take any presentation (U ′ , E ′ ) of Σ0 and put Σ0 hUi := F∅hU ′ ⊔ U|E ′ i.
Then everything follows from the universal properties of all constructions
involved, or from the observation that in this way we get a correct cate-
gory of Σ0 hUi-modules, using 3.3.21 to obtain monad homomorphisms from
functors between categories of modules.
4.5.14. Of course, we can construct a monad Σ0 hU|Ei = Σ0 hUi/hEi over an
algebraic monad Σ0 , starting from an arbitrary graded set U and an arbitrary
set of relations E ⊂ kΣ0 hUi2 k. It has properties similar to those considered
before for Σ0 = F∅, and we introduce similar terminology and notations.
For example, given a monad Σ over Σ0 , i.e. a homomorphism of algebraic
monads ρ : Σ0 → Σ, we say that (U, E) is a presentation of Σ over Σ0 if
Σ∼ = Σ0 hU|Ei. Of course, such a presentation always exists; it can found by
the same reasoning as in 4.5.12.
4.5.15. (Finite presentation and unarity.) Given any algebraic monad Σ
over Σ0 , or equivalently a homomorphism ρ : Σ0 → Σ, we say that Σ is
178                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


finitely presented over Σ0 , or that ρ is of finite presentation, if there exists
a presentation Σ ∼ = Σ0 hU|Ei with both U and E finite. We say that Σ is
generated in arity ≤ r with relations in arity ≤ s over Σ0 if we can find a
presentation with all operations in U of arity ≤ r and all relations in E of
arity ≤ s. If r ≤ s, we can replace U by any other system U ′ of generators
of arity ≤ r, since all the relations expressing operations from U in terms of
new generators from U ′ will be in arity ≤ r ≤ s.
    Finally, we say that Σ is unary over Σ0 , if U can be chosen inside |Σ| =
Σ(1), and E inside |Σ0 hUi2 |. If we have another set U ′ of unary generators
of such a Σ over Σ0 , then the induced equivalence relation on Σ0 hU ′ i will
be necessarily unary, since we can replace in all unary equations from E the
operations from U with their expressions in terms of unary operations from U ′
(and maybe some operations of other arities from Σ0 , but this doesn’t affect
anything).
4.5.16. (Examples.) We know that F1 = F∅h0[0] i, so it is finitely presented
over F∅, but of course not unary. Similarly, F±1 = F1 h−[1] | − (−x) = x,
−0 = 0i = F∅h0[0] , −[1] | − (−x) = x, −0 = 0i is finitely presented over
both F∅ and F1 , and unary over F1 (since we might replace the equation
for constants −0 = 0 with unary equation −0F1 (1) {1} = 0F1 (1) {1}), but not
over F∅. A more interesting example: Z is finitely presented over F∅, since
Z = F∅ 0[0] , −[1] , +[2] | x + y = y + x, x + (−x) = 0, x + 0 = x, (x + y) + z =
x + (y + z) . It is also finitely presented over F1 and F±1 , but not unary over
any of these monads.
4.5.17. (Non-commutative tensor products.) Presentations of algebraic mon-
ads can be used to show existence of “non-commutative tensor products”
Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 , i.e. pushouts of pairs of morphisms ρi : Σ → Σi in the category
of algebraic monads. Indeed, we have just to take any presentations Σi =
ΣhUi |Ei i of Σi , and put Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 := ΣhU1 , U2 |E1 , E2 i = ΣhU1 ⊔ U2 |E1 ⊔ E2 i.
Alternatively, we might take Σ1 hU2 |ρ1,∗ (E2 )i, where ρ1,∗ : kΣ0 hU2 i2 k →
kΣ1 hU2 i2 k is the canonical map induced by ρ1 . Again, the required uni-
versal property of Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 follows from the universal properties of monads
of form ΣhU|Ei. We see that Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 -Mod is isomorphic to the category
of sets X, equipped with both a Σ1 -structure and a Σ2 -structure, restrict-
ing to the same Σ-structures. Actually, since this is a category of algebraic
systems, we could use it to define Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 as the monad defined by the
forgetful functor from this category, applying 3.3.21 to construct monad
homomorphisms from functors between categories of modules.
4.5.18. (Finite presentation, unarity and pushouts.) Of course, the notions
of finite generation and presentation have the usual properties with respect to
pushouts, i.e. NC-tensor products. They are proved essentially in the usual
4.5. Free algebraic monads                                                   179


way, well-known for usual associative and especially commutative algebras,
so we just list them in the order they can be proved, omitting the proofs
themselves.
   • Finitely generated and finitely presented homomorphisms of algebraic
     monads are stable under pushouts.
   • A strict epimorphism Σ ։ Ξ is of finite presentation iff its kernel
     R = Σ ×Ξ Σ is finitely generated as an equivalence relation on Σ.
   • For any homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ the codiagonal (or multiplication)
     map ∇ : Ξ ⊠Σ Ξ → Ξ is a strict epimorphism (i.e. a surjection); if ρ is
     of finite type (i.e. if Ξ is finitely generated over Σ), then ∇ is of finite
     presentation.
   • In the situation Σ → Σ′ → Ξ, if Ξ is finitely presented over Σ, and Σ′
     is finitely generated over Σ, then Ξ is finitely presented over Σ′ .
   • In the same situation if Ξ is finitely generated over Σ, then it is finitely
     generated over Σ′ .
Moreover, we have similar statements about unary and pre-unary homomor-
phisms:
   • Pre-unary and unary homomorphisms are stable under pushouts.
   • A strict epimorphism is always pre-unary; it is unary iff its kernel is a
     unary equivalence relation (cf. 4.4.10).
   • If Ξ is pre-unary over Σ, then the codiagonal map ∇ : Ξ ⊠Σ Ξ → Ξ is
     unary.
   • In the situation Σ → Σ′ → Ξ, if Ξ is unary over Σ, and Σ′ is pre-unary
     over Σ, then Ξ is unary over Σ′ .
   • In the same situation, if Ξ is pre-unary over Σ, the same is true over Σ′ .
4.5.19. (Arbitrary inductive limits of algebraic monads.) Since F∅ is an
initial object of the category of algebraic monads, we see that we have co-
products Σ1 ⊠ Σ2 := Σ1 ⊠F∅ Σ2 and cokernels of pairs of morphisms in this
category as well. Since filtered inductive limits of algebraic monads also ex-
ist (they can be computed componentwise), we deduce first the existence
of infinite coproducts, and then the existence of arbitrary (small) inductive
limits of algebraic monads. So presentations and algebraic systems enable
us to compute inductive limits of algebraic monads, while projective limits
and submonads are better described in terms of algebraic monads themselves
(cf. 4.4).
180                        Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


4.5.20. (Algebraic monads as algebraic structures.) We have seen that the
forgetful functor Σ 7→ kΣk from the category of algebraic monads into the
category of Z≥0 -graded sets Sets /Z≥0 admits a left adjoint U 7→ F∅hUi, hence
we get a monad M over Sets /Z≥0 . Moreover, M : U 7→ kF∅hUik clearly
commutes with filtered inductive limits of graded sets, so it is something
like an algebraic monad over Sets /Z≥0 . On the other hand, we have seen
in 4.3.3 that the structure of an algebraic monad on a graded set kΣk is itself
algebraic, so we might expect the forgetful functor Σ → kΣk to be monadic,
i.e. the category of algebraic monads to be equivalent to (Sets /Z≥0 )M , and
this is indeed the case.
     In fact, we might fix some set S from the very beginning,       F       and consider

Σ : Sets /S → Sets /S are defined by the same requirement to commute with fil-

properties of categories of modules over algebraic monads, at the cost of
making everything less explicit.

4.5.21. (Graded algebraic monads.) One might expect that in the case when
S is a commutative group or at least a commutative monoid, algebraic mon-
ads over Sets /S are something like S-graded algebraic monads (over Sets).
However, this is usually not the case. For example, the degree translation
functors Tt : X 7→ X(t), X(t)s = Xs+t , are usually expected to transform
4.6. Modules over an algebraic monad                                               181


graded modules into graded modules, but in our situation we don’t obtain a
Σ-structure on X(t) from a Σ-structure on X unless we are given a compatible
family of morphisms Σ(s1 , . . . , sn )s → Σ(s1 + t, . . . , sn + t)s+t for each t ∈ S;
if S is a group, then all this morphisms clearly have to be isomorphisms.
    For example, we can construct some canonical maps θ : M(r1 , . . . , rm )n =
F∅ h1i[r1] , . . . , hmi[rm] (n) → M(r1 + 1, . . . , rm + 1)n+1 , t 7→ t̃ by structural
induction in t: we map {k}n into {k}n+1 , and t = hki t1 . . . trk into t̃ :=
hki t̃1 , . . . , t̃rk {n + 1}n+1 , i.e. we add an extra argument {n + 1} to each
operation hki. Of course, these maps θ are injective, but not bijective, so
M is not Z-graded; however, we can take the inductive limit along all these
maps, thus obtaining a Z-graded monad M+ and a monomorphism ρ : M →
M+ . Then the M+ -modules are something like algebraic monads, but they
admit degree translation in both directions, and we obtain functors ρ∗ and
ρ∗ between such things and usual algebraic monads.
4.6. (Modules over an algebraic monad.) Let’s fix an algebraic monad Σ
over C = Sets. We want to study some basic properties of the category
of Σ-modules Σ-Mod = C Σ , as well as the categories of (left, right or two-
sided) Σ-modules in Aalg . These latter categories of “algebraic modules”
over Σ actually behave themselves more like complexes of modules over an
ordinary ring, while Σ-Mod is a close counterpart of category of modules
over an ordinary (associative) ring. In particular, we are going to prove all
properties listed and used before for Σ = Z∞ in 2.14.12.
4.6.1. (Projective limits.) Of course, arbitrary projective limits lim Mα exist

4.6.2. (Submodules.) In particular, f : N → M is a monomorphism in
Σ-Mod iff it is a monomorphism in C = Sets, i.e. an injective map. Therefore,
the subobjects in Σ-Mod of a Σ-module M = (M, ηM ) are given by the
submodules N of M, i.e. those subsets N ⊂ M, which admit a (necessarily
unique) Σ-structure, compatible with that of M, i.e. such that the inclusion
i : N → M is a Σ-homomorphism (cf. 3.1.12). Clearly, N ⊂ M is a

submodule of M iff the image of Σ(N) → Σ(M) → M is contained in N; in
this case it has to be equal to N since ηM ◦ εM = idM .
    Since Σ(N) consists of expressions t({x1 }, . . . , {xn }) with t ∈ Σ(n) and
xi ∈ N (cf. 4.2.10), and ηM : Σ(M) → M maps such an expression into

for any n ≥ 0, t ∈ Σ(n), i.e. N has to be stable under all operations of Σ.

Actually, the set of all operations of Σ, under which N is stable, forms an
algebraic submonad of Σ for any subset N ⊂ M, hence it is sufficient to
check the stability of N under a set of generators of Σ.
4.6.3. (Module structure on sets of maps.) Given any set S and any Σ-

else than the product Σ-structure on HomSets (S, M) ∼ = M S ; the description
of projective limits of Σ-modules given in 4.6.1 shows that all operations
t ∈ Σ(n) act on maps S → M pointwise, i.e.

             for any t ∈ Σ(n), any maps fi : S → M and any s ∈ S. (4.6.3.1)

When N is another Σ-module, HomΣ (N, M) is a subset of Hom(N, M), but

4.6.5. (Free Σ-modules.) Recall that µS : Σ2 (S) → Σ(S) is a Σ-structure
on Σ(S), thus defining a Σ-module LΣ (S) = (Σ(S), µS ), which will be usu-
ally denoted by Σ(S). Moreover, we have seen in 3.3.8 that LΣ is a left
adjoint to the forgetful functor ΓΣ : Σ-Mod → Sets, i.e. there is a canoni-
cal bijection HomΣ (Σ(S), M) ∼  = HomSets (S, M) between Σ-homomorphisms
f : Σ(S) → M and arbitrary maps f ♭ : S → M. Of course, we have a
canonical embedding εS : S → Σ(S), and the above correspondence is given
by f ♭ = f ◦ εS . We say that a Σ-module M is free, if it is isomorphic to some
Σ(S) (cf. 3.3.9); the image of S in M is called a system of free generators
of M. Finally, we say that M is free of (finite) rank n if it is isomorphic
to Σ(n).
4.6.6. (Matrices.) In 3.3.13 and 3.3.16 we have constructed a certain cat-
egory CΣ = Sets Σ and a fully faithful functor QΣ : Sets Σ → Σ-Mod, which
transforms a set S into the corresponding free module (Σ(S), µS ). Clearly,
the essential image of QΣ consists of all free Σ-modules, and QΣ induces an
equivalence of categories Sets Σ and the category of free Σ-modules. Recall
that HomCΣ (S, T ) = HomC (S, Σ(T )) ∼ = HomΣ (Σ(S), Σ(T )).
    We also have the full subcategory NΣ ⊂ Sets Σ , given by the standard
finite sets and corresponding free modules; of course, the essential image
under QΣ of this category consists of all free Σ-modules of finite rank. We
see that HomNΣ (n, m) = HomSets (n, Σ(m)) = Σ(m)n ∼     = HomΣ (Σ(n), Σ(m)).
                                                     n
This is the reason why we put M(m, n; Σ) := Σ(m) and call this “the set of
m × n-matrices with entries in Σ” (cf. 4.3.1,b)). The composition of homo-
morphisms HomΣ (Σ(n), Σ(m)) × HomΣ (Σ(k), Σ(n)) → HomΣ (Σ(k), Σ(m))
defines the “matrix multiplication” M(m, n; Σ) × M(n, k; Σ) → M(m, k; Σ),
                                            (n)
which is essentially given by the maps µm : Σ(n) × Σ(m)n → Σ(m), up to
a permutation of arguments (cf. 4.3.3,b) and 3.3.13). We have the “iden-
tity matrices” In = ({1}n , . . . , {n}n ) ∈ M(n, n; Σ), which correspond to
idΣ(n) (cf. 4.3.3,c)). Moreover, if we put M(1, n; X) := X n for any set X
(“the set of rows over X”), then a Σ-action α on X corresponds to a fam-
ily of maps M(n, k; Σ) × M(1, n; X) → M(1, k; X), essentially given by the
α(n) : Σ(n) × X n → X (cf. 4.3.2,b)), which can be understood as some sort
of multiplication of a row by a matrix.
4.6.7. (Invertible matrices.) Of course, we have the groups of invertible ma-
trices GLn (Σ) = GL(n, Σ) ⊂ M(n, n; Σ), which correspond to AutΣ (Σ(n)) ⊂
EndΣ (Σ(n)). Clearly, a square matrix f = (f1 , f2 , . . . , fn ), fi ∈ Σ(n) is
invertible iff there is another square matrix g = (g1 , . . . , gn ), such that
fi (g1 , . . . , gn ) = {i}n and gi (f1 , . . . , fn ) = {i}n for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n.
4.6.8. (Initial object and ideals.) Notice that 0 := Σ(0) is the initial object
of Σ-Mod. If Σ is a monad without constants, Σ(0) is actually an empty
184                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


set, so we prefer to denote it by ∅ and call it the empty Σ-module; when
Σ is a monad with zero, then 0 = Σ(0) is a one-element set, hence a zero
(both initial and final) object of Σ-Mod. Any module M contains a smallest
submodule, equal to the image of Σ(0) → M; it is called the initial submodule
of M, or the empty or zero submodule of M, and it is denoted by ∅M , ∅ or
0 (depending on the situation). In any case it is a quotient of Σ(0); if Σ has
at most one constant, then it is always isomorphic to Σ(0).
    On the other hand, Σ(0) → Σ(1) is always injective (cf. 4.3.10), so the
set of all ideals (i.e. Σ-submodules of |Σ| = Σ(1)) has a smallest element
— the initial, empty or zero ideal, which is always isomorphic to the initial
object Σ(0).
4.6.9. (Submodule generated by a subset.) If M = (M, ηM ) is a Σ-module,
any subset S ⊂ M induces a Σ-homomorphism f : Σ(S) → M; according
to 4.6.4, the image hSi := f (Σ(S)) ⊂ M is a submodule of M, clearly con-
taining S. We claim that hSi is the smallest submodule of M containing S,
i.e. the submodule of M, generated by S. Indeed, if a submodule N ⊂ M con-
tains S, then hSi = f (Σ(S)) = ηM (Σ(S)) ⊂ ηM (Σ(N)) = N (here we have
identified Σ(S) and Σ(N) with their images in Σ(M)). Since Σ(S) consists
of all expressions t({z1 }, . . . , {zn }) with t ∈ Σ(n) and zi ∈ S (cf. 4.2.10),
we see that hSi consists of all elements of the form tM (z1 , . . . , zn ) ∈ M with
t ∈ Σ(n) and zi ∈ S. In particular, any element of hSi can be expressed in
terms of a finite subset S0 ⊂ S, i.e. belongs to some hS0 i with finite S0 ⊂ S.
4.6.10. (Finitely generated modules.) Of course, we say that S ⊂ M gener-
ates M if hSi = M, i.e. if f : Σ(S) → N is surjective. In this case we also
say that S is a system of generators of M. If M admits a finite system of
generators, i.e. if there exists a surjective homomorphism Σ(n) → M, then
we say that M is finitely generated or of finite type. In this case any system
T of generators of M contains a finite subsystem T0 ⊂ M of generators of M,
since the finite set S is contained in hT0 i for a finite T0 ⊂ T .
4.6.11. (Compatible equivalence relations and strict quotients.) We say that
an equivalence relation R ⊂ M ×M on the underlying set of a Σ-module M =
(M, ηM ) is compatible with its Σ-structure, or that the quotient set M/R is
compatible with the Σ-structure of M, if M/R admits a (necessarily unique)
Σ-structure, for which π : M → M/R becomes a homomorphism. Clearly, in
this case R = M ×M/R M is the kernel of π, and π : M → M/R is the cokernel
of R ⇒ M both in Sets and in Σ-Mod, hence M/R is a strict quotient of M.
Conversely, the kernel R = M ×N M of any Σ-homomorphism f : M → N is
always compatible with the Σ-structure on M, since the image f (M) ∼  = M/R
admits a Σ-structure (cf. 4.6.4), so if f is a strict epimorphism, we must
have N ∼ = M/R in Σ-Mod, hence in Sets as well because of the compatibility
4.6. Modules over an algebraic monad                                                    185


of R. We see that strict epimorphisms of Σ-Mod are precisely the surjective
Σ-homomorphisms, and that the strict quotients of M in Σ-Mod are exactly
the quotients M/R of M modulo compatible equivalence relations R; in
particular, strict quotients of M constitute a set. Observe that in 4.4.7 we
have obtained similar results for the category of algebraic monads; one might
expect this because of 4.5.20.

4.6.12. (EquivalenceTrelation generated by a set of equations.) Notice that
the intersection R = Rα of any family of compatible equivalence relations
on a Σ-module M isQagain a compatible equivalence relation, since R is
the kernel of M → α M/Rα . This means that for any set of equations
(or relations) E on M, i.e. for any subset E ⊂ M × M, we can find the
smallest compatible equivalence relation hEi containing E, simply by taking
the intersection of all such relations. We have an alternative description of
R = hEi: namely, x ≡R y iff this relation can be obtained after a finite
number of applications of rules 0) x ≡ y for any (x, y) ∈ E; 1) x ≡ x; 2)
x ≡ y implies y ≡ x; 3) x ≡ y and y ≡ z imply x ≡ z; 4) the substitution
rule (4.6.11.1).
    Since the kernel R′ of any Σ-homomorphism f : M → N is a compatible
equivalence relation, it contains E iff it contains hEi, i.e. iff f factorizes
through π : M → M/hEi. In other words, π is universal among all Σ-
homomorphisms f : M → N, such that f (x) = f (y) for any (x, y) ∈ E.
4.6.13. (Cokernels of pairs of morphisms.) Suppose M is a Σ-module, and
p, q : S ⇒ M are two maps of sets. Consider the category of all Σ-
homomorphisms f : M → N, such that f ◦ p = f ◦ q. We claim that it
has an initial object: indeed, f ◦ p = f ◦ q iff the kernel of f contains the set
E = (p, q)(S) of all pairs (p(s), q(s)), hence M → M/hEi has the required
universal property. This applies in particular when S is a Σ-module, and p
and q are Σ-homomorphisms; we see that cokernels of pairs of morphisms
exist in Σ-Mod.

4.6.15. (Elements of direct sums.) Notice that if S generates M, and T

case, i.e. the validity of the statement for Σ(n + m) = Σ(n) ⊕ Σ(m), for all

4.6.19. (Scalar extension.) Combining 4.6.17 and 3.3.19, we see that for
any homomorphism of algebraic monads ρ : Σ → Ξ the scalar restriction
functor ρ∗ : Ξ-Mod → Σ-Mod admits a left adjoint — the scalar extension
or base change functor ρ∗ : Σ-Mod → Ξ-Mod. We denote ρ∗ M also by
Ξ⊗Σ M; however, this notation still has to be justified. Of course, in situation
    ρ    σ
Σ → Ξ → Λ we have (σρ)∗ = ρ∗ σ ∗ and (σρ)∗ ∼     = σ∗ ρ∗ , so Λ ⊗Ξ (Ξ ⊗Σ M) can
be identified with Λ ⊗Σ M, i.e. we have some sort of “associativity”. Also
note that HomΞ (Ξ⊗Σ M, N) ∼    = HomΣ (M, ρ∗ N), and Ξ⊗Σ Σ(S) ∼      = Ξ(S). This
is actually a special case of the “associativity”, since Σ ⊗F∅ S = Σ(S) for any
set S. We see that ⊗F∅ corresponds to the left ⊗-action of Aalg ⊂ A on C,
denoted by ⊗ or ; in 3.2.5. Of course, ρ∗ commutes with arbitrary inductive
limits, and in particular it is right exact; for example, Ξ ⊗Σ (M ⊕ M ′ ) ∼      =
                       ′                                               ∗
(Ξ ⊗Σ M) ⊕ (Ξ ⊗Σ M ). Similarly, the scalar restriction functor ρ commutes
with arbitrary projective limits and in particular it is left exact, but in general
not (right) exact, contrary to what one might expect. In fact, we’ll show in
the next chapter that when Σ is commutative, ρ∗ is (right) exact iff ρ : Σ → Ξ
is unary, and in this case ρ∗ commutes with arbitrary inductive limits, and
even admits a right adjoint ρ! .
4.6.20. (Some counterexamples.) Up to now we have seen that Σ-Mod be-
haves in most respects like the category of (left) modules over an associative
ring. However, some properties do not extend to this case. Consider for
example the algebraic monad Σ, such that Σ-Mod is the category of commu-
tative rings. Then Z → Q is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism in
Σ-Mod, but not a strict epimorphism and not an isomorphism. Also note that
the direct sums lose most of their properties: for example, direct sum of two
monomorphisms need not be a monomorphism, since both Z → Q and idZ/2Z
are injective, but their coproduct in the category of commutative rings, i.e.
the tensor product over Z, is not injective. Direct sums don’t commute with
finite direct products as well, since this is not true even in F∅-Mod = Sets.
On the other hand, filtered inductive limits are still left exact, since both fil-
tered inductive limits and finite projective limits of Σ-modules are computed
in Sets.
4.6.21. (Finite presentation.) We say that a compatible equivalence rela-
188                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


tion R on a Σ-module M is finitely generated, if it is generated by a finite set
of equations E ⊂ M × M. Clearly, R is finitely generated iff π : M → M/R
is the universal coequalizer of a pair of maps p′ , q ′ : n ⇒ M (cf. 4.6.13),
or equivalently, if π : M → M/R is the cokernel of a pair of morphisms
p, q : Σ(n) ⇒ M.
    Given a module M, we say that a pair of sets (S, E), where S ⊂ M and
E ⊂ Σ(S) × Σ(S) is a presentation of M if f : Σ(S) → M is surjective and
the kernel of f is generated by E; then M ∼   = Σ(S)/hEi. Equivalently, we can
say that a presentation of M is a pair of maps of sets p′ , q ′ : E ⇒ Σ(S), or a
pair of homomorphisms p, q : Σ(E) ⇒ Σ(S), such that M is the cokernel in
Σ-Mod of this pair of maps.
    We say that M is of finite presentation, or finitely presented, if it ad-
mits a finite presentation (S, E), i.e. if it is a coequalizer of a pair of maps
of sets p′ , q ′ : m ⇒ Σ(n), or equivalently, if it is a cokernel of a pair
of homomorphisms p, q : Σ(m) ⇒ Σ(n) between free modules of finite
rank. Of course, such a pair of morphisms can be given by two matrices
P , Q ∈ Σ(n)m = M(n, m; Σ).
    Notice that the isomorphism classes of all finitely generated (resp. finitely
presented) modules over a fixed algebraic monad Σ constitute a set, since
any such module is isomorphic to a strict quotient of some Σ(n). In other
words, the category of finitely generated (resp. finitely presented) modules is
equivalent to a small category.
    These notions of finite presentation and of finite type have all the usual
properties, which can be shown essentially in the same way as over associative
rings. For example, the cokernel of a pair of homomorphisms from a finitely
generated module into a finitely presented module is itself finitely presented;
conversely, the kernel of a surjective homomorphism from a finitely generated
module to a finitely presented module is finitely generated as a compatible
equivalence relation. Another simple fact: any finite inductive limit (e.g.
finite sum) of finitely generated (resp. finitely presented) modules is itself
finitely generated (resp. finitely presented).
4.6.22. Any Σ-module is a filtered union of its finitely generated submod-
ules, hence it is a filtered inductive limit of a system of finitely generated
modules with injective transition morphisms. Moreover, any Σ-module M
is a filtered inductive limit of finitely presented Σ-modules. To show this we
consider the category D of finitely presented Σ-modules (or any its small
subcategory, equivalent to the whole of D), and observe that the category
D/M of homomorphisms N → M from finitely presented modules into M is
filtering, being stable under finite inductive limits, and limD/M N ∼= M.
                                                           −→
4.6.23. (Direct factors and projective modules.) Recall that N is a direct
4.6. Modules over an algebraic monad                                          189


factor of an object M of some category (e.g. Σ-Mod) if we have two mor-
phisms i : N → M and σ : M → N, such that σi = idN . Then i is a strict
monomorphism, and σ is a strict epimorphism, so N can be considered both
as a submodule and as a strict quotient of M. Moreover, in this situation
p := iσ ∈ EndΣ (M) is an idempotent, i.e. p2 = p, i : N → M is the kernel
of p, idM : M ⇒ M, and σ : M → N is the cokernel of the same pair. Con-
versely, if p2 = p is an idempotent in End(M), then we might reconstruct N
either as the kernel or as the cokernel of p and idM (if any of these exists in
the category under consideration; of course, they both exist in Σ-Mod), thus
obtaining a direct factor of M. In this way we obtain a bijection between
direct factors of M and idempotents in End(M). Notice that the property
of being a direct factor is preserved by all functors, and since direct factors
can be described both as kernels and as cokernels, we see that a direct factor
of a left (resp. right) exact functor is again left (resp. right) exact. Another
consequence: since N = Coker(p, idM : M ⇒ M), if M is finitely generated
(resp. finitely presented), the same is true for any its direct factor N.
    Let’s apply this to projective modules P , i.e. such Σ-modules P , for which
HomΣ (P, −) preserves strict epimorphisms, i.e. transforms surjective homo-
morphisms into surjective maps. Clearly, any free Σ-module Σ(S) is pro-
jective, since HomΣ (Σ(S), −) = HomSets (S, −) (if S is infinite, we need the
axiom of choice here), and any direct factor of a projective module is projec-
tive, so we see that direct factors of free modules are projective. Conversely,
if P is projective, and S is any system of generators of P , then the surjec-
tion σ : Σ(S) → P admits a section, hence P is a direct factor of a free
module Σ(S).

4.7. (Categories of algebraic modules.) Now we would like to prove some
basic properties of algebraic modules over an algebraic monad Σ, i.e. the (left
or right) Σ-modules in Aalg ⊂ A.
4.7.1. (Left Σ-modules.) Let’s begin with the case of a left algebraic Σ-
module F , i.e. an algebraic endofunctor F , together with a Σ-action α :
ΣF → F , such that α ◦ (ε ⋆ F ) = idF and α ◦ (Σ ⋆ α) = α ◦ (µ ⋆ F ) (cf. 3.3.5).
We know that F is given by a collection of sets {F (n)}n≥0 and of maps F (ϕ) :
F (m) → F (n) for each ϕ : m → n (cf. 4.2.1), and α : ΣF → F is given by
        (k)
maps αn : Σ(k)×F (n)k → F (n), subject to certain compatibility conditions

(cf. 4.2.3). Recall that we put [t]F (n) (x1 , . . . , xk ) = αn (t; x1 , . . . , xn ) for any
t ∈ Σ(k) and any xi ∈ F (n).

define a left Σ-module F . Actually, equality of natural transformations of
algebraic functors can be checked on standard finite sets, so we end up with
                 (k)

4.7.2. (Matrix interpretation.) Let F be an algebraic left Σ-module. Then
we put M(n, m; F ) := F (n)m , and interpret this as “the set of n×m-matrices
                                                       (k)
with entries in F ” as before. The action maps αn : Σ(k) × F (n)k →

4.7. Categories of algebraic modules                                        191


associativity and unit relations for α can be understood as associativity of
matrix multiplication M(m, s; Σ) × M(k, m; Σ) × M(n, k; F ) → M(n, s; F ),
and the requirement for Ik = ({1}, . . . , {k}) ∈ M(k, k; Σ) to act identically

4.7.3. (Monad of endomorphisms of an algebraic endofunctor.) If F is an
algebraic left Σ-module, any t ∈ Σ(k) induces a family of compatible maps
[t]F (n) : F (n)k → F (n), i.e. a natural transformation [t]F : F k → F . These
natural transformations have to satisfy a substitution property similar to
that discussed in 4.3.7, and conversely, once we have a family of such nat-
ural transformations, satisfying this property as well as the requirement for
[{s}n ]F : F k → F to coincide with the projection onto the k-th component,
we obtain a left Σ-structure on F .
     This enables us to repeat the reasoning of 4.3.8, and define for any alge-
braic endofunctor F its “absolute endomorphism ring” END(F ) by putting
(END(F ))(n) := HomA (F n , F ), with the multiplication of END(F ) given by
composition of natural transformations. Then END(F ) canonically acts on
F from the left, i.e. we have a natural transformation END(F ) ⊗ F → F ,
and giving a left Σ-module structure on F is equivalent to giving a homo-
morphism of algebraic monads ρ : Σ → END(F ); then the left Σ-structure
on F is recovered from the canonical END(F )-structure by means of scalar
restriction along ρ.
     Similarly to 4.3.8, we denote by ΣF the image of Σ in END(F ), and say
that F is a faithful algebraic left Σ-module if ρ : Σ → END(F ) is injective.
For example, Σ is always a faithful module over itself.

4.7.11. (Algebraic bimodules.) Now suppose we are given two algebraic

In the “cosimplicial set” setting this means that Λ controls the category
Λ-Mod where our “cosimplicial objects” take values, and Σ affects the “index

4.7.13. (Operations with algebraic bimodules.) Equivalence of categories
AΛalg,Σ ∼= Funct(NΣ , Λ-Mod) shows that arbitrary inductive and projective

functors from NΣ into Λ-Mod or Λ′ -Mod with scalar restriction or extension
functors between Λ-Mod and Λ′ -Mod. Therefore, we can fix Λ and study
what happens when we change Σ.
