4.7.15. (Tensor products of bimodules.) Given an algebraic (Ξ, Σ)-bimodule
M and an algebraic (Σ, Λ)-bimodule N, we would like to construct a new
algebraic (Ξ, Λ)-bimodule M ⊗Σ N, and similarly, for any Σ-module X we
would like to obtain a Ξ-module M ⊗Σ X. Interpreting all bimodules involved
as functors between certain categories, we see that all we have to do is to
extend in some way M : NΣ → Ξ-Mod to a functor M̃ : Σ-Mod → Ξ-Mod;
then we’ll put M ⊗Σ N := M̃ ◦ N and M ⊗Σ X := M̃ (X). Since the canonical
functor Q′Σ : NΣ → Σ-Mod is fully faithful (with the essential image equal to
the subcategory of free Σ-modules of finite rank), we have a natural choice of
M̃, given by the left Kan extension: M̃ := Q′Σ,! (M). This defines our tensor
product M ⊗Σ N.
    Clearly, M 7→ M̃ = Q′Σ,! M commutes with arbitrary inductive limits
in M, hence the same can be said about M ⊗Σ N. Another useful observation:
since Q′Σ,! = QΣ,! ◦ JΣ,! , we see that we might first extend M : NΣ → C Λ
to a functor M ′ : CΣ → C Λ by means of JΣ,! , and then extend this M ′
to M̃ : C Σ → C Λ . Since M = M ′ is the algebraic functor corresponding
to M (cf. 4.7.9), we see that for any set S we have M̃(Σ(S)) = M(S), i.e.
M ⊗Σ Σ(S) = M(S).
4.8. Addition. Hypoadditivity and hyperadditivity                                      197


    From this and similar observations we deduce that all scalar restrictions
and extensions with respect to right and left algebraic module structures can
be written in terms of this tensor product in the usual way. For example, if
ρ : Σ → Ξ is a homomorphism, N is any Σ-module, and P is any Ξ-module,
then the scalar extension ρ∗ N is isomorphic to Ξ⊗Σ N, where Ξ is considered
as a (Ξ, Σ)-bimodule, and the scalar restriction ρ∗ P can be identified with
Ξ ⊗Ξ P , where this time Ξ is considered as a (Σ, Ξ)-bimodule.
4.8. (Addition. Hypoadditivity and hyperadditivity.) We have seen that the
multiplication on the underlying set |Σ| of an algebraic monad Σ is always
defined, so in some sense multiplication is more fundamental than addition.
Now we would like to study different versions of addition and additivity of
algebraic monads.
    We fix some algebraic monad Σ and a constant 0 ∈ Σ(0). Since F1 =
F∅h0[0] i, we see that this is equivalent to fixing some ρ : F1 → Σ, i.e. Σ is
an algebraic monad over F1 . In most cases Σ is supposed to be an algebraic
monad with zero, i.e. with exactly one constant (cf. 4.3.12), so we have only
one way of choosing 0 ∈ Σ(0).
4.8.1. (Comparison maps.) Once the zero constant 0 ∈ Σ(0) is fixed, we can
define the comparison maps πn = πΣ,n : Σ(n) → Σ(1)n = |Σ|n as follows.
The k-th component πnk of πn is given by πnk : t 7→ t(0Σ(1) , . . . , {1}1 , . . . , 0Σ(1) )
for any t ∈ Σ(n), i.e. we substitute 0 = 0Σ(1) ∈ Σ(1) for all formal variables
{i}n in t = t({1}n , . . . , {n}n ), with the only exception of {k}n .
      If we are given a monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ, and if we choose the
constant ρ0 (0) ∈ Ξ(0) to construct πΞ,n , then we get πΞ,n ◦ ρn = |ρ|n ◦ πΣ,n ,
i.e. the comparison maps are functorial in Σ.
      Notice that the choice of 0 ∈ Σ(0) gives us a homomorphism 1 → Σ(0)
from the final to the initial Σ-module (when Σ is a monad with zero, this is
an isomorphism), so for any direct sum M ⊕ N in Σ-Mod we get canonical
homomorphisms M ⊕ N → M ⊕ 1 → M ⊕ Σ(0) ∼                 = M and M ⊕ N → N,
which define together a comparison homomorphism πM,N : M ⊕ N → M ×
N. Of course, this construction can be generalized to arbitrary finite and
even
L infinite   Q sums and products, thus defining comparison homomorphisms
    i Mi →     i Mi .
      For example, the comparison homomorphism for n copies of Σ(1) is a
homomorphism Σ(n) = Σ(1) ⊕ · · · ⊕ Σ(1) → Σ(1)n , which is exactly the
comparison map πn considered before.

Definition 4.8.2 (Addition and pseudoaddition.) We say that a binary
operation [+] ∈ Σ(2) is a pseudoaddition (with respect to constant 0 ∈ Σ(0),
when Σ has more than one constant), if π2 ([+]) = (e, e) ∈ Σ(1)2 , in other
198                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


words, if {1} + 0 = {1} = 0 + {1} in |Σ|, i.e. if x + 0 = x = 0 + x for any
Σ-module X and any x ∈ X. We say that [+] is the addition of Σ if [+] is
the only pseudoaddition of an algebraic monad with zero Σ. In this case we
say that Σ is a monad with addition.
Of course, any monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ transforms a pseudoaddi-
tion into a pseudoaddition, and if both Σ and Ξ are monads with addition,
then any ρ : Σ → Ξ respects this addition.
    We can define pseudoadditions of higher arities t ∈ Σ(n) by requiring
πn (t) = (e, e, . . . , e) ∈ Σ(1)n ; if we have a binary pseudoaddition [+], we can
construct pseudoadditions of all higher arities by taking (· · · (({1} + {2}) +
{3}) + · · · ) + {n}.
4.8.3. (Alternative definition of addition.) Arguably better definitions of
addition and zero are these: a zero is simply any central constant in an al-
gebraic monad Σ in the sense of 5.1.1 (such central constant is necessarily
unique, cf. 5.1.7), and an addition in an algebraic monad with zero Σ is
any central pseudoaddition (it is automatically the only pseudoaddition of Σ
by 5.1.8, i.e. is an addition in the sense of 4.8.2). The only reason why
we don’t adopt and study these stronger definitions here is that they require
the commutativity notions of the next Chapter, so we postpone a more de-
tailed study of the relationship between (pseudo)addition and commutativity
until 5.1.8.

Definition 4.8.4 We say that an algebraic monad Σ is hypoadditive (resp.
additive, hyperadditive) if all comparison maps πn : Σ(n) → Σ(1)n are injec-
tive (resp. bijective, surjective).
Clearly, Σ is additive iff it is both hypoadditive and hyperadditive. Notice
that additivity and hypoadditivity imply that π0 : Σ(0) → 1 is injective,
so Σ has at most one constant, so it has to be a monad with zero, and we
don’t need to specify our choice of 0 ∈ Σ(0) while discussing hypoadditivity
or additivity.
    Of course, there can be monads which are neither hypoadditive nor hy-
peradditive; some of them, like F∞ , will play important role in the sequel.
Notice that any submonad Σ′ of a hypoadditive monad Σ, containing the
zero of Σ, is automatically hypoadditive, and similarly, any strict quotient of
a hyperadditive monad is hyperadditive; this follows immediately from the
functoriality of comparison maps.
4.8.5. If Σ is additive, then it has an addition [+] = π2−1 (e, e), i.e. Σ is
then a monad with addition. Conversely, if Σ is hypoadditive and admits
a pseudoaddition [+], it is necessarily unique (since π2 is injective), so Σ
4.8. Addition. Hypoadditivity and hyperadditivity                                199


becomes a monad with addition; moreover, this addition is automatically
commutative, since π2 ({2} + {1}) = (e, e) = π2 ({1} + {2}), and associative,
since both ({1} + {2}) + {3} and {1} + ({2} + {3}) are mapped into (e, e, e)
by π3 . We see that {1} + {2} + · · · + {n} is the unique pseudoaddition of
arity n, and for any choice of unary operations λ1 , . . . , λn ∈ |Σ| we get an
n-ary operation λ1 {1} + · · ·+ λn {n} ∈ Σ(n), mapped into (λ1 , . . . , λn ) by πn ,
so a hypoadditive monad Σ with pseudoaddition [+] is in fact additive, and
in this case any n-ary operation t ∈ Σ(n) can be uniquely written in form
λ1 {1} + · · · + λn {n} with λi ∈ |Σ|.
    One shows, essentially in the same way, that an algebraic monad Σ is
hyperadditive iff it admits a pseudoaddition. Indeed, if Σ is hyperadditive, it
admits a pseudoaddition, π2 : Σ(2) → |Σ|2 being surjective; conversely, if [+]
is a pseudoaddition, then for any λ = (λ1 , . . . , λn ) ∈ |Σ|n we can construct
an n-ary operation (· · · ((λ1 {1} + λ2 {2}) + λ3 {3}) + · · · ) + λn {n}, mapped
into λ by πn .
4.8.6. (Additive monads and semirings.) This implies that an additive
monad Σ is generated (over F∅) by its only constant 0 ∈ Σ(0), the addi-
tion [+] ∈ Σ(2), and the set of its unary operations Σ(1). We have also
some relations: 0 + 0 = 0, the commutativity {1} + {2} = {2} + {1} and
the associativity ({1} + {2}) + {3} = {1} + ({2} + {3}) of the addition,
λ · 0 = 0 for any λ ∈ |Σ|; the addition [+]|Σ| : |Σ|2 → |Σ| gives a family
of relations of form λ = λ′ + λ′′ for all λ′ , λ′′ ∈ |Σ|, we have also a family
of relations λ = λ′ λ′′ coming from the monoid structure of |Σ|, and finally,
we have relations λ({1} + {2}) = λ{1} + λ{2} for any λ ∈ |Σ|, since both
sides are mapped by π2 into (λ, λ). Notice that this list of generators and
relations is a presentation of Σ, since these relations are sufficient to rewrite
any t ∈ Σ(n) in form λ1 {1} + · · · + λn {n}.
      Conversely, if we have any algebraic monad Σ generated by such a list
of generators and relations, i.e. if we are given some set |Σ| together with a
constant 0 ∈ |Σ| and two binary operations +, × : |Σ|2 → |Σ|, subject to a
family of relations which turn out to be exactly the axioms for a semiring
structure (0, +, ×) on |Σ|, then Σ is automatically additive, since the list
of relations given above allows us to write any t ∈ Σ(n) in form λ1 {1} +
· · · + λn {n} with λi ∈ |Σ|, and Σ-Mod is the category of |Σ|-modules, i.e.
additively written commutative monoids with a biadditive action of |Σ|.
      We see that additive algebraic monads Σ are in one-to-one correspondence
with semirings |Σ|.
4.8.7. (Additive monads and rings.) In particular, any monad R = ΣR ,
defined by a ring R, is additive. Conversely, if Σ is additive, and if we have
a unary operation [−] ∈ Σ(1), such that [−]2 = e (giving such a [−] is
200                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


equivalent to giving a homomorphism F±1 = F1 h−[1] |−2 = e, −0 = 0i → Σ),
and such that {1} + (−{1}) = 0 (this condition doesn’t follow from the
others), then R := |Σ| is a ring, and Σ ∼
                                        = ΣR .

phisms πM,N : M ⊕ N → M × N are isomorphisms; (iii’) All comparison

homomorphisms πΣ(n),Σ(1) : Σ(n + 1) ∼  = Σ(n) ⊕ Σ(1) → Σ(n) × Σ(1) are iso-
morphisms for all n ≥ 0; (v) It is possible to introduce on each HomΣ (M, N)
a commutative monoid structure (usually written in additive form), such
that all composition maps HomΣ (N, P ) × HomΣ (M, N) → HomΣ (M, P ) be-
come biadditive; (vi) Σ-Mod is equivalent to the category of modules over a
semiring R.

Proof. (i)⇔(ii) is true by definition, and (ii)⇔(iv) is shown by induction
in n ≥ 0, using πn+1 = (πn × idΣ(1) ) ◦ πΣ(n),Σ(1) . Now (iii)⇔(iii’) by an
easy induction in k, and (iii)⇒(iv) is evident. We know (i)⇒(vi) already.
Let’s show (vi)⇒(v). When we have (vi), we can define an addition on
each HomΣ (M, N) ∼    = HomR (M ′ , N ′ ) pointwise, where M ′ and N ′ are the
R-modules corresponding to M and N: (ϕ1 + ϕ2 )(x) := ϕ1 (x) + ϕ2 (x); it
is immediate that sum of two R-homomorphisms is an R-homomorphism
again, that this addition on HomR (M ′ , N ′ ) ∼= HomΣ (M, N) is commutative
and associative, with the zero map M ′ → 0 → N ′ for zero, and that the
composition maps are biadditive with respect to this addition, so we obtain
(vi)⇒(v).
     It remains to show (v)⇒(iii). First of all, (v) implies that the final object
1 of Σ-Mod is an initial object as well, i.e. Σ-Mod admits a zero object.
Indeed, for any M the set HomΣ (1, M) is a monoid under addition, so it
cannot be empty; on the other hand, EndΣ (1) consists of exactly one element
id1 , so it has to be the zero of this additive monoid, and biadditivity of
HomΣ (1, M) × EndΣ (1) → HomΣ (1, M) implies that for any ϕ : 1 → M we
have ϕ = ϕ ◦ id1 = ϕ ◦ 01 = 0, so HomΣ (1, M) = 0, 1 is the zero object of
Σ-Mod, and for any M and N the composite homomorphism M → 1 → N
is the zero of HomΣ (M, N). In particular, we have shown that Σ(0) ∼      = 1, i.e.
Σ is a monad with zero.
     Now let’s take any two Σ-modules M1 and M2 and prove that πM1 ,M2 :
M1 ⊕ M2 → M1 × M2 is an isomorphism. Let’s denote the projections
M1 × M2 → Mi by pi , and the composite maps Mi → M1 ⊕ M2 → M1 × M2
by λi . These maps are defined by pi λi = idMi , pi λ3−i = 0, and πM1 ,M2
4.8. Addition. Hypoadditivity and hyperadditivity                              201


is an isomorphism iff M1 × M2 together with these maps λi satisfies the
universal property for M1 ⊕ M2 . Notice that λ1 p1 + λ2 p2 = idM1 ×M2 , since
pi (λ1 p1 + λ2 p2 ) = (pi λi )pi + 0 · p3−i = pi . Now for any f : M1 × M2 → N
we have f = f (λ1 p1 + λ2 p2 ) = f1 p1 + f2 p2 , so f is completely determined by
its “components” fi := f λi : Mi → N. Conversely, given any fi : Mi → N,
we can define f : M1 × M2 → N by f := f1 p1 + f2 p2 , and then clearly
f λi = fi , so M1 × M2 is indeed the direct sum of M1 and M2 , and πM1 ,M2 is
an isomorphism.

    This proposition, together with some more similar reasoning, implies the
following corollary:

Corollary 4.8.9 The following conditions for an algebraic monad Σ are
equivalent: (i) Σ ∼
                  = ΣR for some associative ring R; (ii) Σ is additive, and
there is a unary operation [−] ∈ Σ(1), such that {1} + (−{1}) = 0; (iii)
Σ-Mod is equivalent to the category of modules over an associative ring R;
(iv) Σ-Mod is additive; (v) Σ-Mod is abelian.

4.8.10. (Hypoadditivity.) Some of the above conditions generalize to the hy-
poadditive case. For example, Σ is hypoadditive iff all comparison maps Σ(n+
1) ∼= Σ(n) ⊕ Σ(1) → Σ(n) × Σ(1) are injective. One might expect all com-
parison maps M ⊕ N → M × N to be injective for a hypoadditive Σ;
however, this is not true, as shown by the following example. Let’s take
Σ := Z∞ ; since Z∞ is a submonad of an additive monad R, containing
the zero constant of R, it is hypoadditive. Consider the equivalence rela-
tion R on Z∞ (2) = {λ{1} + µ{2} | |λ| + |µ| ≤ 1}, which identifies all
interior points of Z∞ (2), i.e. all elements with |λ| + |µ| < 1, with zero. It
is easy to see that R is compatible with the Z∞ -structure of Z∞ (2), so we
can compute the strict quotient M := Z∞ (2)/R, and let’s denote by π the
canonical projection Z∞ (2) → M. Clearly, M ⊕ M is a strict quotient of
Z∞ (4) = Z∞ (2) ⊕ Z∞ (2); let’s denote the projection by π ′ and its kernel by
R′ . It is easy to check that R′ identifies all interior points of Z∞ (4) together,
and doesn’t identify any boundary points. In particular, x := π ′ ( 12 {1}+ 21 {3})
and y := π ′ ( 21 {2} + 12 {4}) are distinct in M ⊕ M, but the comparison map
M ⊕ M → M × M maps both of them into (0, 0), so it cannot be injective.
4.8.11. (Importance of hypoadditivity.) Notice that any homomorphism
ρ : Σ → Ξ of hypoadditive monads is completely determined by the map
|ρ| = ρ1 : |Σ| → |Ξ|. Indeed, the functoriality of comparison maps πΞ,n ◦ ρn =
|ρ|n ◦πΣ,n shows that ρn is completely determined by |ρ| when πΞ,n is injective.
This can be seen as a manifestation of the following fact: most properties of
a hypoadditive monad Σ can be seen at the level of |Σ|. Conversely, there
202                       Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


are some non-hypoadditive monads, like Aff R ⊂ R (cf. 3.4.12,g)), which are
highly non-trivial (Aff R -Mod is the category of “affine spaces over R”), but
still have | Aff R | = 1, so almost all structure of Aff R is outside of | Aff R |.
This remark will have important consequences in our theory of spectra of
generalized rings, i.e. commutative algebraic monads.
4.8.12. (Examples.) a) Of course, all monads ΣR , defined by some associative
ring R, are additive, hence all their submonads Σ′ ⊂ R, containing the
zero constant of ΣR , are hypoadditive. This applies to almost all examples
from 3.4.12. In particular, Z∞ , Z̄∞ , Z(∞) , F1 and F±1 are hypoadditive.
However, Aff R ⊂ R, ∆ ⊂ R and F∅ ⊂ F1 are not hypoadditive, since all of
them are monads without constants.
     b) Consider the algebraic monad Σ, defined by the category of com-
mutative rings. Then Σ(n) ∼        = Z[T1 , . . . , Tn ]. If we fix some constant c ∈
Σ(0) = Z, say, c = 0, then the comparison maps look like π2 : F (X, Y ) 7→
(F (T, 0), F (0, T )). Clearly, all these maps are surjective, so Σ is hyperaddi-
tive. It admits a lot of different pseudoadditions like X + Y , X + Y + XY
or even X + Y + X 2 Y ; this shows that a pseudoaddition need not be com-
mutative or associative.
     c) We’ll see later that most non-commutative tensor products like Z ⊠F1
Z are hyperadditive. This means that we should not expect to read all
properties of such monads from Σ(1).
     d) All additive monads are generated in arity ≤ 2, and the same is true
for all hypoadditive monads listed in a). Actually, all hypoadditive monads
we encountered so far are generated in arity ≤ 2, and can be embedded into
some additive monads. However, it is not clear why this should be true in
general. Consider the hypoadditive submonad Z√∞ ⊂ R, such that Z√∞ (n)
     p of all formal linear combinations λ1 {1}+· · ·+λn {n} with λi ∈ R and
consists
P
   i    |λi | ≤ 1. It is easy to see that such linear combinations are stable under
substitution, so Z√∞ is indeed a hypoadditive submonad of R. However, it
still turns out to be generated in arity ≤ 2. Another example is given by
A3 := Z∞ ∩ Z[1/3] ⊂ Q, which is hypoadditive and generated over F±1 by
the ternary “averaging operation” s3 := (1/3){1} + (1/3){2} + (1/3){3}, but
can be shown not to be generated in arity ≤ 2.
4.8.13. Let’s construct now a monad with zero, which is neither hypoad-
ditive nor hyperadditive. Consider for this the equivalence relation R on
Z∞ (1) = [−1, 1], which identifies all interior points of Z∞ (1) with zero. We
know that R is compatible with the Z∞ -structure on Z∞ (1), so we obtain a
strict quotient Q = Z∞ /R ∼= {−1, 0, 1} of Z∞ (1), which has been denoted by
F∞ in 2.14.13. The Z∞ -structure on Q defines a homomorphism of algebraic
monads ρ : Z∞ → END(Q), cf. 4.3.8; let’s denote its image by F∞ . Clearly,
4.9. Algebraic monads over a topos                                              203


F∞ is a strict quotient of Z∞ , and two elements t, t′ ∈ Z∞ (n) have the same
image in F∞ (n) iff the induced maps [t]Q and [t′ ]Q : Qn → Q coincide. In
particular, all F∞ (n) ⊂ END(Q)(n) = HomSets (Qn , Q) are finite.PIt is easy

are identified with 0 in F∞ (n), and all remaining elements are identified iff

4.8.14. Notice that F∞ is generated by one constant 0[0] , one unary operation
−[1] , and one binary operation ∗[2] := +?{1}+?{2}. We have some relations
between them, like −0 = 0, 0 ∗ 0 = 0, −(−x) = x, x ∗ 0 = 0, x ∗ x = x,
x ∗ (−x) = 0, (−x) ∗ (−y) = −(x ∗ y), x ∗ y = y ∗ x and (x ∗ y) ∗ z = x ∗ (y ∗ z).
This system of generators and relations constitutes a presentation of F∞ ,
since it already enables us to represent any non-zero element of Σ(n), where
Σ is the generalized ring generated by these operations and relations, in form
±{i1 } ∗ · · · ∗ ±{ik } with some 1 ≤ i1 < · · · < ik ≤ n, hence the surjection
Σ ։ F∞ is an isomorphism, and F∞ = Σ is finitely presented (over F∅).
4.9. (Algebraic monads over a topos.) Most of the results of this chapter
generalize, when properly understood, to the topos case. We start with a
naı̈ve approach:
4.9.1. (Algebraic monads over an arbitrary category.) Recall that in 4.3.3
we have described an algebraic monad Σ over Sets as a sequence of sets
{Σ(n)}n≥0 , together with some maps Σ(ϕ) : Σ(m) → Σ(n) for each ϕ : m →
                                                         (k)
n, an element e ∈ Σ(1), and some multiplication maps µn : Σ(k) × Σ(n)k →
Σ(n), subject to some identities between certain maps, constructed from
these maps by means of finite products and composition. Of course, this
definition generalizes immediately to an arbitrary cartesian category C, if we
                                                                            (k)
require all Σ(n) to be objects of C instead of being sets, all Σ(ϕ) and µn
to be morphisms in C, and choose some e ∈ ΓC (Σ(1)) = HomC (eC , Σ(1)),
where eC is the final object of C. Given any such “algebraic monad” over C,
we can define its action on a object X of C as a collection of morphisms
α(k) : Σ(k) × X k → X, satisfying the conditions of 4.3.2; this defines the
category C Σ = Σ-Mod of Σ-modules in C. Furthermore, we can define left and
right algebraic modules, algebraic monad homomorphisms and so on simply
by copying their descriptions in terms of sets or sequences of sets and maps
204                      Chapter 4. Algebraic monads and algebraic systems


between products of these sets. Notice that “algebraic endofunctors over C”
are nothing else than functors N → C.
    In fact, we can generalize these definitions even to the case when involved
finite products are not representable in C, by identifying C with a full subcat-
egory of the category Cˆ = Funct(C 0 , Sets) of presheaves of sets. Notice that
giving an algebraic monad in Cˆ is equivalent to giving a presheaf of algebraic
monads over C, i.e. a functor from C 0 to the category of algebraic monads
over Sets.
4.9.2. (Application of left exact functors.) The advantage of this approach
is that we can apply any left exact functor h : C → C ′ to any of these
collections of data. For example, if Σ is an algebraic monad over C, then
hΣ, defined by (hΣ)(n) := hΣ(n), is an algebraic monad over C ′ , and for any
Σ-module X we obtain a canonical hΣ-structure on hX. In this way any
such left exact functor h : C → C ′ induces a functor h = hΣ : C Σ → C ′ hΣ
between corresponding categories of modules.
4.9.3. (Application to topoi.) This is especially useful for the left exact
functors that arise from morphisms of topoi f : E ′ → E, i.e. the pullback
functor f ∗ : E → E ′ and the direct image functor f∗ : E ′ → E. In this way f ∗

i.e. a sheaf of algebraic monads over S, as a presheaf of monads iΣ, and
conversely, to “sheafify” any presheaf of algebraic monads, obtaining a sheaf

4.9.4. (Monadicity of forgetful functors.) Given any algebraic monad Σ over
a topos E, we have a forgetful functor ΓΣ : E Σ → E (not to be confused with
the global sections functor ΓE : E → Sets). We claim that ΓΣ : E Σ → E is
monadic, i.e. it admits a left adjoint LΣ : E → E Σ , and induced functor E Σ →
E Σ̃ , where Σ̃ := ΓΣ LΣ is a monad over E, is an equivalence of categories. We
are going to show this in several steps.
4.9.5. First of all, let’s show the existence of a left adjoint LΣ̃ to ΓΣ . Any
topos E is equivalent to the category S̃ of presheaves on some site S, which
can be chosen to be small. Consider first the category of presheaves Ŝ ⊃ S̃.
The collection of sheaves Σ = {Σ(n)} is an “algebraic monad” over Ŝ as
well, so we have a forgetful functor ΓΣ̂ : SˆΣ → Ŝ. On the other hand, Σ
defines an algebraic monad Σ[S] over Sets for any object S ∈ Ob S, once we
apply to Σ the left exact functor F 7→ F (S). We see that a Σ-structure α
on a presheaf F ∈ Ob Ŝ, given by a collection of morphisms of presheaves
α(k) : Σ(k) × F k → F , is nothing else than a collection of Σ[S] -structures
on each set F (S), compatible with the “restriction maps” F (S) → F (S ′ )
and Σ[S] → Σ[S ′ ] for any morphism ϕ : S ′ → S in S. Now we can define a
left adjoint LΣ̂ to ΓΣ̂ by putting (LΣ̂ F )(S) := LΣ[S] (F (S)) for any presheaf
of sets F . Clearly, Σ̂ := ΓΣ̂ LΣ̂ is given by (Σ̂F )(S) := Σ[S] (F (S)). The
monadicity of ΓΣ̂ : SˆΣ → Ŝ follows now pointwise from the monadicity of
all ΓΣ[S] .
    We extend these results from Sˆ to S˜ in the usual way by putting LΣ̃ :=
aLΣ̂ i and Σ̃ := ΓΣ̃ LΣ̃ = aΣ̂i, where a : Ŝ → S̃ and i : S˜ → Sˆ denote
the “sheafification” and inclusion functors as usual; in the first expression a
actually denotes the extension aΣ : Ŝ iΣ → S̃ aiΣ = S˜Σ ; it exists because of the
left exactness of a and full faithfullness of i. Now the adjointness of LΣ̃ and ΓΣ̃
is immediate: HomS̃ Σ (LΣ̃ F, G) = HomS̃ Σ (aLΣ̂ iF, G) = HomŜ Σ (LΣ̂ iF, iG) =
HomŜ (iF, ΓΣ̂ iG) = HomŜ (iF, iΓΣ̃ G) = HomS̃ (F, ΓΣ̃ G).
    It remains to show the monadicity of ΓΣ̃ ; however, we postpone this proof
until 4.9.11.

4.9.9. (Algebraic inner endofunctors and filtered inner inductive limits.) In
the case E = Sets we had an equivalent description of the category of alge-
braic endofunctors Endof alg (Sets) ⊂ Endof (Sets): it was the full subcate-
gory, consisting of those endofunctors, which commute with filtered inductive
limits. In the topos case all algebraic endofunctors are easily seen to commute
with arbitrary filtered inductive limits; however, this property is insufficient
to be an algebraic endofunctor over a topos E, since in general an arbitrary
object X of E cannot be represented as a filtered inductive limit of finite
constant objects nE .
     It is possible to save the situation by considering the category of algebraic
inner endofunctors InnEndof alg (E) ⊂ InnEndof (E): these inner endofunctors
can be characterized by their property to commute with filtered inner (or lo-
cal ) inductive limits, i.e. inductive limits along filtered inner index categories
I in E (recall that this means that I has an object of objects I0 and an object
of morphisms I1 instead of the sets of objects and morphisms, together with
some morphisms i : I0 → I1 , s, t : I1 → I0 , m : I1 ×t,s I1 → I1 , subject
to certain conditions which need not be written here). For example, any
X ∈ Ob E can be written as an F      inner filtered inductive
                                                           F limit along  a certain
                                             n                       n
inner category IX , with IX,0 = n≥0 X and IX,1 = ϕ:m→n X . If we write
down explicitly the requirement for an inner endofunctor Σ′ = (Σ′ , α′ ) to
commute with this particular inner inductive limit, we obtain Σ′ ∼      = J˜E JE∗ Σ′ ,
and one can check that any functor of form J˜E Σ commutes with filtered inner
inductive limits, essentially in the same way as in 4.1.4.
     Such an approach has its advantages. For example, it shows immediately
that the composite of two algebraic inner endofunctors is again algebraic.
However, we don’t want to follow this path, since it would require to explain
4.9. Algebraic monads over a topos                                         209

the above statement about composites of algebraic endofunctors directly:

4.9.11. Once we know that InnEndof alg (E) ⊂ InnEndof (E) is stable under
composition, arbitrary inductive, and finite projective limits, and that mor-
phisms Σ̃(X) → Y admit a description similar to that given in 4.2.2 for any
algebraic endofunctor Σ on E and any two objects X and Y of E, we can ex-
tend all statements from 4.2 and 4.3 to the topos case. In particular, we see
that an algebraic inner monad Σ over E, i.e. an algebra in InnEndof alg (E),
can be described in the same way as in 4.3.1 and 4.3.3, so we obtain the
same notion of an algebraic monad over E as in 4.9.1, and the same notions
of modules over such an algebraic monad. This proves the monadicity of
ΓΣ : E Σ → E, claimed in 4.9.4.
4.9.12. Most statements and definitions given before in this chapter for
algebraic monads over Sets generalize directly to the topos case, at least
those of them which are intuitionistic, i.e. don’t involve the logical law of
excluded middle and the axiom of choice. However, we have to interpret these
statements in the so-called Kripke–Joyal semantics, where existence is always
understood as local existence, i.e. existence after restricting everything to a
suitable cover. Consider for example 4.2.10, which tells us that any element
ξ of Σ(X) can be written in form t({x1 }, . . . , {xn }) for some n ≥ 0, t ∈ Σ(n)
and xi ∈ X. In the topos case we can denote by t({x1 }, . . . , {xn }) the image
of (t, x1 , . . . , xn ) ∈ Σ(n)(S) × X(S)n in Σ(X)(S), for any S ∈ Ob E (or in
Ob S, when E = S)        ˜ and any t ∈ Σ(n)(S) and xi ∈ X(S). However, the above
statement has to be interpreted as follows: for any ξ ∈ (Σ(X))(S) we can find
a cover {ϕα : Sα → S}, some integers nα ≥ 0, elements tα ∈ (Σ(nα ))(Sα )
and xα,i ∈ X(Sα ), 1 ≤ i ≤ nα , such that ϕ∗α ξ = tα ({xα,1 }, . . . , {xα,nα }) in
(Σ(X))(Sα ) for any α.
4.9.13. However, some statements over Sets have been proved before with
the aid of the axiom of choice. We need to find other proofs of such state-
ments, or to extend these results over Sets first to the categories of presheaves
Ŝ, applying already known results componentwise, and then extend these
statements to arbitrary E = S̃ by sheafification.
    For example, we have seen that algebraic monads (even endofunctors)
over Sets preserve epimorphisms and monomorphisms (cf. 4.3.10 and 4.6.4);
however, our proofs used the axiom of choice, so they cannot be generalized
to the topos case directly. Nevertheless, we claim that any algebraic endo-
functor Σ over a topos E preserves monomorphisms and epimorphisms.
    The statement about monomorphisms is easily deduced from the known
case by sheafification, since both i : S̃ → Sˆ and a : Sˆ → S̃ are left exact, and
4.9. Algebraic monads over a topos                                             211


Σ̃ = aΣ̂i. The statement about epimorphisms cannot be easily shown in this
way, since i doesn’t respect epimorphisms; however, it can be deduced from
the fact that any finite product of epimorphisms in a topos is an epimorphism
           F for any epimorphism f : X → Y the induced morphism H0 (f ) :

any morphism of Σ-modules in E admits a Σ-structure. Most statements
after 4.6.4 can be deduced from this fact in the same way as before. For
example, arbitrary projective and inductive limits exist in E Σ .
4.9.14. Some statements that involve the law of excluded middle also need
to be reconsidered. For example, an algebraic monad Σ over a topos E is
said to be a monad without constants (resp. with zero, with at most one
constant) iff Σ(0) is isomorphic to the initial object ∅E of E (resp. iff the
canonical morphism Σ(0) → eE is an isomorphism, or a monomorphism for
the last case). We see that Σ(0) can be a non-trivial open object of E (i.e.
a subobject of the final object eE , different from both ∅E and eE ); in this
case Σ is a monad with at most one constant, but neither a monad without
constants nor a monad with zero.

4.9.16. (Open and closed subtopoi.) Let E be a topos, Σ an algebraic monad
over E, U ⊂ eE an open object of E, U the open subtopos of E defined by U,
and F the complementary closed subtopos of E (cf. SGA 4 IV 9.3). Let’s
denote the corresponding embeddings by j : U → E and i : F → E; recall
that U ∼  = E/U , and i∗ : F → E is a fully faithful functor, the essential image
of which consists of all X ∈ Ob E, such that j ∗ X = X|U is isomorphic to
the final object of U = E/U . We obtain a left exact gluing functor ρ :=
i∗ j∗ : U → F , and we know that E is canonically equivalent to the “comma
category” (F , U, ρ), the objects of which are triples (A, B, f ), with A ∈ Ob F ,
B ∈ Ob U and f : A → ρB a morphism in F . Recall that this equivalence
Φ : E → (F , U, ρ) transforms X ∈ Ob E into (i∗ X, j ∗ X, h(X) : i∗ X → ρj ∗ X),
where h(X) is obtained by applying i∗ to adjointness morphism X → j∗ j ∗ X
(cf. SGA 4 IV 9.5). All functors j! , j ∗ , j∗ , i∗ and i∗ admit descriptions in
terms of this equivalence: j! : B 7→ (∅F , B, ∅F → ρB), j ∗ : (A, B, f ) 7→ B,
j∗ : B 7→ (ρB, B, idρB ), i∗ : (A, B, f ) 7→ A, and i∗ : A 7→ (A, eU , A → ρeU =
eF ).
      Since all functors i∗ , j ∗ and ρ are left exact, we can extend the above
results to the category of modules over an algebraic monad Σ; we see that E Σ
                                            ∗     ∗

i∗ i! X → X is a monomorphism, and that i! commutes with scalar restriction,
essentially in the same way as in SGA 4 IV 14.5.
4.9.17. (Sheaves of homomorphisms.) Let Σ be an algebraic monad over a
topos E, and M, N be two Σ-modules. Then we can construct the “sheaf
of local homomorphisms” HomΣ (M, N) ⊂ HomE (M, N) in two different
ways. On one hand, we can repeat the reasoning of SGA 4 IV 12 and define
HomΣ (M, N) by requiring HomE (S, HomΣ (M, N)) ∼        = HomΣ|S (M|S , N|S );
this notion turns out to have almost all properties of SGA 4 IV 12, which
can be proved essentially in the same way. On the other hand, Σ admits a
canonical plain inner structure, so we might use 3.5.18 instead. Both these
definitions yield the same subobject of HomE (M, N). We don’t give a de-
tailed proof since we are not going to use this fact anyway; it can be shown,
for example, by reduction to the case E = S.ˆ
4.9. Algebraic monads over a topos                                        213


4.9.18. (Small families of generators.) Notice that E Σ admits a small family
of generators. Indeed, any topos admits a small family of generators, so let
G ⊂ Ob E be such a family for E. Then the corresponding free Σ-modules
{Σ(S)}S∈G are easily seen to constitute a small family of generators of E Σ .
4.9.19. (Algebraic bimodules.) Of course, we can consider algebraic bimod-
ules (and left or right modules) over E, i.e. bimodules in InnEndof alg (E).
Most statements made in 4.7 generalize directly to the topos case. For
example, we have matrix interpretations for all these notions, if we put
M(m, n; Σ) := Σ(m)n as before; of course, now these are objects of E, not just
sets. However, (Σ, Λ)-bimodules cannot be interpreted as functors NΛ → E Σ
when Λ is non-constant, at least if we don’t want to replace NΛ with an inner
category in E.
4.9.20. (Local END’s.) For any X ∈ Ob E we can construct an alge-
braic monad END(X) over E, such that giving an action of some alge-
braic monad Σ on X is equivalent to giving a monad homomorphism ρ :
Σ → END(X). Indeed, we can put (END(X))(n) := HomE (X n , X), sim-
ilarly to 4.3.8. We can also consider the algebraic monad END(X) :=
ΓE (END(X)) over Sets; then (END(X))(n) = HomE (X n , X), and monad
homomorphisms Σ → END(X) are in one-to-one correspondence with ac-
tions of constant algebraic monads Σ on X. These notions generalize to the
case of algebraic endofunctor X over E, similarly to 4.7.3.

Chapter 5. Commutative monads                                                     215


5     Commutative monads
This chapter is dedicated to the notion of commutativity of algebraic monads,
and to the properties of generalized rings, i.e. commutative algebraic mon-
ads, and categories of modules over them. We’ll see that they have indeed
properties very similar to classical commutative rings, so our terminology is
justified. Moreover, sometimes we even consider arbitrary algebraic monads
as (non-commutative) generalized rings; however, they can have properties
very different from those of classical (non-commutative) rings.
    We do some basic linear algebra over generalized rings; we construct a
theory of exterior powers and determinants, at least for alternating gener-
alized rings, and define and compute some K-groups. We are also able to
construct a reasonable theory of traces, notwithstanding the absence of addi-
tion. The properties of these theories are illustrated by a series of important
examples.
5.0. Notation. Given an algebraic monad homomorphism ρ : Σ → Ξ, we
denote by a ρ∗ : Σ-Mod → Ξ-Mod or even by ρ∗ the base change functor
(already denoted by ρ∗ in 4.6.19), and by a ρ∗ : Ξ-Mod → Σ-Mod or even
ρ∗ the scalar restriction functor (denoted before by ρ∗ ). This change of
notation may seem slightly confusing, since a ρ∗ is covariant in ρ, and a ρ∗ is
contravariant; the idea, of course, is that we think of pullback and direct
image functors for the corresponding morphism of (generalized) schemes a ρ :
Spec Ξ → Spec Σ. This new notation has its advantages: for example, a ρ∗ is
now a left adjoint to a ρ∗ .
    Unless otherwise specified, all monads are supposed to be algebraic. We
denote them by letters like Σ, Ξ, . . . , and also by A, B, C, . . . , especially
when they are commutative; thus our notation reminds of classical rings.
We also denote free A-module LA (S) by A(S) or A(S) ; when S = n =
{1, 2, . . . , n}, we write A(n) or A(n) , but never An ; the latter notation actually
means the product of n copies of A = A(1) , which is usually not isomorphic
to A(n) , at least for a non-additive A.
    We preserve the notation |A| for A(1), considered both as a monoid (with
identity e ∈F|A|), and an A-module. We denote by kAk the (graded) set of
operations n≥0 A(n).
5.1. (Definition of commutativity.)

Definition 5.1.1 Let Σ be an algebraic monad.

    a) We say that two operations t ∈ Σ(n) and t′ ∈ Σ(m) commute on
       a Σ-module X if for any collection of elements {xij }, 1 ≤ i ≤ n,
216                                              Chapter 5. Commutative monads


      1 ≤ j ≤ m of X we have t(x1. , . . . , xn. ) = t′ (x.1 , . . . , x.m ), where we put
      xi. = t′ (xi1 , . . . , xim ) and x.j = t(x1j , . . . , xnj ).

  b) We say that two operations t, t′ ∈ kΣk commute if they commute on
     any Σ-module X; clearly, it suffices to require them to commute on the
     set of free generators of Σ(n × m) ∼= Σ(mn).

  c) For any subset S ⊂ kΣk we denote by S ′ ⊂ kΣk the commutant of Σ,
     i.e. the set of all operations of Σ, commuting with all operations from S.
     We’ll show in a moment that S ′ is the underlying set of a certain
     submonad of Σ, which will be also denoted by S ′ . Finally, if Λ ⊂ Σ
     is a submonad, we denote by Λ′ the commutant of its underlying set
     kΛk ⊂ kΣk.

  d) We say that t ∈ kΣk is a central operation of Σ if it commutes with all
     operations of Σ. All such operations form a submonad Σ′ ⊂ Σ, called
     the center of Σ.

  e) We say that Σ is commutative, if any two its operations commute, i.e.
     if Σ coincides with its center Σ′ .

5.1.2. Let’s show that the commutant
                                T            S ′ of any subset S ⊂ kΣk is indeed a
submonad of Σ. Since S ′ = t∈S {t}′ , we see that it is sufficient to show this
for a one-element set S = {t}, with t ∈ Σ(n). Given any two Σ-modules M
and N, and any map of sets f : M → N, we say that an operation t′ ∈ Σ(m)
commutes with f , if [t′ ]N ◦ f m = f ◦ [t′ ]M : M m → N. It follows immediately
from the definitions that t′ commutes with t iff it commutes with all maps
[t]Σ(k) : Σ(k)n → Σ(k), k ≥ 0; actually, k = mn would suffice for t′ ∈ Σ(m).
Thus we are reduced to proving the following statement:
5.1.3. The operations of Σ, commuting with a given map f : M → N between
two Σ-modules M and N, constitute a submonad Σ0 ⊂ Σ. The map f is a Σ0 -
homomorphism, and Σ0 is the largest submonad of Σ with this property. First
of all, given any set X and any subset Y ⊂ X, we can consider the submonad
(Y : Y ) of END(X), given by (Y : Y )(n) = {f : X n → X | f (Y n ) ⊂ Y }
(cf. 4.3.8), i.e. (Y : Y ) consists of those maps f : X n → X, which stabilize Y .
It is immediate that such maps are stable under composition, hence (Y : Y )
is indeed a submonad of END(X).
    Now suppose that X is a Σ-module, i.e. we have a monad homomorphism
ρ : Σ → END(X). Consider the pullback Σ0 := ρ−1 (Y : Y ); clearly, this is
the submonad Σ0 of Σ, consisting of all operations t ∈ Σ(n) that stabilize Y
(i.e. such that [t]X (Y n ) ⊂ Y ), hence Σ0 is the largest submonad of Σ, such
that Y is a Σ0 -submodule of X.
5.1. Definition of commutativity                                                217


   Finally, let’s consider any map f : M → N of Σ-modules as above. Its
graph Γf ⊂ M × N is a subset of the Σ-module M × N, and we see that an
operation t ∈ Σ(n) commutes with f , i.e. f ◦ [t]M = [t]N ◦ f n , iff t stabilizes
the graph Γf ⊂ M × N, i.e. [t]M ×N (Γnf ) ⊂ Γf , and we have just seen that all
such operations constitute a submonad Σ0 ⊂ Σ.
5.1.4. Notice that our notion of commutant of sets S ⊂ kΣk enjoys the usual
properties, e.g. S ⊂ T implies T ′ ⊂ S ′ , and we have S ⊂ S ′′ and S ′ = S ′′′ for
any S. We have seen that S ′ is always a submonad of Σ. This implies that for
any subset S ⊂ kΣk its commutant S ′ coincides with the commutant hSi′ of
the algebraic submonad hSi ⊂ Σ generated by S (cf. 4.4.2). Indeed, S ⊂ hSi
(we deliberately confuse submonads of Σ with their underlying sets), hence
hSi′ ⊂ S ′ . Conversely, S ⊂ S ′′ implies hSi ⊂ S ′′ , S ′′ being a submonad,
hence S ′ = S ′′′ ⊂ hSi′ . In particular, if S is a set of generators of Σ, then S ′
coincides with the center of Σ. Therefore, Σ is commutative iff S ′ = Σ = hSi,
i.e. iff S ⊂ S ′ , i.e. iff any two operations from S commute.
5.1.5. Given any two operations t ∈ Σ(n), t′ ∈ Σ(m), we denote by [t, t′ ] ∈
Σ(mn)2 the commutator of t and t′ , i.e. the relation between the free gen-
erators of Σ(m × n) ∼  = Σ(mn), described in 5.1.1. In this way [t, t′ ] holds
in Σ iff t and t′ commute. Notice that the actual element [t, t′ ] ∈ Σ(mn)2
depends on the choice of bijection m × n ∼  = mn, and on the order of t and t′ ,
but the compatible equivalence relation h[t, t′ ]i generated by [t, t′ ] (cf. 4.4.9)
doesn’t depend on these choices, since Σ/h[t, t′ ]i is the largest strict quotient
of Σ, such that the images of t and t′ commute in this quotient. Similarly,
for any two subsets S, T ⊂ kΣk we denote by [S, T ] the set of all relations
[s, t] for s ∈ S, t ∈ T ; sometimes we denote the corresponding compatible
equivalence relation h[S, T ]i on Σ simply by [S, T ], especially when we form
quotients like Σ/[S, T ]. Clearly, this is the largest strict quotient of Σ, on
which all operations from the image of S commute with those from the image
of T . In particular, Σab := Σ/[Σ, Σ] is the largest commutative quotient of Σ,
i.e. Σ 7→ Σab is the left adjoint to the inclusion functor from the category
of commutative algebraic monads into the category of all algebraic monads.
Notice that for any two subsets S, T ⊂ kΣk we have [hSi, hT i] = h[S, T ]i;
this is shown by the same reasoning as in 5.1.4.
5.1.6. (Category of generalized rings.) We denote by GenR the category of
generalized rings, i.e. the full subcategory of the category Monads alg (Sets)
of algebraic monads, consisting of commutative algebraic monads. Clearly,
GenR is stable under subobjects, strict quotients, and arbitrary projec-
tive limits of Monads alg (Sets); in particular, arbitrary projective limits exist
in GenR. As to inductive limits, their existence in GenR follows from their
existence in Monads alg (Sets) (cf. 4.5.19), and from the existence of a left
218                                          Chapter 5. Commutative monads


adjoint Σ → Σab to the inclusion functor GenR → Monads alg (Sets). Indeed,
we have just to compute limα Σα in the category of algebraic monads, and
                              −→
then take (limα Σα )ab . For example, pushouts exist in GenR: given two ho-
              −→
momorphisms of generalized rings ρi : Σ → Σi , we construct their pushout,
i.e. the “tensor product of Σ-algebras” Σ1 ⊗Σ Σ2 , by computing first the non-
commutative tensor product Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 (cf. 4.5.17), and then taking quotient
by the compatible equivalence relation, generated by all commutators be-
tween pairs of operations of this non-commutative tensor product. Since
Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 is generated by λ1 (Σ1 ) ∪ λ2 (Σ2 ), where λi : Σi → Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 is the
canonical “inclusion” homomorphism, we see that this equivalence relation is
generated by commutators between elements of this sort. Now the elements
of λ1 (Σ1 ) will automatically commute between themselves in Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 , and
similarly for λ2 (Σ2 ); hence Σ1 ⊗Σ Σ2 = (Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 )/[λ1 (Σ1 ), λ2 (Σ2 )].
     Notice that GenR is stable under filtered inductive limits of the cate-

5.1.7. (Commutativity for operations of lower arities.) Now we want to study
the shape of commutativity relations between operations of lower arities, and
their immediate consequences.
     a) Commutativity between two constants c, c′ ∈ Σ(0) means simply that
c = c′ , i.e. a commutative monad has at most one constant, hence is either
a monad without constants or a monad with zero. So we can denote all
constants of commutative monads by the same symbol, say 0 ∈ Σ(0).
     b) Commutativity between a constant 0 ∈ Σ(0) and a unary operation
u ∈ Σ(1) means that u(0) = 0, i.e. the zero constant of a commutative monad
(if it exists) is necessarily fixed by all unary operations of Σ.
     c) Similarly, commutativity between a constant 0 ∈ Σ(0) and an n-ary
operation t ∈ Σ(n) means t(0, 0, . . . , 0) = 0, so the zero constant of a com-
mutative monad has to be respected by operations of all arities.
     d) Commutativity between two unary operations u, u′ ∈ |Σ| = Σ(1)
means that uu′ {1} = u′ u{1}, i.e. uu′ = u′u inside the monoid |Σ| (cf. 4.3.5
and 3.4.9), so |Σ| has to be a commutative monoid for any commutative
algebraic monad Σ.
     e) Commutativity between a unary operation u and an n-ary operation
t means t(u{1}, . . . , u{n}) = ut({1}, . . . , {n}). In particular, commutativity
between unary u and binary + actually means some sort of distributivity:
u({1} + {2}) = u{1} + u{2}.
     f) Finally, the commutativity between two binary operations + and ∗
means ({1}+{2})∗({3}+{4}) = ({1}∗{3})+({2}∗{4}), i.e. (x+y)∗(z+t) =
(x ∗ z) + (y ∗ t) for free variables x, y, z, t (or for any four elements of any Σ-
5.1. Definition of commutativity                                                            219


module X). Notice that any operation of arity ≤ 1 automatically commutes
with itself, while this is not true for operations of higher arities: a binary
operation + commutes with itself iff (x + y) + (z + t) = (x + z) + (y + t).

5.1.8. (Commutativity and addition.) Now we want to study the relation-
ship between commutativity and additivity notions of 4.8. Notice that these
notions make sense only if we fix some constant 0 ∈ Σ(0); however, com-
mutative monads have at most one constant, so we don’t have to specify it
explicitly.
     a) Any two pseudoadditions + and ∗ of a commutative monad Σ coincide.
Indeed, we have 0 + x = x = x + 0 and 0 ∗ x = x = x ∗ 0 by definition of
a pseudoaddition, and (x + y) ∗ (z + t) = (x ∗ z) + (y ∗ t) because of the
commutativity between + and ∗. We obtain x + y = (x ∗ 0) + (0 ∗ y) =
(x+ 0)∗ (0 + y) = x∗ y. A similar proof is valid for pseudoadditions t and t′ of
same arity n ≥ 3: we just have to apply the commutativity relation between
t and t′ to the set of elements xij = 0 for i 6= j, xii = {i} in Σ(n). This
implies that any pseudoaddition in a commutative monad is unique, i.e. an
addition, and it is automatically commutative and associative: we just apply
uniqueness to + and {2} + {1} for the first property, and to ({1} + {2}) + {3}
and {1} + ({2} + {3}) for the second; alternatively, we might put z = 0 in
(x + y) + (z + t) = (x + z) + (y + t). Actually, all these statements are true
for a central pseudoaddition + in an arbitrary algebraic monad Σ.
     b) Now we show that any hyperadditive commutative monad Σ is in fact
additive; in other words, if a commutative monad admits a pseudoaddition,
it is necessarily additive. Indeed, any hyperadditive monad Σ admits a pseu-
doaddition + (cf. 4.8.5), and commutativity implies that + is an associative
and commutative addition. Now let t ∈ Σ(n) be an arbitrary operation
of Σ, and let λ = (λ1 , . . . , λn ) be the image of t under the comparison map
πn : Σ(n) → |Σ|n . Let us denote by +̃ the n-ary pseudoaddition (necessarily
unique), constructed from +. We apply the commutativity relation between
t and +̃ to the collection xij = 0 if i 6= j, xii = {i} of elements of Σ(n).
We have xi. = [+̃](0, . . . , {i}, . . . , 0) = 0 + · · · + {i} + · · · + 0 = {i}, x.j =
t(0, . . . , {j}, . . . , 0) = λj {j} by the definition of comparison map πn , hence
t = t({1}, . . . , {n}) = t(x1. , . . . , xn. ) = [+̃](x.1 , . . . , x.n ) = λ1 {1}+· · ·+λn {n},
i.e. t is uniquely determined by its image under πn , hence πn is bijective and
Σ is additive. Notice that the same proof actually shows that if an algebraic
monad admits a central pseudoaddition, it is automatically additive.
     c) We know that any additive monad Σ is of form ΣR for a uniquely
determined semiring R; in fact, R = |Σ| (cf. 4.8.6). We claim that an ad-
ditive monad Σ is commutative iff the semiring |Σ| is commutative. Indeed,
the necessity of this condition has been shown in 5.1.7,d); its sufficience
220                                         Chapter 5. Commutative monads


follows from the fact that Σ is generated by 0[0] , +[2] and all its unary oper-
ations |Σ| (cf. 4.8.6), and the relations between these generators imply all
necessary commutativity relations between them, with the only exception of
commutativity among unary operations (cf. 5.1.7 and 4.8.6). Therefore, the
commutativity of |Σ| implies that of Σ.
    d) Similarly, classical commutative rings R correspond to commutative
additive monads Σ that admit a symmetry [−], i.e. a unary operation − ∈
Σ(1), such that e + (−e) = 0 (this automatically implies −2 = e; cf. 4.8.7).
Notice that if these properties hold in Σ (i.e. Σ admits a pseudoaddition and
a symmetry), and if we have any homomorphism of commutative monads
ρ : Σ → Ξ, they hold in Ξ as well, ρ(+) and ρ(−) being a pseudoaddition
and a symmetry in Ξ, hence if Σ is given by a classical ring, the same is true
for Ξ. Of course, we obtain similar results for semirings as well.
    e) In general a commutative algebraic monad need not be additive. For
example, Z∞ ⊂ R, as well as F∅ ⊂ F1 ⊂ F±1 ⊂ Z(∞) ⊂ Q are examples of
hypoadditive commutative monads that are not additive (they are commu-
tative, being submonads of commutative monad R). In fact, a commutative
algebraic monad needn’t be even hypoadditive, as shown by F∞ (cf. 4.8.13;
notice that F∞ is commutative, being a strict quotient of Z∞ ).

5.1.9. (Algebras over a generalized ring.) Let Λ be a generalized ring, i.e. a
commutative algebraic monad. A (commutative) Λ-algebra Σ is by definition
a homomorphism of generalized rings ρ : Λ → Σ. We denote the category
of (commutative) Λ-algebras by Λ-CommAlg. Clearly, arbitrary projective
and inductive limits exist in this category; for example, coproducts of Λ-
algebras are given by pushouts of GenR, i.e. the “tensor products” Σ1 ⊗Λ Σ2
(cf. 5.1.6).
     Similarly, we define a (not necessarily commutative) Λ-algebra Σ to be a
central homomorphism of algebraic monads ρ : Λ → Σ, i.e. we require ρ(Λ) to
lie in the center of Σ. Clearly, if Λ is not commutative, any such ρ factorizes
through Λab , so it doesn’t really make much sense to allow Λ to be non-
commutative. Therefore, we shall consider algebras only over commutative
monads, i.e. generalized rings Λ. We denote the category of (all) Λ-algebras
by Λ-Alg. Notice that this category has arbitrary projective and inductive
limits: all projective and filtered inductive limits are computed in the usual
way (i.e. componentwise), id : Λ → Λ is the initial object, and the pushouts
are given by the non-commutative tensor products Σ1 ⊠Σ Σ2 of 4.5.17. We
can also consider the commutative tensor products Σ1 ⊗Σ Σ2 := (Σ1 ⊠Σ
Σ2 )/[Σ1 , Σ2 ]; they also lie in Λ-Alg, being strict quotients of corresponding
non-commutative tensor products, and they have a universal property with
respect to all Λ-algebras Ξ that fit into a commutative square with given
5.1. Definition of commutativity                                               221


Σ → Σ1 and Σ → Σ2 , and such that the images of Σ1 and Σ2 in Ξ commute.
5.1.10. (Algebras over an additive generalized ring.) If Λ is additive, i.e.
given by a commutative semiring |Λ|, then any Λ-algebra Σ is additive as
well: indeed, the structural homomorphism ρ : Λ → Σ has to be central,
hence ρ(+) is a central pseudoaddition of Σ, and we have seen in 5.1.8,b)
that this implies additivity of Σ, so Σ is given by a semiring |Σ| and a
central homomorphism |ρ| : |Λ| → |Σ|. Similarly, if Λ is additive and admits
a symmetry −, i.e. if Λ corresponds to a classical commutative ring |Λ|,
then any Λ-algebra Σ admits a central pseudoaddition and a symmetry as
well, hence it is given by a classical ring |Σ| and a central homomorphism
|ρ| : |Λ| → |Σ|, i.e. a classical |Λ|-algebra. This explains our terminology.
    Here is another result of the same kind: if Λ is a generalized ring with
zero, then any Λ-algebra Σ is also a monad with zero. Indeed, Σ has at
least one constant, namely, ρ(0); and this constant is central, so any other
constant must be equal to it (cf. 5.1.7,a)).
5.1.11. (Scalar restriction and base change.) If σ : Λ → Λ′ is a homomor-
phism of generalized rings, we can define the scalar restriction of a Λ′ -algebra
ρ′ : Λ′ → Σ′ by considering ρ′ ◦ σ : Λ → Σ′ . We denote this Λ-algebra by
a
  σ∗ (Σ′ ), σ∗ Σ′ or σ Σ′ . This scalar restriction functor has an obvious left ad-
joint — the base change functor σ ∗ , given by the commutative tensor product:
σ ∗ Σ := Λ′ ⊗Λ Σ. These considerations are valid both for the categories of all
(non-commutative) algebras and for the categories of commutative algebras.
5.1.12. (Central elements.) We see directly from 5.1.1 that t ∈ Σ(n) is a
central element iff the maps [t]X : X n → X are Σ-homomorphisms for all
Σ-modules X (or just for all X = Σ(m)). Another description: the center
of Σ is the largest submonad Σ0 ⊂ Σ, such that for all t ∈ Σ(n) and all
Σ-modules X (or just for all X = Σ(m)) the maps [t]X : X n → X are Σ0 -
homomorphisms. In particular, Σ is commutative iff all maps [t]X : X n → X
are Σ-homomorphisms, and ρ : Λ → Σ is central iff [t]X : X n → X is a
Λ-homomorphism for any t ∈ Σ(n) and any Σ-module X (again, X = Σ(m)
suffice).
    We can generalize this a bit: the actions of two submonads Σ1 , Σ2 ⊂ Ξ
commute on a Ξ-module X (i.e. any two operations t ∈ kΣ1 k, t′ ∈ kΣ2 k
commute on X) iff for any t ∈ Σ1 (n) the map [t]X : X n → X is a Σ2 -
homomorphism. If this is true for any X (or for any X = Ξ(m)), then Σ1
and Σ2 commute inside Ξ.
    We can apply this to Ξ = Σ1 ⊠Λ Σ2 , where Σ1 and Σ2 are Λ-algebras. We
see that a Ξ-module X is just a set X with a Σ1 and a Σ2 -structure, restricting
to same Λ-structure (this actually follows from the universal property of Ξ,
applied to Ξ → END(X)), and a Σ1 ⊗Λ Σ2 -module X is a set X with two
222                                         Chapter 5. Commutative monads


commuting Σ1 and Σ2 -structures, restricting to the same Λ-structure, i.e. we
require Σ1 to act by Σ2 -homomorphisms on X, or equivalently, Σ2 to act by
Σ1 -homomorphisms.
5.1.13. (GeneratorsFand relations.) Let’s fix a generalized ring Λ. Then for
any graded set S = n≥0 Sn we can construct the free (non-commutative) Λ-
algebra Λ{S} (resp. the free commutative Λ-algebra Λ[S]), enjoying the usual
universal property with respect to non-commutative (resp. commutative) Λ-
algebras Σ and graded maps S → kΣk. Indeed, we just have to put Λ{S} :=
ΛhS | [S, Λ]i = ΛhSi/h[S, Λ]i (cf. 4.5.11), resp. Λ[S] := ΛhS | [S, Λ], [S, S]i.
If all operations from S are unary, then Λ{S} is “the ring of polynomials in
non-commuting variables from S” (that are nevertheless assumed to commute
with constants from Λ), and Λ[S] is the ring of polynomials in commuting
variables from S.
    Suppose that we are also given a system of “equations” or “relations”
E ⊂ kΛ{S}k2 (resp. E ⊂ kΛ[S]k2 ); since ΛhSi → Λ{S} (resp. · · · → Λ[S])
is surjective, we can assume that E comes from a system of relations Ẽ ⊂
kΛhSik2, which will be usually denoted by the same letter E. Then we
can construct a (non-commutative) algebra Λ{S|E} = Λ{S}/hEi = ΛhS | Ẽ,
[Λ, S]i, resp. a commutative algebra Λ[S|E] = Λ[S]/hEi = ΛhS | Ẽ, [Λ, S],
[S, S]i = Λ{S | E, [S, S]}, having the usual universal property. When a non-
commutative (resp. commutative) Λ-algebra Σ is represented in form Λ{S|E}
(resp. Λ[S|E]), we say that (S, E) is a presentation of the non-commutative
(resp. commutative) Λ-algebra Σ.
5.1.14. (Finitely generated and pre-unary algebras.) We say that a subset
S ⊂ kΣk generates the non-commutative (resp. commutative) Λ-algebra Σ
if the induced homomorphism of Λ-algebras Λ{S} → Σ (resp. Λ[S] → Σ)
is surjective, i.e. a strict epimorphism. Since ΛhSi → Λ{S} → Λ[S] are
also strict epimorphisms, we see that this condition is equivalent to the sur-
jectivity of ΛhSi → Σ, i.e. to S being a set of generators of Σ over Λ in
the sense of 4.4.4. In particular, S is a set of generators of a commutative
Λ-algebra Σ iff it generates Σ as a non-commutative algebra. This means
that we can safely transfer all terminology from 4.4.4 and 4.4.5; we obtain
the notions of finitely generated Λ-algebras (or Λ-algebras of finite type),
pre-unary Λ-algebras, and Λ-algebras, generated in arity ≤ n, both in the
commutative and non-commutative case.
5.1.15. (Finitely presented and unary algebras.) We can go further on and
define the finitely presented and unary Λ-algebras to be those (commuta-
tive or non-commutative) Λ-algebras that admit a finite presentation (S, E)
(resp. admit a unary presentation (S, E), i.e. a presentation with all opera-
tions from S and all relations from E unary). Relation Λ[S|E] = Λ{S | E,
5.1. Definition of commutativity                                              223


[S, S]i shows that a commutative Λ-algebra is finitely presented iff it is
finitely presented as a non-commutative algebra, and similarly for unarity
(note that [u, u′] is a unary relation when both u and u′ are unary). How-
ever, these notions of finite presentation and unarity do not coincide with
those of 4.5.15; henceforth finite presentation and unarity of algebras over
generalized rings will be understood as just defined. Nevertheless, they have
essentially the same properties as listed before in 4.5.18, when they are prop-
erly understood. For example, in the commutative case we have to replace
the NC-tensor product ⊠ with its commutative counterpart ⊗, and in the
non-commutative case we compute base change of a Λ-algebra Σ only with
respect to homomorphisms of generalized rings Λ → Λ′ ; such base change
functors preserve finite generation and presentation, unarity and pre-unarity,
due to the usual property Λ′ ⊗Λ Λ{S|E} = Λ′ {S|E} and its commutative ver-
sion. Another consequence is that if a Λ′ -algebra Σ′ is finitely presented (resp.
unary) over Λ, and Λ′ is finitely generated (resp. pre-unary) over Λ, then Σ′
is finitely presented (resp. unary) over Λ′ .

5.1.17. (Some tensor products.) Since Λ[S|E] ⊗Λ Λ[S ′ |E ′ ] = Λ[S, S ′ |E, E ′ ],

5.1.18. (NC-epimorphisms.) We see that a homomorphism ρ : Λ → Σ in
GenR can be an epimorphism in GenR without being an epimorphism in the
category of all algebraic monads. To distinguish between these two situations
we say that a homomorphism of generalized rings ρ : Λ → Σ is an NC-
epimorphism if it is an epimorphism in the category of all algebraic monads.
Of course, any NC-epimorphism is automatically an epimorphism (in GenR).
Applying the definition to homomorphisms Σ → END(X) we see that ρ is
an NC-epimorphism iff any Λ-module X admits at most one compatible Σ-
structure (this is the behavior one expects from localization morphisms like
Λ → Λ[S −1 ], and in the next chapter we’ll see that this expectation turns
out to be well-founded). To show the sufficience of this condition we observe
that the category of Σ ⊠Λ Σ-modules is the category of sets, equipped with
two different Σ-structures, restricting to the same Λ-structure;
                                                                  if any two
such Σ-structures necessarily coincide, we have Σ ⊠Λ Σ -Mod ∼      = Σ-Mod,
hence Σ ⊠Λ Σ ∼  = Σ (any monad is completely determined by its category of
modules, together with the forgetful functor).
    Notice that while epimorphisms in GenR and in the category of algebraic
monads are different, monomorphisms and strict epimorphisms coincide, so
we can freely use these notions in both contexts, as well as notions of sub-
monads and strict quotients, without any risk of confusion.
5.1.19. (Semirings and Z≥0 -algebras.) We have seen in 5.1.10 that any Z≥0 -
algebra Σ admits a central pseudoaddition and a central constant, hence it
is additive. Conversely, if Σ is an additive algebraic monad, it has exactly
one constant 0, so this constant is automatically central, and its addition +
is also automatically central, a statement easily checked by applying the
comparison map π2n to both sides of the commutativity relation [+, t] for an
arbitrary t ∈ Σ(n). We know that Z≥0 = F∅[0[0] , +[2] | 0 + e = e = e + 0],
so we obtain a unique central homomorphism Z≥0 → Σ, i.e. any additive
algebraic monad Σ admits a unique Z≥0 -algebra structure. On the other
hand, the list of generators and relations given in 4.8.6 shows that any such
Σ is generated as a (non-commutative) Z≥0 -algebra by the set of its unary
operations |Σ|, subject to unary relations of form λ′ + λ′′ = λ and λ′ λ′′ = λ;
5.1. Definition of commutativity                                                225


all other relations of loc.cit. (associativity, commutativity and distributivity)
are either consequences of similar relations in Z≥0 , or consequences of implied
commutativity relations between Z≥0 and the generators from |Σ| (cf. 5.1.7).
Therefore, any such Σ is a unary Z≥0 -algebra. We have just proved the
following statement:

Proposition. The following categories are canonically isomorphic: a) the
category of additive algebraic monads; b) the category of (non-commutative)
Z≥0 -algebras; c) the category of (non-commutative) unary Z≥0 -algebras.
5.1.20. (Rings and Z-algebras.) Of course, the above equivalence of cate-
gories establishes an equivalence between the category of (unary) commu-
tative Z≥0 -algebras and the category of additive generalized rings. Another
consequence: If Λ is an additive generalized ring, any Λ-algebra Σ is auto-
matically additive and unary (over Λ). Indeed, Z≥0 → Λ → Σ defines a
Z≥0 -algebra structure on Σ, hence Σ is additive and unary over Z≥0 , hence
it is unary over Λ as well, Λ being pre-unary over Z≥0 (cf. 5.1.15). This
is applicable to Z = Z≥0 [−[1] | (−e) + e = 0]: we see that all Z-algebras
are additive and unary (over Z), and that the category of Z-algebras con-
sists of those Z≥0 -algebras, i.e. additive monads, that admit a symmetry [−];
clearly, this is just the category of classical semirings with symmetry, i.e. of
classical rings. Similarly, any algebra Σ over a commutative Z-algebra Λ,
corresponding to a commutative classical ring |Λ|, is automatically additive
and unary over Λ, hence given by classical ring |Σ| and a central homomor-
phism |Λ| → |Σ|, i.e. a |Λ|-algebra in the classical sense. This means that
when we work over a classical base ring Λ, all arising algebras turn out to be
unary, additive and classical, so we don’t obtain anything new over such Λ.
This also explains why we cannot observe the importance of unarity in the
classical case, since in this case it turns out to be always fulfilled.
5.1.21. (Some examples: affine group schemes.) Consider, for example, the
functor Mn : Σ 7→ M(n, n; Σ) = Σ(n)n on the category of commutative
F∅-algebras, i.e. generalized rings. It is easily seen to be representable by
                                                                     [n]     [n]
a certain commutative F∅-algebra An , namely, An := F∅[T1 , . . . , Tn ]. Of
course, An is not unary over F∅ for n ≥ 2 (indeed, if A2 would be unary, its
universal property would enable us to express any central binary operation
in terms of some unary operations, hence any generalized ring generated in
arity ≤ 2 would be also generated in arity ≤ 1; however, this is not true
for Z). But if we extend the base to Z, we obtain a commutative Z-algebra
An,Z = Z ⊗ An = Z ⊗F∅ An , representing the restriction of the same functor
to the category of commutative Z-algebras; of course, this algebra is additive
and unary, and in fact it equals Z[T11 , T12 , . . . , Tnn ]; so a non-unary algebra
226                                             Chapter 5. Commutative monads


becomes unary over Z.
    Another example is given by GLn : Σ 7→ GLn (Σ) ⊂ Mn (Σ). It is rep-
                              [n]        [n] [n]       [n]
resentable by A′n = F∅ T1 , . . . , Tn , U1 , . . . , Un Ui (T1 , . . . , Tn ) = {i}n =
Ti (U1 , . . . , Un ) . Again, A′n is not unary over F∅ for n ≥ 2, but it becomes

by abelian groups A, e.g. the split tori Gnm ∼    = D(Zn ).
5.1.22. (Tensor square of Z.) We have seen in 5.1.20 that for any generalized
ring Σ there is at most one homomorphism Z → Σ. By definition this is
equivalent to saying that F∅ → Z is an epimorphism in GenR, or to Z⊗F∅ Z ∼      =
Z. This statement can be also shown directly starting from the presentation
of Z ⊗ Z obtained from the presentation Z = F∅[0[0] , −[1] , +[2] | e + 0 = e =
0 + e, (−e) + e = 0]: we see that Z ⊗ Z is generated by two constants 0
and 0′ , two binary operations + and +′ , and two unary operations − and
−′ , and we use 5.1.7 to show first 0 = 0′ , then [+] = [+′ ], and finally deduce
[−] = [−′ ], hence Z ⊗ Z ∼
                         = Z. Yet another proof: use the well-known lemma
which states that any two commuting group structures on the same set H
coincide and are abelian (cf. e.g. SGA 3 II 3.10).
     Of course, once we know that F∅ → Z is an epimorphism, we deduce
that F1 → Z and F±1 → Z are epimorphisms as well, and we can compose
them with strict epimorphisms Z → Z/nZ, thus obtaining statements like
Z/nZ⊗F1 Z/nZ ∼   = Z/nZ. This is a phenomenon of commutativity: one easily
checks that a countable set admits different Fp -vector space structures, even
if we fix in advance the zero and the symmetry, hence Fp ⊠F±1 Fp ∼     6 = Fp .
     Another important consequence is that for any two Z-algebras Σ and Σ′
(commutative or not) we have Σ ⊗Z Σ′ ∼   = Σ ⊗F∅ Σ′ , so we can freely use the
                      ′
usual notation Σ ⊗ Σ for such tensor products.
5.2. (Topos case.) Now we want to indicate a way to transfer all our previous
results to the topos case. Everything here turns out to be quite similar to
the classical case.
5.2.1. (Commutativity diagrams.) Notice that the commutativily of an alge-
braic monad Σ is equivalent to the commutativity of the following diagrams
for all k, n, m ≥ 0:

            Σ(n) × Σ(m) × Σ(k)n×m                / Σ(n) × Σ(k)n               (5.2.1.1)
                                                               (n)
                                                              µk
                                        (m)              
                                        µk
                  Σ(m) × Σ(k)m                        / Σ(k)
5.2. Topos case                                                              227

                                                                       (n)   (m)
Of course, the two remaining arrows are also given by products of µk , µk ,
so the commutativity of this diagram makes sense also if we are given an
“algebraic monad” Σ over an arbitrary cartesian category C in the sense
of 4.9.1. We thus obtain the notion of a “commutative algebraic monad” or
a “generalized ring” over such C, and this commutativity property is stable
under any left exact functors h : C → C ′ , i.e. if Σ is commutative, the same is
true for hΣ. We define the notion of a central homomorphism ρ : Λ → Σ by
means of similar diagrams (comparing two morphisms from Λ(n) × Σ(m) ×
Σ(k)m×n into Σ(k)), so we obtain the notion of a Λ-algebra (commutative or
not) as well. These notions have essentially the same properties as before:
we can either repeat the proofs or embed C into the category of presheaves
Cˆ as a full subcategory, and prove all statements for Cˆ componentwise.
5.2.2. (Topos case.) Of course, we immediately obtain the notion of a com-
mutative algebraic monad or a generalized ring in a topos E, i.e. the notion
of a sheaf of generalized rings on a site S, if we consider E = S̃. Since the
pullback, direct image and global section functors are left exact, they pre-
serve commutativity of algebraic monads. Conversely, if Σ is an algebraic
monad over E, such that Σ[U ] = Γ(U, Σ) is commutative for all U from a
system of generating objects of E, then Σ is commutative. If we are given
a homomorphism ρ : Λ → Λ′ of generalized rings in E, we obtain a scalar
                            ′
restriction functor ρ∗ : E Λ → E Λ ; as usual, it admits a left adjoint, the base
change functor ρ∗ , denoted also by Λ′ ⊗Λ −; one can deduce its existence
from the presheaf case by applying the “sheafification” functor a : Ŝ → S̃.
5.2.3. (Generalized ringed spaces and topoi.) This means that we can define
a generalized ringed topos E = (E, Λ) as a topos E, together with a generalized
ring Λ in E (the “structural sheaf” of E). A morphism f : (E ′ , Λ′) → (E, Λ)
is defined in the usual way: f = (ϕ, θ), with ϕ : E ′ → E a morphism of topoi,
and θ : Λ → ϕ∗ Λ′ a homomorphism of generalized rings. We obtain a pair of
                                  ′              ′
adjoint functors f ∗ : E Λ → E ′ Λ and f∗ : E ′ Λ → E Λ in the usual way: f∗ by
               ′     ′        ′
composing ϕΛ∗ : E ′ Λ → E ϕ∗ Λ with scalar restriction with respect to θ, and f ∗
                                ∗
by composing ϕ∗,Λ : E Λ → E ′ ϕ Λ with the base change functor Λ′ ⊗ϕ∗ Λ − with
respect to θ♯ : ϕ∗ Λ → Λ′ . Sometimes we denote the underlying morphism of
topoi ϕ by the same letter f ; then we write f −1 for the pullback functor ϕ∗
of sheaves of sets, and f ∗ for the functor just defined.
    In this way we obtain the 2-category of generalized ringed topoi. Of
course, we can consider topoi defined by some sites, thus obtaining the no-
tions of generalized ringed sites and their morphisms. In particular, we can
consider topoi defined by topological spaces; then we obtain the category of
generalized ringed spaces.
    We postpone until the next chapter the definitions of generalized locally
228                                         Chapter 5. Commutative monads


ringed spaces and topoi, since they depend considerably on the choice of
theory of spectra (or localization theory): E = (E, A) is locally ringed iff for
any X ∈ Ob E the morphism of ringed topoi (E/X , A/X ) → (Sets, A(X))
factorizes through Spec A(X).
5.2.4. (Commutativity in terms of plain inner structures.) Recall that an al-
gebraic monad Σ over a topos E admits also a description in terms of certain
plain inner monads (cf. 4.9.11), so we get a monad Σ : E → E over E, and a
canonical plain inner structure α, αX,Y : X ×Σ(Y ) → Σ(X ×Y ). We can con-
struct a diagonal inner structure ρ on endofunctor Σ, ρX,Y : Σ(X) × Σ(Y ) →
Σ(X × Y ), and then ask whether this ρX,Y is commutative (cf. 3.5.17); one
knows that in this case ρ is even compatible with the monad structure of Σ
(loc. cit.) It turns out that ρ is commutative iff Σ is commutative in the
sense of 5.2.1. One checks this directly for E = Sets, using the explicit
description of the plain inner structure maps αX,Y : X × Σ(Y ) → Σ(X × Y )
and the construction of ρ from α, and then generalizes this result first to the
categories of presheaves Ŝ, and then by sheafification to arbitrary E ∼
                                                                       = S̃.
5.3. (Modules over generalized rings.) Now we want to study some proper-
ties of the category Λ-Mod of modules over a generalized ring Λ; sometimes
we also need another generalized ring Λ′ and a homomorphism ρ : Λ → Λ′ .
Of course, all general properties obtained in 4.6 hold in the commutative
case as well, e.g. Λ-Mod has arbitrary inductive and projective limits and so
on. We want to study properties specific to the commutative case. The most
important among them is the existence of a canonical ACU ⊗-structure on
Λ-Mod, and of inner Homs with respect to this tensor product. This implies
a theory of bilinear and multilinear forms, which admit a more direct descrip-
tion as well, and in particular of symmetric forms; we postpone the study of
alternating forms, since it requires some additional structure on Λ. We can
also use this ⊗-structure to consider the category of algebras (commutative
or all) in Λ-Mod; this category turns out to be equivalent to the category of
unary Λ-algebras.
5.3.1. (Σ-structure on HomΣ (N, P ).) Recall that for any algebraic monad Σ,
any Σ-module P and any set N we have a canonical Σ-structure on the
set Hom(N, P ) = HomSets (N, P ) ∼= P N , namely, the product structure; in
other words, operations of Σ are applied to functions N → P pointwise
(cf. 4.6.3). Now suppose that N is also a Σ-module; then we have a subset
HomΣ (N, P ) ⊂ Hom(N, P ) ∼= P N , in general not stable under all operations
of Σ. We claim the following:

Proposition. An algebraic monad Σ is commutative iff HomΣ (N, P ) is a
Σ-submodule of HomSets (N, P ) for any two Σ-modules N and P (or just
5.3. Modules over generalized rings                                          229


for N and P free of finite rank, i.e. ∼
                                      = Σ(k)). If this be the case, we denote
by HomΣ (N, P ) the set HomΣ (N, P ), endowed with the Σ-structure induced
from Hom(N, P ) ⊃ HomΣ (N, P ).
We deduce this statement from its more precise form:

Proposition 5.3.2 An operation t ∈ Σ(n) is central iff HomΣ (N, P ) ⊂
Hom(N, P ) is stable under t for all Σ-modules N and P (or just for N and
P free of finite rank). This condition is true for fixed t and P and variable N
iff tP : P n → P is a Σ-homomorphism.

Proof. Put H := Hom(N, P ) ∼        = P N , H ′ := HomΣ (N, P ) ⊂ H. Then
by definition tH : Hom(N, P )n ∼   = Hom(N, P n ) → Hom(N, P ) is given by
composing maps N → P n with tP : P n → P . Now H ′ n ⊂ H n is identified
with HomΣ (N, P n ) ⊂ Hom(N, P n ). Therefore, if tP : P n → P is a Σ-
homomorphism, then tH maps H ′ n into H ′ = HomΣ (N, P ), the composite of
two Σ-homomorphisms being a Σ-homomorphism. Conversely, taking N :=
P n and considering the image under tH of idN ∈ HomΣ (N, P n ) ∼        n
                                                                   = H ′ , equal
to tP , we see that the stability of HomΣ (P n , P ) ⊂ Hom(P n , P ) under t
implies that tP is a Σ-homomorphism.
    This proves the second statement of our proposition; notice that it would
suffice to require the stability under t of HomΣ (N, P ) ⊂ Hom(N, P ) not for
all N, but only for all N = Σ(k), k ≥ 0: indeed, stability for such N’s implies
stability for arbitrary filtered inductive limits of these, in particular for all
Σ(S); now we can represent any N as a cokernel of a pair of morphisms
Σ(R) ⇒ Σ(S) (cf. 3.3.20), and a simple diagram chasing shows that the
stability for Σ(R) and Σ(S) implies the stability for N.
    Now the first statement follows from the second, in its stronger form
given above, and from the following observation, already mentioned before
on several occasions (cf. 5.1.12): t is central iff all tP : P n → P are Σ-
homomorphisms iff all tΣ(k) : Σ(k)n → Σ(k) are Σ-homomorphisms.

Definition 5.3.3 (Bilinear forms.) Given three Λ-modules M, N and P
over a generalized ring Λ and a map Φ : M × N → P , we say that Φ is
Λ-bilinear if for any x ∈ M the map sΦ (x) : N → P , y 7→ Φ(x, y), is a
Λ-homomorphism, and for any y ∈ N the map dΦ (y) : M → P , x 7→ Φ(x, y)
is a Λ-homomorphism as well. We denote by BilinΛ (M, N; P ) the set of all
Λ-bilinear maps M × N → P .
5.3.4. Notice that BilinΛ (M, N; P ) ⊂ Hom(M × N, P ) ∼
                                                      = P M ×N , and the
latter set is canonically isomorphic to Hom(M, Hom(N, P )), and this iso-
morphism is clearly Λ-linear (i.e. a Λ-homomorphism). We see that this
230                                            Chapter 5. Commutative monads


bijection transforms a Φ ∈ Hom(M × N, P ) into sΦ ∈ Hom(M, Hom(N, P )).
Now the first condition in the definition of bilinearity actually requires sΦ ∈
Hom(M, HomΛ (N, P )) ⊂ Hom(M, Hom(N, P )); on the other hand, we have a
canonical Λ-structure on Hom(N, P ) ∼   = P N , and the second condition for the
bilinearity of Φ is easily seen to be equivalent to sΦ ∈ HomΛ (M, Hom(N, P )).
Now we know that HomΛ (N, P ) is a Λ-submodule of Hom(N, P ), so we
get BilinΛ (M, N; P ) ∼ = Hom(M, HomΛ (N, P )) ∩ HomΛ (M, Hom(N, P )) =
HomΛ (M, HomΛ (N, P )), as expected.
    The latter set admits a canonical Λ-structure, so we obtain a Λ-module
BilinΛ (M, N; P ), canonically isomorphic to HomΛ (M, HomΛ (N, P )). This
Λ-structure is actually induced by that of P M ×N ∼      = Hom(M × N, P ) ⊃
BilinΛ (M, N; P ).
5.3.5. (Tensor products.) We have just proved that HomΛ (N, P ) represents
BilinΛ (−, N; P ); what about the representability of BilinΛ (M, N; −)?

Proposition. For any Λ-modules M and N the functor BilinΛ (M, N; −) is
representable by a Λ-module M ⊗Λ N, called the tensor product of M and N,
and a Λ-bilinear map ⊗ : M × N → M ⊗ N.

Proof. We construct M ⊗Λ N in the usual way. Consider first the free
Λ-module L := Λ(M × N); let’s denote its basis elements {(x, y)}, x ∈ M,
y ∈ N, simply by {x, y}. Now consider the set of relations E ⊂ L × L, given
by the union of the following two families of relations:
                               
  t {x1 , y}, . . . , {xn , y} ≡ {t(x1 , . . . , xn ), y}
                            for any t ∈ Λ(n), x1 , . . . , xn ∈ M and y ∈ N; (5.3.5.1)

                              
  t {x, y1 }, . . . , {x, yn } ≡ {x, t(y1 , . . . , yn )}
                           for any t ∈ Λ(n), x ∈ M, and y1 , . . . , yn ∈ N. (5.3.5.2)

We consider the compatible equivalence relation ≡ on L, generated by this
set of relations, and put M ⊗Λ N := L/≡. We have a canonical map M ×N →
Λ(M × N) = L → M ⊗Λ N, and its bilinearity and universal property follow
immediately from the construction.
5.3.6. (Multilinear maps and closed ACU ⊗-structure.) Of course, we can
define Λ-multilinear maps M1 ×· · ·×Mn → N in a similar fashion, by requir-
ing them to become Λ-linear (i.e. Λ-homomorphisms) after we fix arbitrary
values for all arguments but one. The set of multilinear maps from the prod-
uct of fixed Λ-modules Mi into a variable Λ-module N is easily seen to be
representable by a multiple tensor product M1 ⊗Λ M2 ⊗Λ · · · ⊗Λ Mn .
5.3. Modules over generalized rings                                         231


    Clearly, (M1 ⊗Λ M2 ) ⊗Λ M3 ∼  = M1 ⊗Λ M2 ⊗Λ M3 ∼  = M1 ⊗Λ (M2 ⊗Λ M3 ), so
we get associativity isomorphisms for this tensor product on Λ-Mod, easily
seen to fit into the pentagon diagram, since all vertices of such a diagram are
canonically isomorphic to a quadruple tensor product. We have a canonical
                                ∼
bijection BilinΛ (M1 , M2 ; N) → BilinΛ (M2 , M1 ; N), hence canonical isomor-
phisms M1 ⊗Λ M2 ∼    = M2 ⊗Λ M1 , fitting into the hexagon diagram.
    We have inner Hom’s as well: HomΛ (M ⊗Λ N, P ) ∼      = BilinΛ (M, N; P ) ∼=
HomΛ (M, HomΛ (N, P )). The free Λ-module |Λ| = Λ(1) is easily seen to be
the unit for this tensor product: indeed, HomΛ (Λ(1), P ) ∼  = HomSets (1, P ) ∼
                                                                               =
P , and this bijection is easily seen to preserve the Λ-structures, so we have
